docs.title: Ansible Mastery Path
docs.text:
Mastery Path BOOTCAMP VINOD BHANUJA

Most Ansible problems are not exotic. A playbook that is green because it never changed anything. A command task that reports changed on every run. A removed task that leaves the old configuration on every server. Two roles that fight over one file and never converge. A --limit that matches nothing and exits zero. A rolling update whose failure budget silently stops working. None of these are bugs in the tool. They follow from how Ansible actually works, and this course shows each one, with an experiment or a test wherever it could be run.

It assumes you can use a terminal and edit YAML. It doesn't assume any automation experience.

Level 1 is the foundation: what Ansible is, ad-hoc commands, inventory, playbooks, idempotency and check mode, variables and facts, conditionals and loops, templates and handlers, debugging, ending with a tested baseline playbook. Level 2 adds structure and safety: roles, a measured variable-precedence table, Jinja2 filters, error handling, Vault, collections, tags and limits, delegation and batches, linting and testing, ending with a tested role. Level 3 extends Ansible: custom modules and plugins, dynamic inventory, command and shell pitfalls, async, performance, rolling updates, drift and convergence, network and Windows targets, ending with a tested module. Level 4 is operations: controllers and execution environments, CI, secrets, pull mode, Terraform together with Ansible, drift audits, incidents, migration, governance and a fleet capstone.

Every lesson has a How It Actually Works section: why a second run is the best test you can write, why -e beats every other variable, why a handler can be skipped after a failure, why lookup() joins a list into one string, and why check mode cannot see what command does.

Read this first: what was actually run

This course was written on a Mac with ansible-core 2.21.5 (Python 3.14.7) and no remote servers, SSH targets, Windows hosts, network devices, container runtime or automation controller. Every playbook shown with output was run with the real ansible-playbook, but all "servers" use ansible_connection=local and are directories under a sandbox. What that means:

  • Run and measured: the playbook language, modules for files, templates and lines, variables and precedence (14 sources ranked by experiment), handlers, roles, blocks and rescue, Vault with real encryption, tags and limits, serial and failure budgets, delegation, ansible-lint, custom modules and plugins, dynamic inventory (script and plugin), async, forks and fact-gathering timings, ansible-pull against a local Git repository, callback plugins, and ansible-builder (build context only).
  • Tested code: 130 pytest tests that run the real Ansible: a baseline playbook, a role, two modules, filter/lookup/inventory plugins, a rolling-update playbook, a drift auditor, a no_log linter, a Terraform-output inventory script (on a hand-written fixture), a preflight guard and a 12-node fleet capstone.
  • Described, not run: SSH and become, Linux packages and systemd, Windows and network targets (their collections were installed only to read documentation), AWX/AAP, container builds, GitHub Actions, Terraform, secret managers, Molecule. These come from docs.ansible.com and general knowledge as read in October 2026 and are marked "not run".

Where an experiment surprised me (a boolean string that is now an error, an always: block that defeated max_fail_percentage, an async timeout reported as "unparsable results", a guard that approved the case it was meant to block), the lesson says so rather than inventing a clean story. Behaviour changes between Ansible versions; check yours with ansible --version.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
• Get something to practise on: two small VMs or containers you can break, or just use connection: local and a sandbox directory as this course does. Never experiment on machines you care about.
  • Read the "what was run" note at the top of each lesson: it tells you whether an output was observed, modelled, or described from documentation.
  • Run the code in the src/ folder of the course repository (see its README): pytest runs 130 tests against real Ansible.
  • Run every playbook twice. The second run is the lesson.
  • Do the exercises, especially "predict, then run".

docs.title: Level 1 · Ansible Foundations
docs.text:
Level 1 builds the working model: how Ansible reaches hosts, how an inventory and a playbook describe them and their desired state, what idempotency means in practice, and how to read what happened. Every playbook shown with output was run with the real ansible-playbook.

What was run, and what wasn't

ansible-core 2.21.5 on a Mac, with all "servers" using ansible_connection=local and acting on sandbox directories. Not exercised: SSH, become, Linux packages and services, Windows and network targets, and automation controllers. Those are labelled "not run" where they come up, and drawn from docs.ansible.com as read in October 2026.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. What Ansible Is and How It Works: agentless push, the model, and the comparison with scripts, Terraform and agent-based tools.
  2. Ad-Hoc Commands, Modules and ansible-doc: one module, many hosts; why command always says changed.
  3. Inventory: INI and YAML, groups, patterns, variable merging; a pattern that matches nothing exits 0.
  4. Playbook Anatomy: plays, tasks, run order, and a YAML mistake that broke a real task.
  5. Idempotency, Changed and Check Mode: the second-run recap, creates, check and diff.
  6. Variables and Facts: sources, set_fact, -e beating everything, facts and magic variables.
  7. Conditionals, Loops and Register: and a boolean-string error in ansible-core 2.21.5.
  8. Templates and Handlers: handlers fire once; a failure can leave a stale service.
  9. Debugging and Reading Failures: error anatomy, verbosity, assert, --start-at-task pitfalls.
  10. Project: A Verified Baseline Playbook: 8 tests that run real Ansible.

docs.title: After Level 1
docs.text: Level 2 adds structure and safety: roles, a measured variable-precedence table, Jinja2 filters, error handling, Vault with real encryption, collections, tags and limits, delegation and serial batches, linting and testing, and a tested role.

docs.title: 01 · What Ansible Is and How It Works
docs.text:
Ansible is a tool for describing the state you want a machine to be in and making it so. You write a playbook in YAML, point it at an inventory of machines, and Ansible connects to each one, runs small programs called modules, and reports what changed. There is nothing to install on the managed machines beyond an SSH server and Python, which is why it is called agentless.

About this course and what was run

This course was written on a Mac with ansible-core 2.21.5 installed in a Python 3.14.7 virtual environment. Every playbook that is shown with output was run with the real ansible-playbook against hosts that use ansible_connection=local, which means they all execute on the same laptop, and the "servers" are directories under a sandbox path. That is faithful for the playbook language, modules such as file, copy, template, lineinfile, variables, handlers, roles, vault, and the plugin APIs. It does not exercise: SSH connections, SSH keys and multiplexing, become (privilege escalation), Linux package managers and systemd, Windows or network devices, or a real automation controller such as AWX. Those lessons say "described, not run" and cite the Ansible documentation (docs.ansible.com) as read in October 2026. Versions and defaults change; check yours with ansible --version.

docs.title: The model in one picture
docs.text:
control node (your laptop or a CI runner)            managed nodes
  ┌────────────────────────────────────┐   SSH     ┌────────────────────┐
  │ inventory + playbook + roles        │ ───────▶ │ sshd + Python       │
  │ ansible-playbook (the only program) │          │ (no Ansible daemon) │
  └────────────────────────────────────┘          └────────────────────┘
        for each task, for each host:  copy a module, run it, collect JSON, delete it

Ansible is a push tool: the control node decides when to run and reaches out. Contrast with pull tools such as Puppet and Chef, where an agent on each machine periodically fetches its configuration. Push is simple to start and easy to reason about (you run it, you see the result), and it makes "run this now on exactly these hosts" natural. The cost is that nothing corrects drift between runs unless you schedule runs (Level 4 covers pull mode and scheduling).

docs.title: Declarative-ish, with an honest caveat
docs.text:
A task says what should be true, not how to get there:

- name: app config directory exists with the right mode
  ansible.builtin.file:
    path: /etc/app
    state: directory
    mode: "0755"

If the directory already exists with that mode, the module does nothing and reports ok. If not, it creates or fixes it and reports changed. That property, idempotency (running it again changes nothing), is the heart of Ansible and the subject of Lesson 05. The caveat: Ansible is not purely declarative. A playbook is an ordered list of tasks, run top to bottom, and tasks that run arbitrary commands (command, shell) have no idea what state they leave behind. Idempotency is a property of each module, not of Ansible as a whole, and you can write non-idempotent playbooks easily. This course measures that rather than assuming it.

docs.title: What you actually write
docs.text: Piece What it is Lesson Inventory The hosts and groups you manage, and variables for them 03 Playbook A YAML file: one or more plays, each mapping a set of hosts to a list of tasks 04 Module The unit of work (file, copy, template, user, package ...) 02 Task One module call with arguments, a name, and optional conditions 04 Variables and facts Data from inventory, files, the command line, and information discovered on the host 06 Handler A task that runs only when notified by a task that changed something 08 Role A packaged directory structure of tasks, templates, defaults and handlers Level 2 Collection A distribution unit for modules, roles and plugins (Galaxy) Level 2 Vault Encryption for secret values in files Level 2

docs.title: Ansible compared with neighbours
docs.text:
• Shell scripts. A script is a procedure; if it is run twice it may fail or duplicate work. Ansible modules check state first. Scripts are fine for one-off glue, and Ansible can run them (with care, Level 3).
  • Terraform / OpenTofu. Terraform provisions infrastructure (networks, VMs, databases) by comparing desired and recorded state, with a plan step. Ansible mostly configures what runs on machines, keeps no state file, and discovers state by asking the host. They are commonly combined (Level 4 · 05). Ansible can create cloud resources too, but without a plan/state model you must be careful.
  • Puppet / Chef / Salt. Agent-based, pull by default, with their own languages (Puppet DSL, Ruby, Salt YAML+Jinja). Ansible's selling point is the low barrier (YAML, SSH). The trade-offs are speed at scale (SSH-per-task is slower than local agents) and the lack of continuous enforcement out of the box.
  • Containers / immutable images. If you replace servers rather than modify them, Ansible is used to build images or to bootstrap hosts, and less to patch running machines.

docs.title: A first run, for real
docs.text:
The smallest useful command, executed with ansible-core 2.21.5 on the control node against itself:

$ ansible web -i hosts.ini -m ping
web1 | SUCCESS => {"changed": false, "ping": "pong"}
web2 | SUCCESS => {"changed": false, "ping": "pong"}

ping here is not ICMP. It is the Ansible ping module: Ansible connected to the host, ran a small Python program, and got pong back as JSON. A SUCCESS therefore proves: the connection works, Python is usable on the target, and the module machinery works end to end. With ansible_connection=local the "connection" is a local subprocess, which is why this works without SSH on a laptop; on real servers you would see SSH authentication here, and most first-day failures live in this step.

docs.title: Where Ansible fits in a delivery pipeline
docs.text: You typically use Ansible to (1) bootstrap a fresh machine into a known baseline, (2) configure applications and services, (3) run orchestrated changes across a fleet in a defined order (rolling updates, Level 3), and (4) audit drift with check mode (Level 4 · 06). It is the "configure" step after Terraform provisions and before the application deploy tools take over; Level 4 · 02 of the CI/CD course on this site covers running such jobs from a pipeline.

docs.title: A note on versions
docs.text: Ansible is two things that are versioned separately: ansible-core (the engine and ansible.builtin) and collections (everything else). Behaviour changes between core versions; this course found, for example, that a when: on the string "false" is an error in 2.21.5. Pin both, and read the porting guide for your version before upgrading.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: For each task and each host (in parallel across hosts, up to forks, default 5), Ansible on the control node does roughly this: build the module arguments by evaluating Jinja2 templates against the host's variables; package the module code and its arguments into a temporary file; transfer it to a temporary directory on the target through the connection plugin (SSH by default; with connection=local it simply runs locally); execute it with the target's Python interpreter; read the JSON the module prints (changed, failed, msg, return data); remove the temporary files; and move to the next task. Because the module is shipped fresh for every task and each module is a self-contained program, no agent or long-lived process is needed. Optimisations such as SSH pipelining reduce the round trips (Level 3 · 06). This design explains both its main strengths (simple, nothing to maintain on targets) and its weaknesses (a task costs at least one connection round trip, so very large fleets and very long task lists get slow).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Treating Ansible as a script runner and putting everything in shell:, losing idempotency and check mode.
  • Expecting state tracking like Terraform. Ansible has no memory of what it did last time; it only inspects the host now.
  • Assuming every module is idempotent. Some always report changed (Lesson 05).
  • Confusing the control node and the managed node. Python on the controller and Python on the target can be different versions, and modules run on the target.
  • Using ping as a network test. It tests Ansible's own connection and Python, not reachability in the ICMP sense.
  • Skipping the inventory and running against localhost by accident.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Install ansible-core in a virtual environment (python3 -m venv ans && ans/bin/pip install ansible-core) and run ansible --version. Record the version, the Python version and where the config file is (it printed None here).
  2. Create an inventory with one host whose connection is local and run ansible all -i hosts.ini -m ping. Then break it (point ansible_python_interpreter at a path that does not exist) and read the error.
  3. Write down, for a server you manage, three things you do by hand that would make a good first playbook, and which module might do each.
  4. In two sentences each, explain when you would choose Ansible, Terraform, and an immutable image for the same job.

docs.title: 02 · Ad-Hoc Commands, Modules and ansible-doc
docs.text:
Before writing playbooks, learn the unit they are built from. An ad-hoc command runs one module, once, on a set of hosts: ansible <pattern> -i <inventory> -m <module> -a "<arguments>". It is the right tool for quick checks and one-off actions, and the best way to explore what a module does and returns.

What was run

Run with ansible-core 2.21.5 on macOS, hosts using ansible_connection=local. The facts shown therefore describe a Mac (Darwin), not a Linux server; module names and arguments are the same, but Linux-only modules (apt, dnf, systemd, user on some platforms) were not run.

docs.title: Anatomy of an ad-hoc command
docs.text:
$ ansible web1 -i hosts.ini -m command -a "echo hello"
web1 | CHANGED | rc=0 >>
hello
  • web1 is the host pattern (a host, group, or expression; Lesson 03).
  • -i hosts.ini selects the inventory.
  • -m command selects the module; -a passes its arguments as a string.
  • The output says CHANGED, even though all we did was print text. The command module cannot know whether running a command changed anything, so it always reports changed unless told otherwise (changed_when: in a playbook, or the creates/removes arguments). This one fact explains many "why does my playbook never go green" questions, measured in Lesson 05.

Useful options: -b (become root; not exercised here), -f 10 (forks), -u user, -k (ask for SSH password), --list-hosts (show matches without running), -o (one line per host).

docs.title: Modules are the vocabulary
docs.text:
Modules are grouped by what they manage. A small, high-value set to know by name:

Area Modules Notes Files file, copy, template, lineinfile, blockinfile, stat, fetch, unarchive stat reads state without changing it Packages package, apt, dnf, pip Platform-specific; not run here Services service, systemd Linux; not run here Users user, group, authorized_key Commands command, shell, script, raw Last resort; idempotency is on you Control debug, assert, fail, set_fact, pause, wait_for Helpers inside playbooks Info setup (facts), package_facts, service_facts

Names are best written as fully qualified collection names (FQCN) such as ansible.builtin.copy. Short names like copy still work for built-ins but become ambiguous once you install collections that define a module with the same short name. This course uses FQCNs throughout, and ansible-lint (Level 2 · 09) can enforce it.

docs.title: Reading the documentation offline
docs.text:
ansible-doc shows module documentation from the installed code, so it always matches your version:

$ ansible-doc -l | wc -l          # list modules visible by default
      71
$ ansible-doc ansible.builtin.copy | head
> MODULE ansible.builtin.copy (.../ansible/modules/copy.py)
  The [ansible.builtin.copy] module copies a file or a directory structure from the local or remote machine to a
  location on the remote machine. ...
$ ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.file    # a YAML snippet with every option

On this install ansible-doc -l listed 71 modules in ansible-core alone (the batteries of cloud, network and database modules live in separate collections, Level 2 · 06). ansible-doc -s prints a starter snippet; the full page lists each option's type, default, choices, and whether it is required, plus the return values that you can register and use. Developing the habit of reading ansible-doc for the exact module version you run avoids using arguments from a blog post that your version does not have.

docs.title: Facts: what the host tells you
docs.text:
The setup module gathers facts, data about the host. Filtering keeps output manageable:

$ ansible web1 -i hosts.ini -m setup -a "filter=ansible_distribution*"
web1 | SUCCESS => {
    "ansible_facts": {
        "ansible_distribution": "MacOSX",
        "ansible_distribution_major_version": "27",
        "ansible_distribution_release": "27.0.0",
        "ansible_distribution_version": "27.0.1"
    },
    "changed": false
}

Facts such as ansible_os_family (here Darwin; on Linux Debian, RedHat and so on) are how playbooks branch by platform (Lesson 07). Gathering facts costs time on every host at the start of each play, and Lesson 06 (Level 3) shows how to avoid it when you do not need them.

docs.title: Ad-hoc is for exploration, playbooks are for repeatability
docs.text: Reasonable ad-hoc uses: check connectivity, look at one value across a fleet (-m setup -a filter=..., -m command -a "uptime"), restart one service in an emergency, copy one file. If you run the same ad-hoc command twice, it belongs in a playbook where it is named, reviewed, and version-controlled. Conversely, an ad-hoc command that changes state with no record is exactly the sort of undocumented change that automation exists to eliminate.

docs.title: Return values and changed/failed
docs.text: Every module returns JSON. Three keys matter on every module: changed (did it modify the target), failed (did it fail), and msg (human text). Additional keys are module specific: command returns rc, stdout, stderr, delta; stat returns an object describing the file; file returns the resulting mode, owner, path. The ad-hoc output you see is a pretty-printed version of that JSON; in playbooks you capture it with register (Lesson 07).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The ansible CLI is a one-task playbook runner. It parses the pattern against the inventory, builds a play with a single task module: args, and executes the same task engine as ansible-playbook. Module lookup searches, in order, the collection namespace in the FQCN, then built-ins, then any module paths configured through ANSIBLE_LIBRARY or ansible.cfg; custom modules (Level 3 · 01) are found the same way. Arguments are templated through Jinja2 before the module runs, then validated against the module's argument spec on the target, which is why a misspelled option gives a precise error naming the module and the unsupported parameter rather than a silent ignore.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using command or shell for something a module does (command: mkdir -p /x instead of file).
  • Believing CHANGED from command means the system changed.
  • Short module names that later collide with a collection.
  • Skipping ansible-doc and guessing arguments from old tutorials.
  • Relying on ad-hoc changes that are never recorded.
  • Quoting problems in -a: the whole argument string is parsed by the module, and spaces and quotes need care.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run ansible-doc -l on your install and count modules. Pick one you have never used and read its examples and return values.
  2. Run ansible <host> -m setup unfiltered once, save it to a file, and find five facts you could use to decide behaviour.
  3. Run ansible <host> -m command -a "echo hi" twice and note the status each time. Then run it with -a "echo hi" replaced by the stat module on a file and compare the status.
  4. Use ansible-doc -s ansible.builtin.lineinfile and write down which two arguments decide whether the module edits an existing line or adds a new one.

docs.title: 03 · Inventory: Hosts, Groups and Variables
docs.text:
The inventory tells Ansible what exists. It lists hosts, arranges them into groups, and attaches variables. A good inventory is the foundation for everything else: the same playbook runs against staging or production simply by pointing at a different inventory, and the group structure decides which tasks apply where.

What was run

All output below is from the real ansible-inventory and ansible commands (ansible-core 2.21.5). Hosts use ansible_connection=local, so there are no real remote machines or SSH. Dynamic inventories (cloud, CMDB) are Level 3 · 03.

docs.title: Two static formats
docs.text:
INI (compact):

[web]
web1 ansible_connection=local http_port=8081
web2 ansible_connection=local

[db]
db1 ansible_connection=local

[prod:children]
web
db

[all:vars]
env=staging

[web:vars]
http_port=80

YAML (same idea, nestable, better for complex data and types):

all:
  vars: {ansible_connection: local}
  children:
    web:
      hosts:
        web1: {http_port: 8081}
        web2:
      vars: {http_port: 80}
    db:
      hosts: {db1: }

Use INI for small inventories, YAML when values are lists or dictionaries (INI values are strings, with some parsing, and type surprises). The special group all always exists, and ungrouped holds hosts that are in no other group. A group can contain other groups (:children), so prod here is the union of web and db.

docs.title: Inspect before you trust
docs.text:
ansible-inventory shows how Ansible understood your files:

$ ansible-inventory -i hosts.ini --graph
@all:
  |--@ungrouped:
  |--@prod:
  |  |--@web:
  |  |  |--web1
  |  |  |--web2
  |  |--@db:
  |  |  |--db1

$ ansible-inventory -i hosts.ini --host web1
{ "ansible_connection": "local", "env": "staging", "http_port": 8081, ... }
$ ansible-inventory -i hosts.ini --host web2
{ ..., "env": "staging", "http_port": 80 }

Two things to read here. --graph shows the tree, which confirms prod contains web and db. And --host shows the merged variables for one host: web1 has http_port: 8081 (set on the host) while web2 gets 80 (from the [web:vars] group). A host variable beats a group variable for the same name, one rule of precedence out of many (Level 2 · 02 measures the full order). env=staging came from [all:vars] and applies to everyone. --list prints the whole inventory as JSON, which is also the format dynamic inventory scripts must emit.

docs.title: Host patterns
docs.text:
The first argument to ansible and the hosts: of a play is a pattern. Measured with --list-hosts:

Pattern Meaning Matched web the group web1, web2 web:db union web1, web2, db1 prod:!db in prod but not db web1, web2 web:&prod intersection web1, web2 web1,db1 explicit list web1, db1 nomatch nothing 0 hosts, with a warning

The last row matters operationally: a pattern that matches nothing prints a warning and does nothing, and the play succeeds with zero hosts. I confirmed it with a playbook whose hosts: was nomatch: it printed skipping: no hosts matched and exited with status 0. A typo in a group name in a CI job can therefore pass silently. Defensive options: check --list-hosts in a pre-step, or fail the pipeline when the host count is zero.

docs.title: Where variables live
docs.text:
Ansible reads variables from many places. For inventories, the structured, version-friendly way is directories next to the inventory:

inventory/
  production/
    hosts.yml
    group_vars/
      all.yml            # applies to everyone
      web.yml            # applies to the web group
    host_vars/
      web1.yml           # applies to web1 only

This keeps data out of the host list, lets you review changes per group, and makes it easy to keep secrets in a vaulted file (group_vars/db/vault.yml, Level 2 · 05). A common convention is one inventory directory per environment, with the same group names and different values; the playbooks never mention environments.

docs.title: Connection variables
docs.text: Variables whose names begin with ansible_ control how Ansible reaches a host: ansible_host (the real address if the inventory name is a label), ansible_user, ansible_port, ansible_connection (ssh, local, winrm ...), ansible_python_interpreter, ansible_become. I set ansible_python_interpreter to the virtual environment's Python because otherwise Ansible tries to discover an interpreter on the target, a documented step that can pick a different Python than you expect. On real servers, pin the interpreter explicitly when the system has several.

docs.title: Design advice
docs.text:
• Group by role and by environment, not by one dimension: web, db, staging, production, eu. A host belongs to several groups, and web:&production selects the intersection.
  • Keep names stable and put the real address in ansible_host.
  • Prefer inventory-supplied data over hard-coded values in playbooks.
  • Don't encode behaviour in group names that nobody documents; a short README beside the inventory pays off.
  • Test the shape: a small script can assert that every host is in exactly one environment group; this course's pipeline (Level 4) uses ansible-inventory --list as the data source for such checks.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: On start-up, Ansible loads each inventory source through inventory plugins: ini, yaml, script (executable returning JSON), and others such as cloud plugins. Each plugin adds hosts and groups to an in-memory structure. Then Ansible loads group_vars/ and host_vars/ files that sit next to the inventory source or the playbook, and merges variables per host according to precedence rules. Merging is per variable name, with later and more specific sources winning, and dictionaries are replaced by default, not deep-merged (a setting, hash_behaviour, exists but is discouraged). When the play runs, hosts: is evaluated as a pattern against this structure to produce the play's host list, and each host's merged variables are what templates and conditions see.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Pattern matching nothing and a green run that did nothing.
  • Variables on the wrong level, so a host variable overrides what you thought was a group default.
  • INI type surprises: enabled=false is a string unless parsed as a boolean by the consumer.
  • Putting secrets in plain inventory files committed to Git.
  • Reusing group names with different meanings across environments.
  • Forgetting all:vars is the lowest-precedence group source, not a global override.
  • Using IP addresses as inventory names, making renames painful.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Create the INI inventory above, run ansible-inventory --graph and --host for each host, and predict http_port for each before you look.
  2. Convert it to YAML and confirm the graph output is identical apart from prod. Why might you add prod there too?
  3. Add a group_vars/web.yml file with http_port: 8000 next to the inventory and see which value web2 gets now. (I measured it: web2 went from 80 to 8000, while web1 stayed at 8081. A group_vars file next to the inventory beats a [web:vars] section inside the inventory file, and the host-level value still beats both.) Explain why that ordering is useful.
  4. Write a one-line command that fails (non-zero exit) when a pattern matches zero hosts.

docs.title: 04 · Playbook Anatomy: Plays, Tasks and Modules
docs.text:
A playbook is a YAML list of plays. Each play maps a set of hosts to a list of tasks, executed in order. Understanding exactly what runs, in what order, and on which hosts removes most early confusion.

What was run

Every playbook here was run with ansible-core 2.21.5 against ansible_connection=local hosts. YAML errors and messages are copied from real runs. Remote execution, SSH and privilege escalation were not exercised.

docs.title: The smallest useful playbook
docs.text:
- name: Configure web servers
  hosts: web
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    out: /tmp/demo
  tasks:
    - name: ensure dir
      ansible.builtin.file: {path: "{{ out }}", state: directory}
    - name: write config
      ansible.builtin.copy: {dest: "{{ out }}/app.conf", content: "port=8080\n"}

Parts, outside in:

  1. A play is one item of the top-level list: name, hosts, and keywords such as vars, gather_facts, become, tasks, handlers, roles.
  2. hosts: is an inventory pattern (Lesson 03). A play with zero matching hosts is skipped, not failed.
  3. tasks: run in order; each task runs on all hosts in the play before the next task starts (the default linear strategy; Level 2 · 08 covers alternatives).
  4. A task has an optional name and exactly one module with its arguments, plus keywords such as when, loop, register, notify, tags, become, ignore_errors.

docs.title: Always name tasks
docs.text:
An unnamed task prints as its module name. Named tasks make runs readable and let you use --start-at-task. ansible-playbook --list-tasks shows the plan without running it:

playbook: handlers.yml
  play #1 (web1): web1  TAGS: []
    tasks:
      ensure dir    TAGS: []
      render config TAGS: []
      second notifier of same handler   TAGS: []

--list-tasks is a good CI step too: it parses the whole playbook, including templated task names and imports, and fails on structural errors without touching a host.

docs.title: Argument styles and the YAML trap
docs.text:
Three equivalent ways to give module arguments:

- ansible.builtin.copy: dest=/tmp/x content="hi"          # key=value string (legacy style)
- ansible.builtin.copy: {dest: /tmp/x, content: hi}        # inline mapping
- ansible.builtin.copy:                                    # block mapping (preferred)
    dest: /tmp/x
    content: hi

Use the block form. Inline mappings are compact and break easily. While preparing this course I wrote this task:

ansible.builtin.command: {cmd: touch "{{ target }}/marker", creates: "{{ target }}/marker"}

and ansible-playbook refused with a YAML parse error pointing at column 30, hinting at the quoting problem. The "{{ ... }}" inside a flow mapping, followed by more text, confused the YAML parser. Rewriting as a block mapping fixed it. Rule: a value that starts with {{ must be quoted; inside inline {} prefer not to nest quotes at all.

Other YAML traps seen constantly:

  • yes, no, on, off are booleans in YAML 1.1 (Ansible's parser follows YAML 1.1 for these); quote strings you mean literally.
  • Octal-looking modes: write mode: "0644" as a quoted string. An unquoted 0644 is parsed by YAML as a number, and what the module then does with it is easy to get wrong (the Ansible documentation advises quoting modes or using a leading zero; I did not test the unquoted form).
  • A task list indented inconsistently gives errors like did not find expected key.

docs.title: Syntax checking
docs.text:
--syntax-check parses the playbook without connecting:

$ ansible-playbook bad.yml --syntax-check
[ERROR]: YAML parsing failed: While parsing a block mapping did not find expected key.
Origin: .../bad.yml:4:4

2   tasks:
3     - debug: msg=hi
4    - debug: msg=bad
     ^ column 4

The message gives the file, line and column and prints the surrounding source with a caret. (The file has a task indented one space too few.) Syntax checking does not catch an undefined variable or a wrong module argument; those appear at run time (Lesson 09). ansible-lint (Level 2 · 09) finds many more problems statically.

docs.title: Run order, precisely
docs.text: For one play, Ansible runs: (1) fact gathering, if enabled; (2) pre_tasks; (3) roles and tasks, in the order written (roles: run before tasks: unless you use import_role/include_role inside tasks); (4) notified handlers at the end of each section (pre_tasks, main, post_tasks), or earlier with meta: flush_handlers; (5) post_tasks. A playbook with several plays runs them in order, and a later play can target different hosts, which is how "configure database, then web servers, then run a smoke test from the controller" is written as one file.

docs.title: Multiple plays and import_playbook
docs.text:
- import_playbook: db.yml
- import_playbook: web.yml
- hosts: localhost
  connection: local
  tasks:
    - ansible.builtin.uri: {url: http://web1/health}

import_playbook is resolved when the playbook is parsed, so it can be listed and checked. The final play uses localhost with connection: local to run a check from the controller, a common pattern.

docs.title: Facts at the start of a play
docs.text: By default each play begins by running setup on every host, which costs a connection and a second or two per host. If a play does not use facts, set gather_facts: false (all examples in this course that don't use facts do). If it uses a few, gather_subset limits the work (Level 3 · 06 measures the difference).

docs.title: become and the user a task runs as
docs.text: become: true runs a task with elevated privileges (sudo by default). It can be set per play, per task, or per role. It requires configuration on the target (a sudoers entry, or a password supplied with -K). It was not exercised here because everything ran as my own user. When you move to real servers, add become at the narrowest scope that works and remember that files created by tasks with become are owned by root unless owner: says otherwise.

docs.title: Check mode and diff mode
docs.text: ansible-playbook --check asks each module to report what it would change without changing it; --diff shows the content differences for modules that support it. Lesson 05 measures both. They work only for modules that implement check mode; command and shell are skipped in check mode unless told otherwise (a skipping: line appears).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When you run ansible-playbook, the parser loads the YAML into a tree of Play, Block, Task and Handler objects, resolving imports (static) at load time and leaving includes (dynamic) to run time. For each play it asks the strategy plugin for the next batch of (host, task) pairs. The default linear strategy picks one task, queues it to a worker process per host (up to forks), waits for all to finish, then continues. Module arguments are templated per host immediately before execution, which is why a task can use a fact discovered earlier or a value registered by a previous task but cannot reference a variable that does not yet exist. A failed host is removed from the rest of the play (its recap shows failed=1) while other hosts continue, unless any_errors_fatal is set.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unquoted {{ }} at the start of a value.
  • Unquoted file modes and yes/no strings.
  • Unnamed tasks, producing logs nobody can read.
  • Using key=value strings for complex arguments.
  • Mixing tabs and spaces (YAML forbids tabs for indentation).
  • Assuming tasks run host by host to completion. By default all hosts run task 1, then task 2, and so on.
  • Leaving fact gathering on when facts are not needed.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a three-task playbook that creates a directory, writes a file in it, and prints the file's mode with stat and debug. Run it with --list-tasks, --syntax-check, and then for real.
  2. Introduce a YAML indentation error on purpose and read the message. Fix it.
  3. Add a second play to the same file that runs on a different group and observe the recap.
  4. Run with -v and -vvv and note what extra information each level adds for one task.

docs.title: 05 · Idempotency, changed and Check Mode
docs.text:
The promise of configuration management is convergence: no matter what state a machine starts in, running the playbook brings it to the desired state, and running it again changes nothing. This lesson measures that promise on real runs, shows where it breaks, and explains how check mode and diff mode let you see changes before making them.

What was run

Real ansible-playbook (ansible-core 2.21.5) runs on a Mac with ansible_connection=local, so the modules edited files and directories in a sandbox. Package, service and user modules were not run. The recaps and diff output shown are copied from those runs.

docs.title: First run, second run
docs.text:
A four-task playbook: create a directory with a mode, write a config file, run echo hi with command, and run touch marker with command guarded by creates:.

First run                                    Second run
make dir ........... changed                 make dir ........... ok
write config ....... changed                 write config ....... ok
raw command ........ changed                 raw command ........ changed   <-- still changed
command + creates .. changed                 command + creates .. ok

recap: ok=4 changed=4                        recap: ok=4 changed=1

Three kinds of behaviour:

  1. State-aware modules (file, copy) compare the current state with the request. Second run: ok. That is idempotency.
  2. command/shell with no guard cannot know; it reports changed every time. A pipeline that checks "no changes on the second run" will fail forever on it.
  3. command with creates: is made idempotent by a condition: if the file exists the command is skipped and reported ok. removes: is the mirror image. These two arguments are the cheapest way to make a command idempotent when no module exists.

The recap line is the instrument: the number of changed tasks on a repeat run should be zero for a converged system. A Level 1 project (Lesson 10) turns that into an automated test.

docs.title: changed_when and failed_when
docs.text:
For commands you cannot avoid, tell Ansible how to interpret the result:

- name: query version (read only)
  ansible.builtin.command: myapp --version
  register: ver
  changed_when: false          # reading never changes anything

- name: apply migration
  ansible.builtin.command: myapp migrate
  register: mig
  changed_when: "'applied' in mig.stdout"
  failed_when: mig.rc not in [0, 3]

changed_when: false is the single most common fix for a noisy playbook. changed_when with a stdout test gives truthful reporting when the tool prints something distinct. Do not use changed_when: false on a task that really changes state; you would blind check mode and drift reports (Level 4 · 06).

docs.title: Check mode: "what would you do?"
docs.text:
--check runs the playbook in a dry-run mode where modules that support it report what they would change. After the baseline was applied, a stray line appended to the config file and the playbook was run with --check --diff:

TASK [write config]
--- before: /tmp/demo/app.conf
+++ after: /tmp/demo/app.conf
@@ -1 +1 @@
-port=9999
+port=8080
changed: [localhost]
TASK [raw command (always changed)]
skipping: [localhost]

Observations from real runs:

  • The diff shows exactly the drift: someone had set port=9999; the playbook would restore 8080.
  • The file was not modified: afterwards cat app.conf still showed port=9999.
  • The command task was skipped, because command modules cannot predict their effect. In check mode their results are unknown, so tasks that depend on their registered output may behave differently or fail. Add check_mode: false to a read-only command whose output later tasks need (it will run for real, so it must be safe), or check_mode: true to force dry-run behaviour.
  • A task that notifys a handler reports changed in check mode, and the handler is also simulated, so a check run is a good preview of what would restart.

Check mode is reliable only for modules that implement it faithfully. For file, copy, template, lineinfile, blockinfile and similar, it is good. For modules that depend on earlier tasks' real effects, a check run may be misleading: a task that would only work after a package is installed may fail or report wrong results in check mode because the package was not actually installed. Treat "no changes in check mode" as strong evidence, and "changes in check mode" as a list to read.

docs.title: Diff mode
docs.text: --diff prints before/after for file-content modules (template, copy, lineinfile, blockinfile). It can be used without --check to log what actually changed. Warning: diffs print file content into logs. Files that contain secrets must be protected with no_log: true or diff: false on that task.

docs.title: Idempotency is a design habit, not a switch
docs.text:
• Prefer a module to a command; prefer state: arguments (present, absent, latest, started).
  • Make operations safe to repeat: lineinfile with a regexp replaces a line instead of appending a duplicate each run; blockinfile manages a marked block; file: state=directory instead of mkdir.
  • Avoid state: latest for packages in production runs unless you want upgrades whenever someone runs the playbook.
  • Avoid tasks that depend on the current time or random values in their arguments (a timestamp in a file makes every run changed).
  • Verify by running twice. If the second run reports changes, fix it before shipping.

docs.title: Why "idempotent" is subtler than "no changes"
docs.text: A playbook can report zero changes and still be wrong (it checks the wrong thing), or report changes every run and be harmless (a command that restarts nothing). The aim is: changed means something really changed, and ok means the system already matched. Honest reporting is what makes check mode, drift audits and CI gates trustworthy.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each module implements its own comparison. file calls stat on the path and compares owner, group and mode with the requested values; copy computes a checksum of the destination and compares it with the checksum of the source content; template renders the Jinja2 text on the controller, then behaves as copy. If the comparison shows a difference, the module applies the change and returns changed: true; otherwise it returns changed: false without touching the target. In check mode the module is instructed (via an argument in its input JSON) not to write, and it returns what it would have done. The command module has no way to inspect the effects of an arbitrary command, so it returns changed: true unless creates, removes, changed_when or check mode says otherwise. The PLAY RECAP counts come directly from these changed flags.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Never running twice to verify idempotency.
  • command/shell that changes state with no creates/removes/changed_when.
  • changed_when: false on a real change, blinding drift reports.
  • Trusting check mode for tasks that depend on earlier tasks' real effects.
  • Timestamps or random values in managed content.
  • Appending lines with shell: echo >> file instead of lineinfile.
  • Printing secret content through --diff into CI logs.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the four-task playbook and its two runs. Add a fifth task using shell: date > /tmp/x and watch it change every time; then fix it two different ways.
  2. Change a managed file by hand, run --check --diff, confirm the diff and that the file is untouched, then run for real.
  3. Write a command task that is only ever changed when its output says so, using changed_when.
  4. Explain why a play with changed=0 on the second run is evidence of idempotency but not proof of correctness.

docs.title: 06 · Variables and Facts
docs.text:
Playbooks become reusable when the host-specific and environment-specific parts are variables. Ansible has a rich variable system: you define data in inventory, playbooks, files and on the command line; Ansible discovers more data as facts; and magic variables describe the run itself. This lesson shows the pieces. How conflicts are resolved (precedence) is measured in Level 2 · 02.

What was run

Everything below was run with ansible-core 2.21.5 on a Mac, hosts local. Facts therefore describe macOS (Darwin). The ansible_facts dictionary has the same structure on Linux, with different values.

docs.title: Defining variables
docs.text:
- hosts: web1
  gather_facts: false
  vars:
    greeting: "from play vars"
    cfg: {a: 1, b: {c: 2}}
  tasks:
    - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "{{ greeting }} / {{ http_port }} / {{ env }}"}

Output: from play vars / 8081 / staging. greeting came from the play; http_port (8081) from the host entry in the inventory; env (staging) from [all:vars]. Your task did not care where each came from, which is the point.

Common sources: inventory (host/group vars), group_vars/ and host_vars/ directories, vars: and vars_files: in plays, role defaults/ and vars/, set_fact and register at run time, -e on the command line, and facts.

docs.title: Referencing and defaults
docs.text:
• {{ name }} for a simple value; {{ cfg.b.c }} or {{ cfg['b']['c'] }} for nesting (measured: cfg.b.c=2 cfg['a']=1). Use bracket syntax when a key contains dashes or clashes with a method name.
  • {{ missing | default('fallback') }} gives fallback when missing is undefined. Without default, an undefined variable is an error (Lesson 09 shows the message). Defaults are how roles stay usable with minimal input.
  • Strings with a leading {{ must be quoted in YAML.
  • A variable may refer to another: url: "http://{{ host }}:{{ port }}" is evaluated lazily when used.

docs.title: set_fact and its precedence
docs.text:
set_fact creates or changes a variable for the rest of the play for that host:

debug greeting          -> "from play vars"
set_fact greeting       -> "set by set_fact"
debug greeting again    -> "set by set_fact"

It overrides play vars (it sits higher in precedence). But extra vars (-e) beat everything, including set_fact. Running with -e greeting=CLI printed CLI both before and after the set_fact task. That is intentional: -e is the operator's override, and it is also why you should never put values you want tasks to compute into variables that operators may pass with -e. set_fact values also persist across plays in the same run for that host, and with fact caching they can be cached (Level 3 · 06).

docs.title: Facts
docs.text:
Facts are variables Ansible discovers with the setup module at the start of a play when gather_facts is on. The full dictionary on this Mac had 90 keys (names beginning ansible_). Modern style is to read them from the single dictionary ansible_facts, without the ansible_ prefix:

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "os_family={{ ansible_facts.os_family }} cpus={{ ansible_facts.processor_vcpus | default('n/a') }} py={{ ansible_facts.python_version }}"

printed os_family=Darwin cpus=8 py=3.14.7. The older injected form ansible_os_family pollutes the variable namespace and the Ansible documentation has been moving away from it (I did not test whether it is still injected by default in this version); prefer ansible_facts.*. Facts you will use constantly: os_family, distribution, distribution_major_version, hostname, fqdn, default_ipv4, processor_vcpus, memtotal_mb, mounts, date_time. Gathering them has a cost and a failure mode: if Python is missing on the target, fact gathering fails first.

Custom (local) facts go in /etc/ansible/facts.d/*.fact (INI or JSON, or an executable that prints JSON) and appear under ansible_facts.ansible_local. This is a way for the machine to declare its own attributes without Ansible controlling them (not run here).

docs.title: Magic variables
docs.text:
Ansible always provides variables about the run:

host=web1  groups=['prod', 'web']  in_web=['web1', 'web2']  play_hosts=['web1']
  • inventory_hostname: the name in the inventory (not necessarily the real hostname).
  • group_names: the groups this host belongs to.
  • groups: a dictionary of all groups to their host lists, which lets a task on one host read the whole inventory (for example to build a load balancer config from the web group).
  • hostvars: a dictionary of every host's variables (hostvars['db1'].http_port), including facts if they were gathered.
  • ansible_play_hosts, ansible_play_batch, playbook_dir, role_path, ansible_check_mode, ansible_version.

hostvars is powerful and risky: it couples hosts to each other and to the order of gathering. If a task reads hostvars['db1'].ansible_facts... and db1 was never fact-gathered in this run, it fails.

docs.title: Variables from files and the command line
docs.text:
• vars_files: [vars/common.yml] loads a file in a play. Paths are relative to the playbook.
  • include_vars loads at run time, including per-OS files: include_vars: "{{ ansible_facts.os_family }}.yml" is the classic way to handle differences between platforms.
  • -e @file.yml or -e '{"key": "value"}' passes variables; JSON form keeps types (-e port=80 passes a string that Jinja may auto-convert, but filters such as | int make intent explicit).

docs.title: Types and the string trap
docs.text: Ansible templates return strings unless a literal type is detectable. Task arguments that are pure {{ expr }} are evaluated to native types where possible (a "{{ 5 }}" argument becomes an integer), but a value stored in a variable as a string stays a string. The "false" string is true in Python truthiness, so a condition on it would be wrong; Ansible 2.21 actually refuses it: a when: on a variable whose value was the string "false" failed with Conditionals must have a boolean result (Lesson 07). Use | bool when the value may come from the command line or an INI file.

docs.title: Naming conventions
docs.text: Choose variable names that avoid collisions: prefix role variables with the role name (nginx_port, not port). Avoid names that clash with Ansible's own (environment, name, hosts, ansible_*). Keep data (what) in variables and logic (how) in tasks and templates.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: For each host and each task, Ansible builds a variable context by merging sources in a fixed priority order (Level 2 · 02 measures it), then evaluates Jinja2 expressions against that context. Facts and registered variables are stored per host in the controller's memory (and optionally in a fact cache). Because each host has its own context, two hosts running the same task can render different arguments. Templating is lazy: a variable that refers to another is resolved when used, so the final value can depend on facts set between the definition and the use. Jinja2 runs on the controller, not on the target; this is why filters and lookups are controller-side features (a lookup reads files on the controller), a distinction that matters in Level 3 · 02.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Undefined variables with no default in roles meant to be reusable.
  • Using set_fact for configuration that belongs in inventory.
  • Passing -e variables and wondering why nothing else can override them.
  • Relying on injected ansible_* facts instead of ansible_facts.
  • Reading hostvars of hosts that weren't gathered.
  • Strings that should be booleans or integers.
  • Variable names that collide across roles.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the set_fact and -e experiment. Predict the output of each debug before running.
  2. Gather facts from a host and find the fact for total memory and the default IPv4 address. Write a task that prints both.
  3. Use include_vars with a per-OS file (Darwin.yml, Debian.yml) to set a package name variable, and a default for unknown platforms.
  4. Write a task that builds a comma-separated list of all hosts in the web group using groups.

docs.title: 07 · Conditionals, Loops and Registered Results
docs.text:
Real playbooks branch (only on Debian-family hosts), repeat (create five users) and react to results (restart if the config test passed). when, loop and register are the three tools.

What was run

Run with ansible-core 2.21.5 on macOS, hosts local, so ansible_facts.os_family was Darwin and distribution-specific branches were skipped. The error message in the "boolean strings" section is copied from a real run of this version; older versions were more lenient, so behaviour may differ on yours.

docs.title: when
docs.text:
when takes a Jinja2 expression (without {{ }}) evaluated per host:

- name: only on Debian family
  ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "apt would run"}
  when: ansible_facts.os_family == "Debian"

On the Mac this task printed skipping: [web1]. Combine conditions with and, or, not, or list them (a list means all must be true). Common tests: var is defined, var is not none, result is changed, result is failed, result is skipped, item in list, version is version('2.0', '>='), path is exists (a controller-side test).

Key behaviours:

  • A task skipped by when reports skipping and is not counted as changed.
  • when on a task with loop is evaluated per item (below).
  • A when on a role or import_tasks is applied to every task inside (and evaluated for each), unlike include_tasks, where the condition decides whether the include happens at all.

docs.title: Loops
docs.text:
vars:
  users: [{name: ann, admin: true}, {name: bob, admin: false}, {name: cy, admin: true}]
tasks:
  - name: loop with when
    ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "{{ item.name }} is admin"}
    loop: "{{ users }}"
    loop_control: {label: "{{ item.name }}"}
    when: item.admin

Actual output:

ok: [web1] => (item=ann) => {"msg": "ann is admin"}
skipping: [web1] => (item=bob)
ok: [web1] => (item=cy) => {"msg": "cy is admin"}

loop: is the modern keyword (it replaced most uses of with_items). item is the current element. loop_control lets you rename item (loop_var, important when loops nest or when a role is called inside a loop), set a short label so logs do not dump big dictionaries (done above), add a pause, or access the index (index_var). Useful companions: loop: "{{ dict | dict2items }}" to loop over a mapping, subelements, product, and zip filters.

One module call can often replace a loop (package with a list of names installs them in one transaction, much faster than a loop that calls the package manager once per package). Loop only when the module takes a single item.

docs.title: register: capture the result
docs.text:
- name: run per item
  ansible.builtin.command: echo {{ item }}
  loop: [one, two]
  register: res
  changed_when: false

- ansible.builtin.debug:
    msg: "{{ res.results | map(attribute='stdout') | list }} first_rc={{ res.results[0].rc }}"

Output: ['one', 'two'] first_rc=0. With a loop, the registered variable has a results list with one entry per item, each holding the module's return values (stdout, rc, changed, item). Without a loop, the variable holds the return directly (res.stdout). That structural difference between looped and non-looped registers is a common source of dict has no attribute errors; use ansible.builtin.debug: var=res to look at the structure before writing expressions.

register works with check mode and skipped tasks: a skipped task registers a result with skipped: true, so conditions like res is skipped or res.stdout | default('') are needed when a later task reads it.

docs.title: until, retries, delay
docs.text:
- name: wait until the file exists
  ansible.builtin.command: test -f /tmp/never
  register: r
  until: r.rc == 0
  retries: 2
  delay: 1
  ignore_errors: true

Real output: two lines FAILED - RETRYING: ... (1 retries left) and (0 retries left), then the task failed (ignored here). The recap showed ignored=1. Use this pattern to wait for something asynchronous (a service answering) but prefer purpose-built modules, wait_for or uri with until, which give clear failures instead of retrying a generic command.

docs.title: Boolean strings: a real failure
docs.text:
I wrote a task with vars: {flag: "false"} and when: flag. In ansible-core 2.21.5 the play stopped with:

A 'when' expression failed: Conditional result (True) was derived from value of type 'str' ...
Conditionals must have a boolean result.

Older versions silently evaluated non-empty strings in various ways, which hid bugs like this one. The fix is explicit conversion: when: flag | bool, after which the string "false" converted to false and the task was skipped (two skipping lines appeared in the run). The general rule: conditions must be real booleans. Values from -e on the command line, INI inventories and environment lookups are strings until you convert them.

docs.title: Conditions on registered results
docs.text:
Typical patterns:

- name: config test
  ansible.builtin.command: nginx -t
  register: test
  changed_when: false
  failed_when: false          # we want to inspect the result, not stop

- ansible.builtin.fail: {msg: "bad config: {{ test.stderr }}"}
  when: test.rc != 0

failed_when: false (or ignore_errors: true) lets you handle failure yourself. Prefer failed_when with a precise expression to a blanket ignore_errors, which also hides real problems such as an unreachable host or a Python exception inside the module.

docs.title: Facts-driven branching
docs.text:
Branch on facts, not on the group names you invented, when the difference is platform-specific:

- ansible.builtin.include_vars: "{{ ansible_facts.os_family }}.yml"
- ansible.builtin.package: {name: "{{ web_package }}", state: present}      # name set per OS file

This keeps platform conditionals out of every task. Reserve when: for genuine behavioural differences.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Both when and the loop expression are Jinja2 expressions evaluated on the controller with the host's variable context. For a looped task, the engine evaluates the loop list first, then runs the module once per item on the target (each is a separate module execution, which is why looping is slower than passing a list to a module that supports it) and evaluates when separately for each item with item set. register stores the aggregated result under the variable name for that host. until re-runs the task, re-evaluating the condition after each attempt, up to retries. In the release I used (2.21.5), conditionals are evaluated with strict typing, which is why the string "false" produced an error; I did not check in which release this started, and older versions were more lenient.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• String booleans in when.
  • {{ }} inside when: write when: x == 1, not when: "{{ x == 1 }}".
  • Looping package installs one by one.
  • Forgetting that a looped register has .results.
  • Blanket ignore_errors hiding real failures.
  • Naming conflicts for item in nested loops and roles; use loop_var.
  • Reading a skipped task's register without a default.
  • Using until on a task whose failure mode is not transient.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the loop with when and add loop_control: {index_var: i}; print i.
  2. Reproduce the boolean-string failure on your Ansible version and note whether it errors or warns. Then fix it two ways.
  3. Register the output of a command run in a loop and print only the stdout values as a comma-separated string.
  4. Write a retry loop that waits for a file to appear within 5 seconds, and test it by creating the file from another terminal after 2 seconds.

docs.title: 08 · Templates and Handlers
docs.text:
Configuration files are mostly the same across machines and differ in a few values. A template is a file with variable slots filled in with host values. A handler is an action (restart, reload) that should happen only if something changed. Together they implement "change the config, then reload the service, but only if the config actually changed."

What was run

Real runs, ansible-core 2.21.5, local connection. The "service" is simulated by a debug handler and files in a sandbox; no real daemon was restarted, so service-manager behaviours (systemd reload semantics) were not exercised.

docs.title: Templates
docs.text:
A template is a Jinja2 file, by convention ending in .j2:

# managed by Ansible - do not edit by hand
server {
    listen {{ http_port }};
    server_name {{ inventory_hostname }}{% if env == 'production' %}.example.com{% endif %};
{% for u in upstreams %}
    # upstream {{ loop.index }}: {{ u.name }} weight={{ u.weight | default(1) }}
{% endfor %}
}

Rendered for web1 (port 8081) with upstreams: [{name: a, weight: 3}, {name: b}] it produced the config with comments for each upstream; with upstreams: [{name: a}] on a later run:

# managed by Ansible - do not edit by hand
server {
    listen 8081;
    server_name web1;
    # upstream 1: a weight=1
}

Jinja2 tools you need: {{ expr }} prints a value; {% if %}...{% endif %} and {% for %}...{% endfor %} control flow; {# comment #}; filters (| default, | upper, | join(','), | to_nice_json, Level 2 · 03); loop.index, loop.first, loop.last inside loops. Control lines such as {% for %} leave blank lines unless trimmed: Ansible's template module enables trim_blocks by default, which removes the newline after a block tag (this is why the output above has no blank lines), and lstrip_blocks can be set per task.

Good habits:

  • Put a managed-by header so people know hand edits will be reverted.
  • Keep logic out of templates where you can. Compute lists and flags in variables, and let the template format them.
  • Quote values the target format needs quoted; Jinja does no escaping for config languages.
  • Use the validate: argument of template and copy to check a file before it replaces the live one (validate: nginx -t -c %s); the module runs the command on a temporary file and aborts if it fails, so a bad render cannot break a running service. Not exercised here.
  • Set mode, owner, group, and consider backup: true for important files.

docs.title: Templates and idempotency
docs.text: template renders on the controller, then compares the rendered content's checksum with the destination, exactly like copy. The second run reported ok, no change. Anything that varies between renders defeats this: {{ ansible_date_time.iso8601 }} in a template makes every run changed. If you need to record a time, use a value that changes only when the config really changes (a version variable).

docs.title: Handlers
docs.text:
Handlers are tasks in a handlers: section, triggered with notify::

tasks:
  - name: render config
    ansible.builtin.template: {src: templates/nginx.conf.j2, dest: /tmp/web/site.conf}
    notify: reload service
  - name: second notifier of same handler
    ansible.builtin.copy: {dest: /tmp/web/extra.conf, content: "x=1\n"}
    notify: reload service
handlers:
  - name: reload service
    ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "RELOAD happened"}

Measured over three runs:

Run What changed Handler 1 (fresh) directory, site.conf, extra.conf (3 changes) ran once, even though two tasks notified it 2 (same inputs) nothing did not run (recap changed=0) 3 (upstreams changed) site.conf only ran once

The rules visible there: a handler runs only if at least one notifying task reported changed; it runs once per play no matter how many tasks notified it; it runs after all the tasks in the play (or section), not immediately. This is what makes "reload once at the end" cheap and safe.

Handlers can notify other handlers, can be named with listen: topics so one notify: "restart web stack" triggers several handlers, and can be flushed early:

- ansible.builtin.meta: flush_handlers

Flush when a later task needs the service already reloaded (for example you start a service and then run a smoke test in the same play).

docs.title: When a failure skips the handler
docs.text:
tasks:
  - name: change something
    ansible.builtin.copy: {dest: /tmp/hf.txt, content: "..."}   # reports changed
    notify: h
  - name: boom
    ansible.builtin.command: /usr/bin/false
handlers:
  - name: h
    ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: HANDLER RAN}

Run normally: change something was changed, boom failed with rc=1, and the handler never ran. The config on disk had changed but the service was not reloaded, and the next run would see no change (the file already matches), so the handler would not fire on the next run either. That is a real operational trap: a failed play after a config change can leave the system with new config and an old running process, and a rerun reports ok forever. Mitigations: --force-handlers (or force_handlers: true in the play) runs notified handlers even after a failure (with it, the output did include RUNNING HANDLER [h] and HANDLER RAN); put the notifying task last in the sequence it belongs to; or use blocks with rescue (Level 2 · 04); or make the handler idempotent and have a task that checks the service's actual state.

Note also the side observation in that run: the command task is reported "changed": true in the failure output. A failed command still says changed, consistent with Lesson 05.

docs.title: Check mode and handlers
docs.text: In check mode the notifying task reports changed and the handler is also simulated. That makes --check a faithful preview of "what would restart", which operations teams use before maintenance windows.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a task returns changed: true and has notify, the strategy engine adds the handler's name to a per-host "notified" set. At the end of the current section (pre_tasks, tasks, or post_tasks) or at a flush_handlers meta task, the engine runs every notified handler once, in the order handlers are defined in the play (not in the order notified), and clears the set. A host that has failed is dropped from the play before the flush, which is why handlers are skipped after a failure unless force_handlers is on. template rendering happens on the controller with Jinja2 using the host's variables and then the rendered text is compared and transferred like copy; the validate step, if present, runs on the target against a temporary copy.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Restarting inside a task with command instead of notifying a handler.
  • Expecting handlers to run immediately.
  • Handler order assumed to follow notify order.
  • Failure after change leaving the service stale, with later runs showing ok.
  • Time-dependent templates that change every run.
  • No validate on configs that can break the service.
  • Logic-heavy templates that nobody can test.
  • Handler names that differ by a typo (restart nginx vs Restart nginx): a notify to a handler that does not exist is an error, but a case difference is a different handler.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the three-run handler table. Add a third notifying task and confirm the handler still runs once.
  2. Reproduce the failure case with and without --force-handlers. What is the state of the file and the "service" after each?
  3. Add a validate: command to a template task that rejects any rendered file containing the word FORBIDDEN, and test both outcomes.
  4. Write a template that renders a list of allowed IPs from a variable, one per line, and a task that makes the file unchanged when the list order changes (hint: sort in the variable or the template).

docs.title: 09 · Debugging and Reading Failures
docs.text:
Automation fails in boring ways: a typo, an undefined variable, a wrong assumption about the target. Learning to read Ansible's output quickly is a skill you build once. This lesson walks through the real failures hit while building this course and the tools used to diagnose them.

What was run

All messages and counts are from real runs of ansible-core 2.21.5 on macOS with local connections. Error text changes between versions; the diagnosis technique does not. SSH-specific failures (permission denied, host key checking, unreachable) were not reproduced and are described from documentation.

docs.title: Read the failure top-down
docs.text:
Ansible's error format identifies the task, the host, the module, and (in recent versions) prints the source location with a caret. For an undefined variable:

TASK [ansible.builtin.debug]
[ERROR]: Task failed: Finalization of task args for 'ansible.builtin.debug' failed:
Error while resolving value for 'msg': 'not_defined' is undefined

Origin: .../undef.yml:4:7
2   gather_facts: false
3   tasks:
4     - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "{{ not_defined }}"}

Read: what failed (resolving task arguments), why (not_defined is undefined), where (file:line:column). Most errors are one of these categories:

Symptom Likely cause First step YAML parsing failed ... did not find expected key Indentation, colon/quote problem Look at the origin line and the one above 'x' is undefined Missing variable, typo, wrong scope, fact not gathered debug: var=x, check inventory with ansible-inventory --host couldn't resolve module/action Misspelled module or missing collection ansible-doc <name>, check FQCN Unsupported parameters for module Wrong argument for this version ansible-doc -s <module> Conditionals must have a boolean result String used as a boolean Add | bool or fix the type UNREACHABLE Connection (SSH, host key, network, interpreter) -vvv, try the same ssh command by hand FAILED with rc=... and stderr The command or module ran and failed Read stderr/msg; reproduce by hand Missing sudo password / become errors Privilege escalation not configured Test sudo -n true on the target

docs.title: Verbosity
docs.text:
default : 20 lines for a 3-task playbook
-v      : 16 lines   (shows module return values for each task)
-vvv    : 106 lines  (shows connection and execution details)

Increase only as needed: -v shows results (stdout, rc, diff-like content); -vv shows task file locations and more; -vvv shows the connection method and the remote commands. In the -vvv output:

<web1> ESTABLISH LOCAL CONNECTION FOR USER: bhanuja
<web1> EXEC /bin/sh -c 'echo ~bhanuja'
<web1> EXEC /bin/sh -c '( umask 77 && mkdir -p "` echo /Users/bhanuja/.ansible/tmp `" && mkdir ... )'
Using module file .../ansible/modules/file.py

That is Ansible creating a private temp directory (umask 77), choosing the module file and shipping it. On an SSH connection the same lines show the ssh command line with all options, which you can paste into a terminal to reproduce a connection problem. -vvvv adds connection-plugin debugging. Never paste -vvv logs publicly without scrubbing: they may include usernames, paths and sometimes arguments with secrets (use no_log: true on sensitive tasks).

docs.title: debug, assert, fail
docs.text:
• ansible.builtin.debug: var=name prints a variable's value (including type and structure). msg: prints a templated string. Set verbosity: 2 on a debug task to print only when -vv is used, so you can leave diagnostics in.
  • ansible.builtin.assert states expectations and fails with a clear message:
- ansible.builtin.assert:
    that: ["http_port | int < 1024"]
    fail_msg: "http_port {{ http_port }} needs root"

Output: fatal: [web1]: FAILED! => {"msg": "http_port 8081 needs root"}. Assertions at the top of a play or role (required variables defined, inputs valid, target OS supported) turn confusing mid-run errors into clear early ones, like input validation. - ansible.builtin.fail: msg=... with when: is the same idea for custom conditions.

docs.title: Targeting what you debug
docs.text:
• --limit web1 runs on one host. --tags/--skip-tags (Level 2 · 07) select tasks.
  • --list-hosts and --list-tasks show the plan without running anything.
  • --step asks before each task (interactive).
  • --check --diff previews changes (Lesson 05).
  • --start-at-task "name" begins at a task. Careful: it skips all earlier tasks, including setup tasks that later ones need. While testing it, I ran the handler playbook with --start-at-task "render config" after deleting the sandbox directory; the first task (ensure dir) was skipped, so the template task failed (failed=1 with ok=0) because the directory did not exist. Use it to resume a long play when you know earlier state exists, not to skip setup.
  • ansible-playbook -e 'debug_var=1' style switches in your own playbooks are fine, but prefer -v levels.

docs.title: Debugging templates and Jinja2
docs.text: To see what a template would produce without deploying, render it with the template module into a temporary path (dest: /tmp/rendered) and read it, or use debug: msg="{{ lookup('ansible.builtin.template', 'x.j2') }}". Common template errors: a missing endif/endfor (Jinja reports the line), an undefined variable (use default or check), or whitespace changes (use trim_blocks/lstrip_blocks settings and - markers like {%- if x -%}).

docs.title: Failure handling you can see
docs.text:
Output markers: ok, changed, skipping, failed (task failed, host removed from the play), unreachable (connection failed), rescued (a rescue block recovered, Level 2 · 04), ignored (failure ignored with ignore_errors). The recap's counts tell you at a glance: failed=1 means one task failed for that host; ok=0 failed=1 (as above) means the very first executed task failed.

A failed host is removed from the rest of the play. Other hosts continue. The command exits with a non-zero status if any host failed or was unreachable, so CI sees red. A play with hosts matching nothing exits zero (Lesson 03).

docs.title: A debugging checklist
docs.text:
1. Re-read the error from the top; find the task, module, file and line.
  2. Reproduce on one host: --limit host -v.
  3. Print the inputs: debug: var=... right before the failing task, and ansible-inventory --host host for inventory variables.
  4. Run the underlying command by hand on the target as the same user.
  5. Check module docs for the exact argument names and types for your version.
  6. Check recent changes with git diff; many failures follow the last edit.
  7. Reduce the playbook to the smallest case that still fails.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Errors surface at three stages. At parse time the YAML loader and the playbook compiler detect structural problems (bad indentation, unknown keywords on a play or task) before any host is contacted, which is why --syntax-check is cheap. At templating time per host, argument expressions are evaluated; undefined variables and type errors surface here, as a task failure for that host. At execution time the module runs on the target and returns JSON; module-level validation (unsupported or missing parameters) happens inside the module's argument spec check, and runtime problems come back as failed: true with msg and any stderr. The verbosity flags change only what the controller prints; they do not change what runs, except that -vvv makes the SSH layer print its commands.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Running at full verbosity first and drowning in output.
  • Not limiting to a single host while debugging.
  • --start-at-task skipping prerequisites.
  • ignore_errors left on while debugging, hiding the failing step.
  • Printing secrets with debug or -vvv in shared logs.
  • Trusting a green run that skipped everything because a when was always false.
  • Editing the playbook and the inventory at once, so you don't know which change fixed it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Make each of these errors on purpose and record the message: a bad indent, an undefined variable, a misspelled module name, a wrong module argument. Which are caught by --syntax-check?
  2. Add an assert at the top of a play that checks three required variables are defined and the OS family is supported.
  3. Run a failing playbook with -v and -vvv; list three facts you learn only from the higher level.
  4. Write a one-page personal debugging checklist for your environment, including the exact SSH command you would use to test a connection by hand.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Verified Baseline Playbook
docs.text:
A playbook you have never tested twice is a playbook you hope works. This project builds a small server baseline and, more importantly, an automated test suite that runs the real ansible-playbook and asserts the properties from this level: it converges, it is idempotent, check mode touches nothing, drift is detected and repaired, and handlers fire only when they should.

What was run, and what wasn't

The tests call the real ansible-playbook (ansible-core 2.21.5) on a Mac. The "servers" node1 and node2 are two inventory entries with ansible_connection=local, each owning a directory tree under a temporary sandbox (<sandbox>/<host>/etc/...). No real server, SSH, package manager, systemd, user account, or privilege escalation was involved, so this baseline manages files and directories only. A production baseline would add packages, users, services and firewall rules, each of which needs its own verification on the target OS. All 8 tests passed on the first full run (53 seconds, because each test starts several Ansible processes).

docs.title: What the playbook manages
docs.text:
src/baseline/baseline.yml configures every host in servers:

  1. Directory tree with modes (etc/app 0755, var/log/app 0750, var/lib/app 0700) via a loop with a short label.
  2. Message of the day with copy content.
  3. Application config from a template (templates/app.conf.j2) using a per-host variable app_port (8080 for node1, 9090 for node2) and an optional workers variable. It notifies the restart app handler.
  4. A hardening line in a copy of sshd_config: lineinfile replaces any #?PermitRootLogin line with PermitRootLogin no, creating the file at mode 0600 if absent.
  5. A managed block in sysctl.conf with blockinfile (two settings between marker comments).
