  6. A handler that increments var/lib/app/restart.count, standing in for restarting the service: it lets the tests count how many restarts happened.

Running it for real:

first run : node1 ok=6 changed=6   node2 ok=6 changed=6
second run: node1 ok=5 changed=0   node2 ok=5 changed=0

(The first run is ok=6 because the handler ran once; the second has no handler, so ok=5.)

docs.title: Drift, shown for real
docs.text:
I then vandalised node1 by hand: appended port = 1 to app.conf, set the var/lib/app directory to mode 777, and changed PermitRootLogin no to yes. Running with --check --diff:

TASK [directory tree]
-    "mode": "0777"
+    "mode": "0700"
changed: [node1] => (item=var/lib/app)
TASK [app configuration]
-port = 1
changed: [node1]
TASK [ensure a hardening line in sshd config copy]
-PermitRootLogin yes
+PermitRootLogin no
changed: [node1]
recap: node1 ok=6 changed=4    node2 ok=5 changed=0

Four reported changes on node1 (three drifted items plus the handler that the config change would trigger) and none on node2. Then a real run repaired everything; restart.count ended at 2 (one restart after the first deployment, one after the repair; check mode itself did not write).

This is the whole value of check mode in operations: the diff is the drift report, and it distinguishes hosts that match from hosts that do not.

docs.title: The test suite
docs.text:
src/baseline/test_baseline.py starts Ansible with subprocess, passes the sandbox location with -e sandbox=<tmp path>, parses the PLAY RECAP lines into dictionaries of counters, and asserts:

Test What it proves First run changes everything Both nodes show changed=6, exit status 0 Second run is idempotent changed=0 and failed=0 on every node Check mode writes nothing On a fresh sandbox, --check reports at least 5 changes and the sandbox directory does not exist afterwards Per-host variable reaches template node1 file contains port = 8080, node2 contains port = 9090 Modes are enforced var/lib/app is 0700 and sshd_config is 0600 (stat) Drift detected, then repaired After appending port = 1: check mode reports changes only for node1 and leaves the bad line; a real run removes it; a further run is changed=0 Handler runs only on config change Counter is 1 after the first run, still 1 after an unchanged re-run, 2 after running with -e workers=4 Manual edit of sshd_config is reverted A file containing PermitRootLogin yes is rewritten to PermitRootLogin no

Design notes on the harness:

  • It rewrites the inventory in a temporary copy so the interpreter path points at the Python running pytest, instead of a hard-coded path.
  • It sets ANSIBLE_HOME to a directory beside the test so Ansible's temp files and cache stay out of your real home directory.
  • It skips itself with a clear reason if ansible-playbook is not installed (pytest.mark.skipif).
  • Because every test runs Ansible several times, the suite is slow (53 s). That is the honest cost of testing the real thing. Level 2 · 09 covers lighter-weight checks (ansible-lint, --syntax-check) and how to keep slow tests in a separate stage.

docs.title: How to use this pattern on a real baseline
docs.text:
1. Write the invariant first: "after the playbook, SSH root login is disabled, the log directory is 0750, the service is enabled."
  2. Express each invariant as a task (so Ansible enforces it) and as a test assertion (so you notice if the task is removed).
  3. Always include the second-run-is-zero-changes test. It is the cheapest and most valuable test you can write for a playbook.
  4. Add a drift test for any setting an operator might change by hand.
  5. Run the same tests in CI against disposable machines (containers or VMs), as Level 4 · 02 describes. Containers are good for file and package logic; for anything involving the init system or kernel settings, use a VM, since containers share the host kernel.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Check mode and idempotency both come from how modules are written. Each file-oriented module computes the current state on the target, compares it with the requested state, and only writes if they differ; in check mode the same code runs but the write step is skipped and the module reports changed based on the comparison. The test suite exploits this: because the recap counts come from the modules' own changed flags, changed=0 on the second run is a direct measurement that every module found the system already in the desired state. The handler counter works because handlers run only if at least one notifying task reported changed (Lesson 08), and the check-mode test works because check is a property of the whole run: no module writes, so the sandbox directory never gets created even though file would have created it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Testing only the first run. Idempotency failures appear on the second.
  • Tests that share state between runs. Each test here uses a fresh temporary sandbox.
  • Checking only the exit status. A playbook can exit 0 and have done nothing (zero hosts) or changed the wrong thing.
  • Putting secrets in test inventories.
  • Assuming file-only tests prove package/service behaviour.
  • Letting the suite get too slow and then skipping it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run python3 -m pytest -q src/baseline (with ansible-core installed) and read the recap parsing code. Add a third node with app_port=7070 and extend the tests.
  2. Add a task that sets a file's content from ansible_date_time and watch the idempotency test fail; then fix the task.
  3. Add a managed setting to sysctl.conf, a test that a hand-edited value inside the managed block is reverted, and a test that a line outside the block is preserved.
  4. Write the invariants list for a baseline of a Linux web server (ten items) and mark which could be tested with file-only checks and which need a real VM.

docs.title: Level 2 · Structure and Safety
docs.text:
Level 1 gave you playbooks that converge. Level 2 makes them maintainable and safe to run on more than one machine: roles, a measured variable-precedence table, Jinja2 data shaping, error handling, real Vault encryption, collections as dependencies, targeted and batched runs, and testing with lint and repeated runs.

What was run, and what wasn't

ansible-core 2.21.5 and ansible-lint on a Mac, with all hosts local (ansible_connection=local). The variable-precedence order, tag and limit behaviour, serial/failure-budget results, vault commands and lint findings are measurements from those runs. Not run: SSH, become, real services and packages, Molecule and containers, Galaxy roles beyond installing one collection (ansible.utils 6.1.1), and an automation controller.

Prerequisites: Level 1.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:

docs.title: 01 · Roles: Reusable Structure
docs.text:
A role packages everything needed to configure one thing (tasks, default variables, templates, files, handlers, metadata) into a directory with a known layout, so playbooks can say roles: [webapp] instead of repeating thirty tasks. Roles are the unit of reuse and sharing in Ansible.

What was run

The role in this lesson (src/l2/roles/webapp) was created with ansible-galaxy role init --offline and run with ansible-core 2.21.5 against two local hosts. ansible-lint (production profile) passes on the final version. Shared roles from Galaxy and role dependencies on remote hosts were not exercised.

docs.title: The standard layout
docs.text:
$ ansible-galaxy role init --offline webapp
webapp/README.md
webapp/defaults/main.yml   # low-precedence variables: the role's public interface
webapp/handlers/main.yml
webapp/meta/main.yml       # author, license, platforms, dependencies
webapp/tasks/main.yml      # entry point
webapp/tests/...           # scaffold only; replace with real tests (Lesson 09)
webapp/vars/main.yml       # high-precedence variables: internal constants

Other directories you add as needed: templates/ (Jinja2 files for template), files/ (static files for copy), library/ (custom modules private to the role), filter_plugins/, and tasks/ can contain many files that main.yml includes.

The key design decision is defaults versus vars:

  • defaults/main.yml holds the variables a user is meant to override. They have the lowest precedence of all, so inventory, play variables or the command line win. This file is the role's documented interface.
  • vars/main.yml holds internal constants. They have high precedence. But note what I measured: a role parameter (a variable passed in the roles: entry) still beat vars/main.yml (Lesson 02), so vars/ is not a way to forbid overriding. Prefix internal names with _rolename_ as a convention and do not rely on precedence for protection.

docs.title: The role used in this lesson
docs.text:
defaults/main.yml:

webapp_port: 8080
webapp_root: "/private/tmp/.../webapp/{{ inventory_hostname }}"
webapp_workers: 2

tasks/main.yml validates input, creates a directory, renders a config, and notifies a handler:

- name: Validate inputs
  ansible.builtin.assert:
    that:
      - webapp_port | int > 0
      - webapp_port | int < 65536
      - webapp_workers | int >= 1
    fail_msg: "webapp_port must be 1-65535 and webapp_workers >= 1"
    quiet: true
- name: Create directory
  ansible.builtin.file: {path: "{{ webapp_root }}", state: directory, mode: "0755"}
- name: Render config
  ansible.builtin.template: {src: webapp.conf.j2, dest: "{{ webapp_root }}/webapp.conf", mode: "{{ webapp_config_mode }}"}
  notify: Reload webapp

Used in a play with a role parameter:

- hosts: web
  roles:
    - role: webapp
      vars: {webapp_workers: 4}

Real output of --list-tasks shows role tasks prefixed with the role name: webapp : Validate inputs, webapp : Create directory, webapp : Render config. The inventory gave w2 its own webapp_port=9000, and the rendered files were port=8080 workers=4 host=w1 and port=9000 workers=4 host=w2: the role default (8080) applied to w1, the host variable overrode it for w2, and the role parameter (workers=4) applied to both.

Passing an invalid value stopped the play at the first task: webapp_workers=0 produced fatal: ... "webapp_port must be positive and webapp_workers >= 1" for each host, before any change. Validation at the top of a role is cheap insurance, and a role that checks its inputs gives better errors than whatever breaks later.

docs.title: A bug found by running it: two hosts, one path
docs.text:
My first version of the role used a fixed webapp_root in defaults. Both hosts run on the same laptop in this course, so both rendered the same file. On the first runs the recap showed w2 changed again and again (changed=1 each time, while w1 flipped), and the file contents depended on which host ran last. After changing the default to include {{ inventory_hostname }} in the path, three consecutive runs gave changed=2/2, then 0/0, then 0/0, as expected.

This is an artifact of the local setup, but the lesson is real: when two hosts share a resource, their tasks race. It happens on real fleets with NFS-mounted directories, a shared database, or a delegated task that writes one file for every host (Lesson 08). Idempotency checks, by watching changed on the second run, are what catch it.

docs.title: Using roles in plays
docs.text:
Three ways to apply a role:

  1. roles: section of a play: static, runs before the play's tasks.
  2. ansible.builtin.import_role inside tasks: static, role is parsed at load time; when applies to every task in it; tags apply to all of them.
  3. ansible.builtin.include_role: dynamic, evaluated when reached, so it can be conditional or looped; tags and when apply to the include itself, and with apply: you can pass them down.

Prefer roles: for the common case. Use include_role when the role name or the decision to run is computed (include_role: name="{{ item }}" in a loop), and remember the cost: dynamic includes are invisible to --list-tasks until they run, and tags work differently.

docs.title: Handlers and variables across roles
docs.text: A handler defined in a role is available to the whole play and runs once, however many roles notify it by name. Handlers from different roles with the same name collide (the usual advice is to prefix: webapp : Reload in tasks as notify: Reload webapp). Variables defined in a role's defaults and vars are visible to the entire play after the role loads (a known property of Ansible's variable scope), so names must be unique across roles: use a role-name prefix.

docs.title: Role dependencies
docs.text: meta/main.yml can list dependencies: (other roles that run first). They are convenient but implicit: the dependency runs for every role that lists it, once per unique parameter set, which surprises people. Prefer explicit ordering in the play, or tasks that include_role deliberately. Collections (Lesson 06) are the modern way to share roles, modules and plugins.

docs.title: Size and shape
docs.text: A role should do one thing and have a short interface. Signs a role has grown too large: more than a dozen defaults, tasks full of when branching for unrelated cases, a need to pass lists of lists. Split by responsibility (install, configure, harden) or into several roles composed by the playbook. Document the interface in the README: variables, defaults, examples, supported platforms.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a play loads a role, Ansible resolves it by searching roles/ next to the playbook, then the paths in roles_path (ANSIBLE_ROLES_PATH, or collection namespaces), and then it merges: defaults/main.yml into the lowest variable layer, vars/main.yml into a higher one, role parameters into a still higher one, meta dependencies placed first, tasks/main.yml turned into a block of tasks, and handlers/main.yml appended to the play's handlers. Templates and files are looked up relative to the role first (templates/ inside the role), which is why src: webapp.conf.j2 resolves without a path. A role is therefore not a runtime object; it is a loading convention that expands into the same task, handler and variable structures a plain playbook would contain.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Putting overridable settings in vars/ instead of defaults/.
  • No input validation, so mistakes fail late and obscurely.
  • Un-prefixed variable names that clash between roles.
  • Hard-coded shared paths that make hosts race.
  • Using include_role where a static import is clearer, losing --list-tasks visibility.
  • Implicit dependencies in meta that nobody remembers.
  • Roles that configure several unrelated services.
  • No README documenting the variables.

docs.title: 02 · Variable Precedence, Measured
docs.text:
When the same variable is defined in several places, exactly one value wins. The documentation lists the order; this lesson measures it on the version used for this course by setting one variable x in fourteen places, running a play to see which value wins, removing the winner, and repeating.

What was run

src/l2/prec/run.py generates a fresh project for each trial (inventory, group_vars, host_vars, role, play) and runs the real ansible-playbook (ansible-core 2.21.5, 14 sources, 14 runs). test_precedence.py pins the result. The order below is what this version did. Precedence has been stable for years but has changed in details across releases; the documentation page "Using variables" is the reference for your version, and the test is how you notice a change.

docs.title: The method
docs.text:
For each trial the script writes the active sources, runs the playbook, reads the printed X=<source name> and records the winner. Then it drops that source from the active list and repeats until no source is left. The sources, each setting x to its own name:

role defaults/main.yml; inventory file group [all:vars]; inventory file group [web:vars]; group_vars/all.yml; group_vars/web.yml; inventory file host entry; host_vars/h1.yml; play vars:; play vars_files:; role vars/main.yml; task vars:; include_vars; set_fact; and -e extra vars.

docs.title: The result (highest first)
docs.text:
Rank Source Notes 1 -e extra vars beats everything, including set_fact 2 set_fact 3 include_vars 4 task vars: 5 role vars/main.yml 6 play vars_files: 7 play vars: 8 host_vars/<host>.yml next to the inventory 9 inventory file, host entry h1 x=... 10 group_vars/web.yml specific group 11 group_vars/all.yml 12 inventory file [web:vars] 13 inventory file [all:vars] 14 role defaults/main.yml lowest

Five facts from the table are worth memorising:

  1. Extra vars always win. That makes them the operator's emergency override, and it means a value passed with -e can never be changed by a task.
  2. Host beats group, specific group beats all. At both inventory levels (files in host_vars/group_vars and values inside the inventory file).
  3. group_vars/host_vars files beat variables inside the inventory file at the same specificity (rank 8 versus 9, 10 versus 12 and 11 versus 13). I also saw this in Level 1: a group_vars/web.yml of 8000 overrode [web:vars]'s 80.
  4. Role defaults lose to everything. That is their purpose.
  5. Play vars, vars_files and role vars sit above the inventory. Anything defined in a playbook overrides inventory data for that play, so putting settings in play vars: makes them hard to override per host (they win over host_vars!). Put defaults in the role and per-environment data in the inventory; reserve play vars: for values that are truly fixed for that playbook.

One more measured fact from the Level 2 role project: a role parameter (roles: [{role: webapp, vars: {...}}]) beat the role's own vars/main.yml. So the role's vars/ directory is not protected from callers.

docs.title: Verifying a pairwise rule
docs.text:
Ranking tests are easy to misread, so the test file also checks pairs directly:

  • -e against each of the other 13 sources: -e wins every time.
  • host against group at both inventory levels.
  • group_vars/web.yml against group_vars/all.yml: web wins.
  • role defaults against each of the other 13: defaults lose every time.

These run in a few seconds each and fail with a clear diff if a future Ansible version changes the order.

docs.title: Practical rules
docs.text:
• Defaults in the role, data in the inventory, overrides on the command line. That layering matches the table: defaults < inventory < -e.
  • Do not use set_fact to make "defaults": it outranks inventory, so it silently overrides what the operator configured. Use default() filters or defaults/main.yml. Use set_fact for computed values.
  • Avoid play vars: for anything operators may want to change per host.
  • One definition per variable where possible. If the same variable is defined in four places, you will eventually be debugging precedence. A search for the variable name across the repository should return one definition and the places that use it.
  • Use ansible-inventory --host name to see inventory-level values for a host (it shows inventory sources only, not play vars, role vars or facts). To see the final value a task will use, debug: var=x inside the play.
  • Use a prefix per role/app (webapp_port) so unrelated roles don't collide.
  • Dictionaries replace, they do not merge. If group_vars/all.yml sets app: {a: 1, b: 2} and group_vars/web.yml sets app: {b: 3}, the web value is {b: 3}: key a is gone. Merge explicitly with combine(recursive=True) (Lesson 03) when you want layering, e.g. app_effective: "{{ app_defaults | combine(app_overrides, recursive=True) }}".

docs.title: Debugging a surprising value
docs.text:
1. ansible-inventory -i inv --host h to see inventory-derived values.
  2. ansible-playbook -vvv to see variable files being loaded.
  3. In the play: ansible.builtin.debug: var=x, and var=hostvars[inventory_hostname] to see what everything looks like for the host.
  4. Bisect: comment out the suspected sources (the script above does it mechanically).
  5. Search for set_fact: and include_vars: which are high in the table and often forgotten.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Ansible's variable manager builds a dictionary per host per task by merging layers from lowest to highest priority, so later layers overwrite earlier ones by key. The layers are collected in a documented order: role defaults, inventory sources, play-level data, role vars, task/block vars, include_vars, set_fact and registered values, and finally extra vars. Group variables for several groups containing a host are merged in an order determined by the group's depth in the hierarchy (children over parents) and then alphabetically by group name, with ansible_group_priority available to adjust it (that last part is from the documentation; I did not test group-merge order). Lazy templating means a variable is stored as an unevaluated expression and resolved when used, so "the value of x" can depend on other variables at the time it is read, not when it was defined. This is why a variable can look defined in the file you are reading but resolve differently: a higher layer replaced it before templating.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Defining one variable in many places.
  • Using set_fact or play vars: where a default is meant.
  • Assuming dictionaries merge.
  • Believing vars/main.yml protects a role from caller overrides.
  • Debugging with ansible-inventory only and missing play-level overrides.
  • Forgetting -e beats everything, including in CI jobs that pass -e from a template.
  • Relying on an alphabetical group-merge order instead of explicit priorities.

docs.text:
1. Run python3 src/l2/prec/run.py and compare with the table. Is anything different on your version?

docs.title: 03 · Jinja2 Filters and Expressions
docs.text:
Jinja2 is the expression language in templates, when, and every {{ }}. Ansible adds its own filters, tests and lookups on top. Knowing a dozen filters well lets you shape data without custom code.

What was run

The expressions and outputs below were produced by one playbook (src/l2/filters.yml) run with ansible-core 2.21.5. Filters from collections (ansible.utils) were installed from Galaxy for the last section. Jinja2 runs on the controller, so none of this depends on the target OS.

docs.title: Data used
docs.text:
servers: [{name: a, port: 80, tags: [x, y]}, {name: b, port: 8080, tags: [y]}, {name: c, port: 443, tags: []}]
base: {a: 1, b: {c: 2, d: 3}}
over: {b: {c: 9}, e: 5}
csv: "web1, web2 ,db1"

docs.title: Lists of dictionaries
docs.text:
Expression Result servers \| map(attribute='name') \| list [a, b, c] servers \| map(attribute='name') \| join(',') a,b,c servers \| selectattr('port', 'gt', 100) \| map(attribute='name') \| list [b, c] servers \| rejectattr('tags') \| map(attribute='name') \| list [c] (empty tag list is falsy) servers \| map(attribute='tags') \| flatten \| unique \| sort [x, y] dict(names \| zip(ports)) {a: 80, b: 8080, c: 443}

map, selectattr and rejectattr return generators, so end with | list (or | join) when you need a list. selectattr('port', 'gt', 100) uses a Jinja test by name (gt, lt, eq, in, match, defined).

docs.title: Dictionaries
docs.text:
• base | combine(over) gives a shallow merge: {a: 1, b: {c: 9}, e: 5}; the whole b was replaced, and d: 3 was lost.
  • base | combine(over, recursive=True) gives a deep merge: {a: 1, b: {c: 9, d: 3}, e: 5}.
  • base | dict2items | map(attribute='key') | list gives [a, b]; items2dict goes back.
  • base | to_json printed {"a": 1, "b": {"c": 2, "d": 3}}; to_nice_yaml printed the indented YAML (4-space indentation by default in this version).

The shallow-vs-deep distinction connects to Lesson 02: variables from different layers do not merge on their own, and combine(recursive=True) is how you build layered settings explicitly.

docs.title: Strings and numbers
docs.text:
• csv.split(',') | map('trim') | list gives [web1, web2, db1]; without trim, ' web2 ' keeps its spaces.
  • 'web-01.example.com' | regex_replace('^(\w+)-(\d+).*', '\2:\1') gives 01:web. Note the backslashes: in YAML double quotes they must be doubled ('\\w') or the string put in single quotes.
  • '8080' | int + 1 gives 8081; 'abc' | int(-1) gives -1 (the argument is the default when conversion fails).
  • 'x' ~ 3 concatenates with ~ and gave x3; + on string and int would be an error. [1,2,3] | sum gave 6; 7 // 2 gave 3; 'a' if 3 > 2 else 'b' gave a.

docs.title: default and mandatory
docs.text:
'' | default('x')         -> ''     (empty string is DEFINED, so the default is not used)
'' | default('x', true)   -> 'x'    (second argument: also replace falsy values)

The output line was / x: the first part empty, the second x. This catches people constantly: a variable defined as an empty string is not "undefined". Use default(value, true) to treat empty/false/0 as missing, and omit (default(omit)) to drop an optional module argument entirely when the variable is unset.

mandatory turns silent defaults into early, clear errors:

{{ base.a | mandatory }}                              -> 1
{{ undefined_thing | mandatory('need undefined_thing') }}
 -> The filter plugin 'ansible.builtin.mandatory' failed: need undefined_thing

Use it in roles for required inputs, or use assert for several checks at once (Lesson 01).

docs.title: Tests
docs.text: Jinja tests are used with is: x is defined, x is none, x is string, path is file, r is changed, r is failed, v is version('2.0', '>='), x is match('^web'), x is in list. In conditions when: x is not defined is clearer than comparing with strings.

docs.title: Collection filters, and what happens when they are missing
docs.text:
IP address work lives in ansible.utils, not in ansible-core. Installed with ansible-galaxy collection install ansible.utils -p ./collections (it installed version 6.1.1; the filters also need the Python library netaddr on the controller, which I installed with pip). Then:

'10.0.0.5' is ansible.utils.ip                  -> True
'10.0.0.5/24' | ansible.utils.ipaddr('network')  -> 10.0.0.0
'10.0.0.5/24' | ansible.utils.ipaddr('netmask')  -> 255.255.255.0

Before installation, the same expression failed with Syntax error in template: No test named 'ansible.utils.ip'. A filter name from a collection that is absent fails at templating time with that message, and ignore_errors: true let the play continue. An unknown module in a task is worse: nosuch.collection.thing made the whole play fail at load time (couldn't resolve module/action), before any task ran, and ignore_errors cannot help. Dependencies on collections belong in requirements.yml (Lesson 06).

docs.title: Where templating happens and its limits
docs.text:
All filters run on the controller, with the controller's Python. A filter that needs a library (netaddr, jmespath for json_query) needs it on the controller, not the target. Use | to_json/from_json, from_yaml, b64encode, hash('sha256'), password_hash (needs a library) and quote (shell-quote a value; use it whenever a variable goes into a shell: string) as needed.

Keep templates and expressions readable. When an expression gets longer than a line, compute it in a vars: block or a set_fact with a clear name, or write a small filter plugin (Level 3 · 02) which you can unit test. Long Jinja is hard to debug and impossible to unit test.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Ansible hands each string containing {{ }} to a Jinja2 environment configured with Ansible's filter and test plugins (found by name through the plugin loader, including collection-qualified names such as ansible.utils.ipaddr). The environment compiles the expression and evaluates it against the variable context. If the whole string is a single expression, Ansible tries to convert the result back to a native type (so "{{ 5 }}" can produce an integer), whereas an expression embedded in surrounding text always yields a string. Errors inside a filter are wrapped as Finalization of task args ... failed with the original message, which is why the origin line points at the task, not the position in the expression. undefined values propagate as special Undefined objects until something uses them in a way that is not allowed; most filters then raise, while default explicitly handles them.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting | list after map/select.
  • default with an empty string that is defined but empty.
  • Shallow merging when you wanted deep.
  • Unescaped backslashes in regex strings.
  • Long expressions nobody can read or test.
  • Using + between a string and a number.
  • Filters from a collection you did not install (or its Python dependency).
  • Unquoted variables in shell strings; use | quote.

docs.title: 04 · Blocks, Errors and Rescue
docs.text:
By default, when a task fails on a host, Ansible stops running that host's remaining tasks and moves on with the others. That default is right most of the time, but real automation needs finer control: roll back a partial change, clean up in all cases, treat some non-zero exit codes as success, or stop the entire run if any host fails.

What was run

All outputs are from a real run of src/l2/blocks.yml on ansible-core 2.21.5, localhost. Behaviours involving several hosts (any_errors_fatal, max_fail_percentage) were measured in Lesson 08 with serial.

docs.title: Blocks group tasks
docs.text:
A block groups tasks so you can apply keywords once (when, become, tags, vars, ignore_errors) and attach error handling:

- name: deploy with rollback
  block:
    - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "1 apply new config"}
    - name: 2 health check (fails)
      ansible.builtin.command: /usr/bin/false
    - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "3 never reached"}
  rescue:
    - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "R rollback; failed task was '{{ ansible_failed_task.name }}' rc={{ ansible_failed_result.rc }}"}
  always:
    - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "A always: cleanup"}
- ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "play continues after rescue"}

Actual sequence printed: 1 apply new config, then the failure of 2 health check (fails), then R rollback; failed task was '2 health check (fails)' rc=1, then A always: cleanup, then play continues after rescue. Task 3 never ran. The recap said rescued=1, failed=0.

How it works: if any task in block fails, the remaining block tasks are skipped and rescue runs, where the special variables ansible_failed_task and ansible_failed_result describe what went wrong. If rescue completes successfully, the host is considered recovered: the play carries on and the host is not counted as failed. always runs whether or not the block failed. This is Ansible's try / except / finally.

Rescue is not magic rollback. It runs the tasks you wrote. A rollback task must itself be idempotent and safe to run when the failure happened at any point in the block (including before anything changed). Typical rescue content: restore a backup, flip a load balancer back, send an alert, then optionally fail so the run still reports failure.

A failing rescue task fails the host, and the always section still runs. In the experiment, a block whose rescue raised fail: second was marked with ignore_errors: true on the block, and the recap showed ignored=1 while the play continued.

docs.title: Failing on purpose, and telling the truth about success
docs.text:
• ansible.builtin.fail: msg=... stops a host with a message (usually with when:).
  • ansible.builtin.assert states several expectations and fails with fail_msg (Level 1 · 09).
  • failed_when: redefines failure for a task. Many tools use non-zero exit codes for non-error states:
- name: grep-like command
  ansible.builtin.command: sh -c 'echo warn >&2; exit 3'
  register: r
  failed_when: r.rc not in [0, 3]
  changed_when: false

With rc=3 the task passed, and the next task could read stderr=warn. failed_when: false means "never fail; I'll inspect the result" (and is clearer than ignore_errors because it states intent and leaves genuine unreachable errors visible).

  • ignore_errors: true continues after a failure of this task but still reports the failure in output (...ignoring) and counts ignored in the recap. It does not ignore unreachable hosts, and a failure inside a module's argument templating (like the undefined-variable error in Level 1 · 09) also counts as a failure that is then ignored, which can hide typos. Use it sparingly.
  • ignore_unreachable: true is the separate switch for unreachable hosts.

docs.title: What happens to the rest of the play
docs.text:
Per host, the default: first failure removes that host from the rest of the play. In check mode the same. Two keywords change that:

  • any_errors_fatal: true (on the play or a block): if any host fails the task, the whole play stops for all hosts. Good for steps where partial application is dangerous (a schema migration that must succeed everywhere or nowhere).
  • max_fail_percentage with serial (Lesson 08): tolerates failures up to a limit within each batch.

Handlers do not run after a failure unless force_handlers: true (Lesson 08 of Level 1 measured this). A rescue that succeeds restores normal handler behaviour for that host.

docs.title: Retrying and waiting
docs.text: until / retries / delay repeat a task (Level 1 · 07). For waiting on a TCP port, an HTTP status or a file, prefer wait_for and uri with until; they report timeouts clearly. For an operation that may take a long time, see async tasks (Level 3 · 05).

docs.title: Error handling on blocks: patterns
docs.text:
1. Deploy with rollback. block: apply; rescue: restore; always: remove temp files.
  2. Try an optional thing. block: read an optional file; rescue: use a default (ansible.builtin.set_fact).
  3. Guard rails. Use assert at the top of the play to fail fast before changing anything.
  4. Notify on failure only. rescue: send a message, then ansible.builtin.fail to preserve the failure.
  5. Cleanup always. always: remove locks, restore maintenance mode, close tickets.

docs.title: Check mode and blocks
docs.text: In check mode, blocks and rescue behave the same way, but the commands inside may be skipped (Lesson 05 of Level 1), so a "failure" that depends on a real command's result may not occur; do not use check mode as a rescue-path test. To test rescue paths, write a test playbook that forces the failure (like the /usr/bin/false above) in a throwaway sandbox.

docs.title: Reading the recap
docs.text: Counters: ok, changed, unreachable, failed, skipped, rescued, ignored. A run with rescued=1 exited 0, which can mislead a pipeline into believing everything went well; if a rescue means "something went wrong", end it with fail or write an artifact (a summary line) that the pipeline checks. In the experiment the exit status was 0 even though the health check had failed and the rollback ran.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A block is parsed into a Block object with three task lists. The strategy plugin executes the main list; when a task returns failure for a host, the executor marks the host as "in rescue" for that block, discards the rest of the block's main tasks for that host, and executes the rescue list with the failure details available as variables. After rescue (or without it), always runs. If rescue succeeded, the host's failed state is cleared for the enclosing scope and the recap increments rescued. Because state is tracked per host, one host can be in rescue while others complete the block normally, and under the linear strategy the rescue and always tasks are scheduled at their natural position, so hosts may wait at the next task boundary for each other.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using ignore_errors to silence a problem instead of deciding what failure means.
  • Rescue blocks that assume a particular failure point.
  • A rescued run treated as success by the pipeline.
  • Forgetting always for cleanup of locks and temp files.
  • Failing in rescue with no log of the original error.
  • Not using any_errors_fatal for steps that must be all-or-nothing.
  • Relying on failed_when strings that vary between tool versions.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the block/rescue/always sequence and change the failing task to succeed; note which sections run.
  2. Add any_errors_fatal: true to a two-host play where one host fails, and observe the difference.
  3. Write a deploy block whose rescue restores a backed-up file and then fails the host so CI turns red.
  4. Use failed_when to treat a command that returns 1 for "nothing to do" as success, and test both outcomes.

docs.title: 05 · Ansible Vault and Secrets
docs.text:
Playbooks need secrets: database passwords, API tokens, private keys. Committing them in plain text is a breach waiting to happen. Ansible Vault encrypts files or individual values so they can live in version control, and decrypts them in memory at run time.

What was run

Every command below was run with ansible-vault and ansible-playbook from ansible-core 2.21.5, with real encryption. The passwords used (correct-horse) and secrets (s3cr3t-value) are throwaway examples. External secret managers (HashiCorp Vault, cloud KMS) were not used; Level 4 · 03 describes them.

docs.title: Encrypting a file
docs.text:
$ ansible-vault encrypt secrets.yml --vault-password-file .pw
$ head -c 120 secrets.yml
$ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
66356235386462613565353263663334363165303233323565616465323762383430316330313338
...
$ ansible-vault view secrets.yml --vault-password-file .pw
db_password: s3cr3t-value
api_key: abc123

The file now starts with a header ($ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256) followed by hex-encoded ciphertext, 7 lines for this two-line file. It is safe to commit. view decrypts to the terminal; edit opens it in $EDITOR and re-encrypts on save; decrypt writes plain text (careful: it overwrites the file unless you use --output). The documented cipher is AES-256 in counter mode with an HMAC for integrity, with a key derived from your password by PBKDF2 and a random salt; I did not audit this and describe it from the documentation.

Same plaintext, different ciphertext. Encrypting the identical content twice with the same password gave different files (I compared them with cmp). The random salt means you cannot tell whether two secrets are equal, and that every re-encryption is a full-file change in Git, even when only one value changed: reviewing a vaulted file's diff tells you nothing about what changed. Convention: keep vaulted files small and separate from non-secret variables.

docs.title: Wrong or missing password
docs.text:
• No vault secret supplied when a play needs one: Invalid vars_files file ...: Attempting to decrypt but no vault secrets found. and the play does not start.
  • A wrong password: Decryption failed (no vault secrets were found that could decrypt).
  • Rekeying changes the password without changing contents: ansible-vault rekey a.yml --vault-password-file .pw --new-vault-password-file .bad printed Rekey successful, and the file then opened only with the new password.

Note that vault errors happen at load time, so a missing password is caught immediately, before any host is touched.

docs.title: Encrypting a single value
docs.text:
Instead of encrypting a whole file you can embed an encrypted value in a normal variables file:

$ ansible-vault encrypt_string 's3cr3t-value' --name db_password --vault-password-file .pw
db_password: !vault |
          $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.1;AES256
          66653235626435393734656233656461...

This keeps non-secret variables readable and diff-friendly, and only the secret is opaque. Both styles are common. The trade-off: with encrypt_string the names of secrets are visible in the file, which can be useful (reviewers see which secrets exist) or undesirable. Many teams use the pattern group_vars/db/vars.yml (plain, references db_password: "{{ vault_db_password }}") plus group_vars/db/vault.yml (encrypted, defines vault_db_password). That keeps variable names greppable while the values stay encrypted.

docs.title: Using vaulted data in a play
docs.text:
vars_files: [a.yml] with --vault-password-file .pw loaded the secret into db_password. Things to know, from the experiment:

  • A task that prints the variable leaks it. debug: msg="pw={{ db_password }}" printed pw=s3cr3t-value in the output. Vault protects data at rest, not in output.
  • no_log: true hides a task's results. A failing command with no_log: true printed only {"censored": "the output has been hidden due to the fact that 'no_log: true' was specified for this result", "changed": true}. Without no_log, a failing command whose arguments contain the secret would print the command line, including the secret. Put no_log: true on any task that handles secrets (copy/template of key material, uri with tokens, user with passwords). It also hides useful error details, so debug without it in a safe environment.
  • Secrets in -vvv output, --diff output and retained logs. --diff prints file contents for template/copy unless diff: false or no_log: true.
  • Secrets on the target. copy with a secret creates a file with whatever mode you give it: set mode: "0600" and the right owner (I did). Tools that read secrets from process arguments leak them to ps.
  • Check mode and handlers do not change any of this.

docs.title: Providing the password
docs.text:
Options, from least to most careful:

  1. --ask-vault-pass: prompts interactively; fine for people, impossible for CI.
  2. --vault-password-file path: a file containing the password (keep it out of Git, mode 0600). A file that is executable is run and its stdout is used as the password, so you can fetch it from a secret manager or keychain.
  3. The ANSIBLE_VAULT_PASSWORD_FILE environment variable or the config file setting.
  4. In CI, a pipeline secret written to a temporary file for the run, or an executable script that reads it from the CI system's environment.

Never put the password in the repository next to the vault. Rotate it when someone with access leaves (rekey all files) and treat the vault password as the single most sensitive value.

docs.title: Vault IDs
docs.text:
Different secrets often need different passwords (dev vs prod). --vault-id label@source supports several:

$ ansible-vault encrypt_string --vault-id prod@.pw 'x' --name k
k: !vault |
          $ANSIBLE_VAULT;1.2;AES256;prod

The header becomes version 1.2 and includes the label (prod), so Ansible can pick the right password among several supplied with multiple --vault-id options. Without labels it tries all supplied passwords in order, which is slower and ambiguous.

docs.title: What Vault does not do
docs.text:
• It does not hide secrets from anyone who can run the playbook with the password: they can debug the variable. Authorisation is controlled by who gets the password.
  • It does not provide rotation, audit trails, dynamic or short-lived secrets, or per-secret access control. Those need a secrets manager (Level 4 · 03).
  • It does not protect the control node's memory or logs, and the target machine sees the decrypted value.
  • Git history keeps old ciphertexts. If the vault password was ever exposed, every previous version of the file is readable by the attacker, so you must change the secrets themselves, not just rekey.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The vault file format is text: a header line carrying the format version, cipher and optional label, then hex of an encrypted payload that itself contains a salt, an HMAC and the ciphertext. To decrypt, Ansible derives keys from the password and salt with PBKDF2, verifies the HMAC (which is why a wrong password fails cleanly rather than yielding garbage), and decrypts. Loading a vaulted vars_files entry or an inline !vault value happens in the controller's variable loader; the decrypted text is then parsed as YAML and merged like any other variable. For encrypt_string, the value is stored as a custom YAML tag (!vault), which the loader decrypts lazily when the variable is first used. Since decryption happens on the controller, the target never sees the vault password, only the decrypted values sent to modules.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Committing .vault_pass or leaving it world-readable.
  • Printing secrets with debug, -vvv or --diff.
  • Missing no_log on secret-handling tasks.
  • Rekeying after a leak and assuming old secrets are safe.
  • Encrypting a huge file so every change is an unreviewable diff.
  • One vault password for everything, including dev contributors and production.
  • No procedure for rotating the vault password and the secrets.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Encrypt a file, view it, edit it, rekey it, and confirm the old password no longer works. Commit the encrypted file to a scratch Git repository and look at the diff after changing one value.
  2. Write a play that uses a vaulted variable in a copy with mode: "0600" and no_log: true; verify the output shows no secret even with -v.
  3. Set up the vars.yml + vault.yml split for a database password and show that grep -r db_password finds the usage.
  4. Write a short rotation procedure for your vault password: who is told, in what order files are rekeyed, and how you verify nothing still uses the old one.

docs.title: 06 · Collections, Galaxy and Dependencies
docs.text:
ansible-core is deliberately small: it contains the engine and the ansible.builtin modules and plugins. Everything else (cloud providers, databases, network vendors, utilities) is distributed as collections, versioned packages of modules, plugins, roles and documentation. Managing collections is managing your automation's dependencies.

What was run

On this install ansible-galaxy collection list found no collections (only the built-ins that live inside ansible-core). I installed ansible.utils 6.1.1 from Galaxy into a project directory with ansible-galaxy collection install ansible.utils -p ./collections, which took about 9 seconds, and used its filters and tests. The larger ansible community package (which bundles many collections) was not installed. Network access to Galaxy worked in this environment; yours may be proxied or offline.

docs.title: What is in ansible-core
docs.text: ansible-doc -l listed 71 modules on this install: all ansible.builtin (file, copy, template, command, debug, assert, uri, get_url, user, service ...). Anything else needs a collection. The community-maintained ansible package is a convenience bundle that installs ansible-core plus many collections; production setups usually install only the collections they use, pinned.

docs.title: Naming: namespace.collection.plugin
docs.text:
A fully qualified collection name has three parts: ansible.utils.ipaddr is the filter ipaddr in the collection utils of the namespace ansible. Modules, filters, tests, lookups, callbacks and inventory plugins are all addressed this way. With FQCNs there is no ambiguity about which implementation runs, which matters because two collections can ship a module with the same short name.

Resolution failures give precise messages (all real):

couldn't resolve module/action 'nosuch.collection.thing'. This often indicates a misspelling, missing collection, or incorrect module path.
No filter named 'ansible.utils.nonexistent'.
No test named 'ansible.utils.ip'.      # collection not installed (before I installed it)

An unknown module/action aborts the whole play at load time (ignore_errors does not help, because it is a parse-time error), while an unknown filter or test fails only when the task is templated, as an ordinary task failure.

docs.title: Where collections live
docs.text:
Ansible searches collections_paths (the ANSIBLE_COLLECTIONS_PATH environment variable or ansible.cfg), a list of directories each containing ansible_collections/<namespace>/<name>/. Installing with -p ./collections creates ./collections/ansible_collections/ansible/utils. Per-project collection directories are good practice: the project carries its dependencies and does not depend on whatever happens to be installed in a user's home directory. With ANSIBLE_COLLECTIONS_PATH=./collections the earlier collection list showed:

# .../collections/ansible_collections
Collection    Version
ansible.utils 6.1.1

docs.title: requirements.yml
docs.text:
Declare dependencies in a file and install them in one command:

---
collections:
  - name: ansible.utils
    version: ">=6.0.0,<7.0.0"
  - name: community.general
    version: "11.0.0"
roles:
  - name: some.role
    version: v1.2.3

ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml -p ./collections installs them. Choices that matter:

  • Pin versions, or at least a major range. An unpinned install gets whatever is latest, so a pipeline can break with no commit on your side. A fully reproducible setup pins exact versions and updates them deliberately (a bot or a scheduled task).
  • Pin ansible-core too (in requirements.txt for pip): collections declare a minimum ansible-core version, and upgrades of core change behaviour (this course found when: with a string failing on 2.21.5).
  • Python dependencies of plugins (netaddr for ipaddr, jmespath for json_query, cloud SDKs) are not installed by ansible-galaxy. Put them in requirements.txt (and in the execution environment, Level 4 · 01). I had to pip install netaddr before the IP filters worked.
  • Trust. A collection is code that runs on your controller and, as modules, on your targets. Install from sources you trust, review release notes, and consider an internal Galaxy/Automation Hub mirror. A typosquatted collection name is a supply-chain risk (CI/CD course, Level 3 · 08).

docs.title: Roles from Galaxy and from Git
docs.text: Roles can be installed with ansible-galaxy role install -r requirements.yml into roles_path, from Galaxy names or Git URLs (src: https://...git, version: <tag or commit>). Pin to a tag or commit SHA. Consider vendoring the role into your repository when it is small and you need to review every line.

docs.title: Building your own collection
docs.text: When roles, modules and plugins are shared across projects, package them as a collection: ansible-galaxy collection init mycompany.platform creates the skeleton (galaxy.yml, roles/, plugins/modules/, plugins/filter/, docs/), ansible-galaxy collection build makes a tarball, and install accepts a path or a tarball. Use semantic versioning and a changelog, tested in CI, and publish to a private repository. Level 3 builds a custom module and a plugin; they can be dropped into such a collection unchanged.

docs.title: Using collections in playbooks
docs.text: A play can set a search order with collections: (so you may write short names), but that reintroduces ambiguity; this course and ansible-lint prefer FQCNs everywhere. Lint flagged short names in the bad example in Lesson 09: fqcn[action-core]: Use FQCN for builtin module actions (shell).

docs.title: Reproducibility checklist
docs.text:
1. requirements.txt with pinned ansible-core and Python libraries.
  2. requirements.yml with pinned collections and roles.
  3. A documented bootstrap command (or a container image, Level 4 · 01).
  4. The same versions in CI as on workstations.
  5. A scheduled job that tries the latest versions in a branch, so upgrades are discovered before they are forced.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The plugin loader keeps a mapping from FQCN to files discovered by scanning each directory in collections_paths for ansible_collections/<ns>/<name>/plugins/<type>/. When a task names ansible.utils.ipaddr, the loader finds the collection, imports the plugin file, and caches the loaded plugin. Each collection can include a meta/runtime.yml with redirects and deprecations (a module renamed between collections keeps working through a redirect for a while, printing a deprecation warning), and requires_ansible to state compatible core versions. For module plugins, the controller packages the module file with Ansiballz, a self-extracting zip containing the module and its Python helpers from ansible.module_utils, and ships it to the target, which is why a collection's modules do not have to be pre-installed on the managed hosts.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unpinned collections and core, so builds change on their own.
  • Forgetting the Python dependency of a filter or module.
  • Installing into the user's home and relying on it silently.
  • Short module names that resolve differently once a collection is added.
  • Treating a collection as trusted because it is on Galaxy.
  • Not testing upgrades.
  • A missing collection discovered mid-pipeline, not at the start; install and ansible-doc check first.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Install ansible.utils into a project directory with -p, point ANSIBLE_COLLECTIONS_PATH at it, and run an ipaddr filter. Then unset the variable and read the error.
  2. Write a requirements.yml for your project with pinned versions and a bootstrap script that installs it and checks ansible-doc for one module from each collection.
  3. Create a collection skeleton with ansible-galaxy collection init and move one role into it. Run it with its FQCN.
  4. Write the upgrade procedure for ansible-core in your environment: branch, install, run the test suite, compare lint output, roll forward.

docs.title: 07 · Tags, Limits and Targeting
docs.text:
A playbook that configures a whole fleet is the wrong thing to run when you want to change one setting on one host. Ansible gives you three ways to narrow a run: tags (which tasks), limits (which hosts) and check mode (whether to change anything). Used well they make a large playbook safe to run; used carelessly they cause partial, inconsistent states.

What was run

The tag and limit results below were produced by a real run of src/l2/tags.yml against two local hosts, and the exit-status checks come from the shell. Behaviour is for ansible-core 2.21.5.

docs.title: Tags: which tasks run
docs.text:
tasks:
  - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "install"}
    tags: [install, setup]
  - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "configure"}
    tags: [configure, setup]
  - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "always runs"}
    tags: [always]
  - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "never unless asked"}
    tags: [never, debug_only]
  - ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "untagged"}

Measured results (messages printed on host w1):

Command Tasks that ran (no options) install, configure, always runs, untagged --tags configure configure, always runs --skip-tags setup always runs, untagged --tags debug_only always runs, never unless asked --tags nonexistent always runs --tags setup --skip-tags configure install, always runs

Rules shown by the table:

  • No options runs untagged and tagged tasks alike, except tasks tagged never.
  • --tags X runs only tasks with tag X, so untagged tasks do not run; this is a frequent surprise when you tag only some tasks.
  • always tasks run regardless of --tags (not if you --skip-tags always). Use it for tasks other tasks depend on, such as loading variables or fact gathering helpers.
  • never tasks are excluded unless you explicitly select another tag they carry. Good for destructive or diagnostic tasks.
  • --skip-tags wins over --tags when both match the same task.
  • A task selected by tag still has its when: evaluated.
  • --list-tags shows the tag set: [always, configure, debug_only, install, never, setup].

docs.title: Tag hygiene
docs.text:
Tags are easy to misuse. A tag selects a task but does not include its dependencies: --tags configure skips an earlier install task. If configure needs a variable set by an untagged task earlier, it will fail in an odd way. Keep tagged tasks independent, or tag the prerequisite always. For roles, tags set on the role entry apply to all of the role's tasks; import_role tags are inherited statically; include_role needs apply: {tags: ...}. Use a small, documented vocabulary (packages, config, service, users) rather than a tag per task.

Do not make tags a substitute for structure. A playbook that has to be run with the right tags to work is a playbook that should be split into several playbooks or roles.

docs.title: Limits: which hosts run
docs.text:
--limit narrows the hosts of every play to an intersection with the given pattern:

  • --limit w1 or -l w1: one host.
  • --limit 'web:!w2': pattern expression (Lesson 03).
  • --limit @hosts.txt: hosts listed one per line in a file. Running with --limit @lim.txt (containing w2) executed on w2 only: ok: [w2].
  • --limit nope (matches nothing): printed Specified inventory, host pattern and/or --limit leaves us with no hosts to target. and exited with status 1. This is different from a play whose hosts: matches nothing, which exits 0 (Level 1 · 03). A --limit that leaves nothing is treated as an error, which is the safer behaviour.

--limit with serial and run_once interacts: run_once runs on the first host of the limited set, so limiting can change which host performs the one-time action. Test that if you rely on it.

A very common operational workflow:

  1. ansible-playbook site.yml --limit canary --check --diff to preview.
  2. ansible-playbook site.yml --limit canary to apply to a canary host or group.
  3. Verify (smoke tests, monitoring).
  4. ansible-playbook site.yml --limit 'prod:!canary' for the rest, perhaps in batches with serial (Lesson 08).

docs.title: --check, --diff, --step, --start-at-task
docs.text:
Check mode (Level 1 · 05) combines with limits and tags for targeted previews: --tags config --limit web --check --diff answers "what would a config change do to the web hosts?" without touching anything. Be aware of the caveat from Level 1: tasks that depend on earlier tasks' real effects (a package install) can mislead a check run that skips them.

--step prompts before each task. --start-at-task resumes at a named task but skips the earlier ones, which broke the sandbox setup in Level 1 · 09.

docs.title: Variables that depend on the run
docs.text:
Magic variables expose the selection: ansible_run_tags, ansible_skip_tags, ansible_limit, ansible_check_mode, ansible_play_hosts, ansible_play_batch. You can make playbooks refuse to run unsafely:

- ansible.builtin.assert:
    that: ansible_limit is defined
    fail_msg: "Refusing to run against production without --limit. Use --limit canary first."
  run_once: true
  when: "'production' in group_names"

Guard rails like this are cheap; the cost is a little friction. I checked the variables: with no options ansible_limit was undefined (so is defined works as a test), ansible_run_tags was ['all'], ansible_skip_tags was [] and ansible_check_mode was False; with --limit n2 --tags all --skip-tags x --check they were n2, ['all'], ['x'] and True. The assert guard itself was not run.

docs.title: Separate playbooks vs tags
docs.text: A playbook per operation (site.yml, deploy.yml, rotate-keys.yml, patch.yml) is easier to understand and review than one giant playbook with twenty tags. Use tags for modest sub-selection inside a playbook. Build an index (a README or Makefile targets) of the commands people should run, so operators do not invent their own tag combinations.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Tag selection is applied when the play's task list is compiled for execution: each task has a set of tags (its own plus those inherited from blocks, roles and play), and the engine keeps a task if the run's tag filter says so. always and never are special tags handled in that filter. Limits are applied earlier, when the play's host pattern is evaluated: the effective host list is the intersection of the pattern and the limit. If the intersection is empty and a limit was given, the CLI aborts with the error shown above; if the pattern alone matched nothing, the play is skipped. The restriction is applied on the controller, so tasks excluded by tags or limits never reach a target and no connection is made to hosts outside the limit (which is one reason limits are also a performance tool).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting --tags to run untagged setup tasks.
  • Tagged tasks with hidden dependencies on untagged ones.
  • --limit forgotten, so production is changed along with the intended host.
  • Different behaviour assumed between an empty hosts: match and an empty --limit.
  • Tags that mean different things in different roles.
  • Using tags where separate playbooks would be clearer.
  • No guard rails against running on production without limits.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the table with your own playbook and add a --tags combination you have not seen; predict the result first.
  2. Show that --limit with a typo exits non-zero and that a hosts: typo does not; add a CI pre-step that catches both.
  3. Write a guard-rail assertion that fails when the play would touch more than five hosts without an explicit -e confirm=yes.
  4. Convert a tag-heavy playbook into three smaller playbooks and a Makefile with the commands operators should run.

docs.title: 08 · Delegation, Serial Batches and Strategies
docs.text:
Some tasks must run on a different machine from the one being configured (take a host out of a load balancer, register it in a monitoring system). Some must happen only once for the whole group. Some must proceed in small batches so a mistake does not take everything down. Ansible provides delegate_to, run_once, serial, and execution strategies for these.

What was run

Four local hosts n1..n4 (ansible_connection=local) and the playbooks serial.yml, deleg.yml and strat.yml in src/l2, run with ansible-core 2.21.5. Real load balancers, rolling restarts of services and SSH delegation were not exercised.

docs.title: delegate_to
docs.text:
delegate_to: host runs the task on another host while keeping the variable context of the original one. A typical use:

- name: remove this host from the load balancer
  ansible.builtin.uri: {url: "http://lb.example/api/drain/{{ inventory_hostname }}", method: POST}
  delegate_to: lb1

Each web host triggers one call from lb1's side (or localhost to call an API from the controller), and {{ inventory_hostname }} is still the web host. The task's own connection settings come from the delegated host. In my test, a delegated command ran on n4 for each of four hosts; the output was the right messages with all four hosts' names.

Gotchas:

  • ansible_delegated_vars exists only inside the delegated task's context. I referenced ansible_delegated_vars['n4'] from a later, ordinary debug task and got 'ansible_delegated_vars' is undefined. To use delegated host data later, register the result or use hostvars['n4'].
  • Facts gathered during a delegated task are assigned to the delegated host only with delegate_facts: true; otherwise they attach to the original host.
  • command is not a shell. My delegated command used $(basename $PWD) and printed it literally (registering n1 from $(basename /Users/.../l2)): the command module does not run a shell, so $() is not evaluated. Use shell when you need substitution (and then own the idempotency and quoting).
  • Parallel delegated tasks against one host can race: all four hosts ran the delegated task on n4 at once. If the delegated action is not safe to run concurrently (editing one file), use serial: 1 or a throttle.

docs.title: run_once
docs.text:
- ansible.builtin.debug: {msg: "run_once ran for {{ inventory_hostname }}"}
  run_once: true

Printed run_once ran for n1: the task ran on the first host of the play batch only. Its result is copied to the other hosts' variable context, so a set_fact with run_once is visible everywhere: my token variable showed the same value (tok12839) on n1..n4. Typical uses: database migrations (once per cluster), sending one notification, creating one shared resource. Warnings:

  • With serial, run_once runs once per batch, not once overall. Combine carefully (when: inventory_hostname == ansible_play_hosts_all[0] is the explicit alternative).
  • It runs on the first host, so if you --limit the run, the first limited host does the work.
  • If the first host fails the task, the whole group is treated as failed for that task.

docs.title: serial: rolling batches
docs.text:
serial: 2 on four hosts ran the entire play in two passes: first n1+n2 for all tasks (A and B), then n3+n4:

PLAY [app]  A on n1  A on n2  B on n1  B on n2
PLAY [app]  A on n3  A on n4  B on n3  B on n4

serial also accepts a percentage ("25%") or a list for a ramp ([1, 3, "100%"]): one host as a canary, then three, then everyone. Batches are the basic mechanism of a rolling update (Level 3 · 07).

docs.title: Failure budgets
docs.text:
max_fail_percentage stops the play if too large a share of a batch fails. Measured on four hosts with a task that fails on chosen hosts:

Setting Failing hosts Result serial: 1, default (0%) n1 n1 failed; n2..n4 never ran (the play aborted) serial: 2, max_fail_percentage: 50 n1 (1 of 2 = 50%) batch continued; n2 finished; n3 and n4 ran serial: 2, max_fail_percentage: 50 n1 and n2 (100% > 50%) play aborted; n3 and n4 never ran

Two details to remember: the threshold is "strictly more than" (50% failures of a batch of two does not abort at 50), and with the default of 0 any failure in a batch stops later batches. With serial: 1 and a default budget, one bad host protects the rest of the fleet, which is the point: a broken change is stopped after one machine. any_errors_fatal: true is the stricter setting (stop everything on the first failure, even within a batch).

docs.title: Strategies
docs.text:
The strategy: keyword selects how tasks are scheduled across hosts:

  • linear (default): every host finishes task N before any host starts N+1.
  • free: each host runs through the tasks as fast as it can.
  • host_pinned and debug exist for special cases (not run).

Measured: host n1 sleeps 2 seconds on task 1, the others 0; the second task prints the seconds of the clock.

linear: second task on n1, n2, n3, n4 all at :45   total ~2.96 s
free:   n4, n2, n3 at :46; n1 at :48               total ~2.99 s

Under linear the fast hosts waited for n1 and all printed the same second. Under free they ran ahead by two seconds. Total time was the same here (the slow host dominates in both), but free helps when tasks take very different times per host and later tasks do not depend on other hosts. Output ordering under free is non-deterministic, and tasks that expect other hosts to be at the same point (a "wait until everyone is done" step) break.

docs.title: throttle and forks
docs.text: throttle: 1 on a task limits it to one host at a time without changing the rest of the play (useful for a step that hits a rate-limited API). forks (-f, default 5) caps how many hosts run a task concurrently across the whole run. A play on 100 hosts with forks=5 takes at least 20 rounds per task (Level 3 · 06 measures fork effects).

docs.title: Orchestrating a rolling change
docs.text:
A common structure for a service update:

- hosts: web
  serial: [1, "25%", "100%"]
  max_fail_percentage: 0
  tasks:
    - ansible.builtin.include_tasks: drain.yml        # delegate_to: lb
    - ansible.builtin.include_role: {name: webapp}
    - ansible.builtin.include_tasks: smoke_test.yml   # fail the batch if unhealthy
    - ansible.builtin.include_tasks: undrain.yml

One canary host, a quarter of the fleet, then everyone; any failure stops the rollout. This is the CI/CD course's rolling and canary ideas (Level 3 · 01) applied with Ansible primitives.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: serial makes the play executor split the matching host list into batches and run the whole task list for each batch in turn, re-evaluating the play for each (including run_once and handlers per batch). delegate_to changes only the connection: the task's templated arguments use the original host's variables, but the executor opens (or reuses) a connection to the delegated target. run_once selects the first host in the current batch and runs the task there, then copies the result to the others through register/set_fact machinery. The linear strategy is a loop that sends task N to all hosts' workers and waits for all results before proceeding; free gives each host's worker its own iterator over the task list. max_fail_percentage is evaluated after each batch finishes a task, against the number of hosts in the batch.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• run_once with serial and expecting one run in total.
  • Delegated tasks racing on a shared target.
  • Using ansible_delegated_vars outside the delegated task.
  • Assuming command evaluates shell syntax.
  • No failure budget on a rolling change, so a bad change reaches the whole fleet.
  • free strategy with cross-host dependencies.
  • Draining and undraining in separate plays so a failure leaves a host out of rotation; wrap in block with always.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the serial and max_fail_percentage table on four local hosts and add a case with serial: [1, 3].
  2. Write a play that gets a token with run_once and delegate_to: localhost, stores it with set_fact, and uses it on every host. Run it with --limit for two hosts and note who performs the run_once.
  3. Make a task slow on one host and compare the wall-clock time of linear and free with 8 hosts and forks=3.
  4. Add a drain/undrain pair to a rolling play so the host is always put back, even when the middle task fails.

docs.title: 09 · Testing and Linting Ansible
docs.text:
Infrastructure code deserves tests as much as application code. Fortunately Ansible has a testing ladder, from instant static checks to full runs in disposable environments. This lesson works up the ladder with real runs and says where each rung stops being informative.

What was run

ansible-lint and ansible-playbook (syntax checks, repeated runs, check mode) were run for real, ansible-core 2.21.5 and ansible-lint from the same venv. Molecule (the usual role testing framework) and container-based testing were not run (no container runtime). Findings are copied from an actual lint run on a deliberately bad playbook.

docs.title: Rung 1: syntax check
docs.text: ansible-playbook --syntax-check site.yml parses the playbook without connecting. It catches YAML and structural errors (Level 1 · 04), not undefined variables or wrong arguments. It is instant; run it everywhere, including editor hooks.

docs.title: Rung 2: ansible-lint
docs.text:
ansible-lint applies a catalogue of rules. On this playbook:

- hosts: all
  tasks:
    - shell: echo hello > /tmp/x
    - name: copy file
      copy: src=a dest=/tmp/a mode=0644
    - command: mkdir /tmp/foo
    - name: Ensure latest
      package: name=foo state=latest

it reported 13 violations and failed, summarised as:

Rule Count Meaning fqcn 4 Use ansible.builtin.shell, not shell name (missing/casing/play) 4 Name plays and tasks, start names uppercase no-changed-when 2 command/shell without changed_when (breaks idempotency reporting, Level 1 · 05) no-free-form 2 Avoid copy: src=a dest=b free-form arguments package-latest 1 state: latest makes runs non-reproducible

Each message gives the rule, the file and line, and a suggested fix. The corrected playbook:

---
- name: Example
  hosts: all
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - name: Create directory
      ansible.builtin.file:
        path: /tmp/foo
        state: directory
        mode: "0755"

passed with Last profile that met the validation criteria was 'production'. ansible-lint has profiles (min, basic, moderate, safety, shared, production) in increasing strictness; the output tells you the highest your content satisfies. Start by getting to basic, then raise the bar.

Linting my own role was instructive: the first run of ansible-lint roles/webapp failed on meta/main.yml because galaxy_info.min_ansible_version was the number 2.2 instead of a string (YAML parsed 2.2 as a float), plus sample metadata left by galaxy init and two YAML formatting issues. After fixing them the production profile passed. The scaffold created by ansible-galaxy role init does not pass lint without editing.

Lint cannot know whether your logic is right. It is fast, deterministic and finds a lot, so run it on every pull request, with a project config (.ansible-lint) that documents any disabled rules and the reason. It needs to be pinned like any dependency, because a new version adds rules that suddenly fail old code.

docs.title: Rung 3: idempotence and check mode on a real run
docs.text:
The cheapest dynamic test: apply twice and assert changed=0 on the second run. Add a check-mode run after the apply and assert changed=0 too. The Level 1 baseline project does this with pytest calling the real ansible-playbook (8 tests, 53 s), and the Level 2 role project does it (below). It requires a target to apply to:

  • localhost with connection: local and a sandbox directory (as in this course) is good for file, template and variable logic.
  • Containers are good for package and file logic across distributions; start from the distribution image, run the playbook, run it again, and run assertions. Not for systemd, kernel parameters or anything needing a real init system.
  • Virtual machines (Vagrant, cloud instances created in CI) are slower but test the real thing, including services and reboots.

Molecule automates this: it creates instances, runs converge (your role), idempotence (second run must report no changes), and verify (assertions with Ansible, Testinfra or other), then destroys the instances. I describe it from its documentation and did not run it. The test strategy it embodies is exactly the one you can build with pytest and subprocess.

docs.title: Rung 4: assertions about the result
docs.text:
Check the state, not just the exit code:

- name: Verify config
  ansible.builtin.stat: {path: /etc/app/app.conf}
  register: st
- ansible.builtin.assert:
    that: [st.stat.exists, st.stat.mode == "0644"]

Put such verification tasks in a separate playbook (verify.yml) so they can be run against production as a read-only audit (Level 4 · 06), or use a dedicated testing library to check ports, services and packages.

docs.title: Rung 5: negative tests
docs.text: Test that invalid input fails and that failure is clean. In the role project, webapp_port=70000 and webapp_workers=0 both failed before changing anything (the sandbox directory did not exist afterwards). Test the guard rails; they are the most valuable and least exercised code.

docs.title: Test the right thing at the right cost
docs.text:
Rung Catches Time Needs Syntax check YAML/structure ms nothing Lint Style, risky patterns, FQCN, naming seconds ansible-lint Check mode on real hosts Drift, wrong values seconds-minutes a target Converge + idempotence Non-idempotent tasks, ordering minutes disposable target Verify assertions Wrong end state minutes disposable target Integration across roles/hosts Cross-host ordering, real services many minutes VMs / test fleet

Run the cheap rungs on every commit and the expensive ones on pull requests or nightly. A common trap is skipping the expensive rungs because they are slow; keep one fast converge+idempotence test per role and let the slow ones run less often.

docs.title: Testing the playbooks that call roles
docs.text: Test roles in isolation (each role with its own converge playbook and tests) and the integrated playbook in a staging environment. For variables, test the defaults and each documented override. For templates, render them in a test and compare the output to a golden file where the output is stable.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: ansible-lint loads each file with Ansible's own parsers (so it needs a working Ansible install), builds a normalised representation of plays, tasks and roles, and runs each rule class over it. Rules are Python classes tagged with identifiers (fqcn[action-core], no-changed-when); the profile is a set of rules that must pass. Because it uses the real parser it sees through includes and imports to some extent, but it cannot evaluate templates or know variable values. The dynamic tests rely on the contract of modules (Level 1 · 05): a module reports changed: false when no change was needed, so changed=0 in the recap is a machine-checkable statement about convergence. That contract is also the limit of the test: a module that lies about changed makes the test meaningless, which is why changed_when on commands matters.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No lint at all, or lint with half the rules turned off and no record why.
  • Unpinned lint version whose new rules break builds without a code change.
  • Testing only on the first run.
  • Treating a container test as proof for service or kernel behaviour.
  • Tests that share state across cases.
  • No negative tests for input validation.
  • Never running the verify step against production as a read-only audit.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run ansible-lint on one of your playbooks and fix everything until it passes the production profile. Note which rule took longest to satisfy.
  2. Write a pytest that applies a role twice in a temporary directory and asserts changed=0 the second time, then add a check-mode assertion.
  3. Add a negative test that proves an invalid variable value fails before any change.
  4. Draft a CI job for a roles repository: which rungs run on every push, which nightly, and what environment each needs.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Tested Role
docs.text:
This project turns the Level 2 ideas into a small, finished artefact: a role with a documented interface, validation, a handler, and a test suite that proves it behaves. The tests run the real ansible-playbook against local hosts and the real ansible-lint.

What was run, and what wasn't

The role is src/l2/roles/webapp; the tests are src/l2/test_role.py (9 tests, all passed, 16 seconds) and run on a Mac with ansible-core 2.21.5 and ansible-lint in the same virtual environment. They run two inventory hosts with ansible_connection=local; the role manages a config file and directory, so nothing about packages, services or privilege escalation is tested. The suite was written after the role and one assumption in it was wrong (below), which is reported rather than hidden.

docs.title: The role
docs.text:
• Interface (defaults/main.yml): webapp_port (8080), webapp_workers (2), webapp_root (a per-host directory under a sandbox, derived from inventory_hostname so two hosts never share a file).
  • Internal constant (vars/main.yml): webapp_config_mode: "0644".
  • Tasks: validate (assert on port range 1..65535 and workers >= 1, quiet: true), create the directory (0755), render webapp.conf from a template (mode from the constant) and notify: Reload webapp.
  • Handler: Reload webapp (a debug message standing in for a service reload).
  • Docs: a README with a table of variables, defaults and meanings. meta/main.yml has real metadata (author, license, a string min_ansible_version, platform list).

docs.title: The tests
docs.text:
Test Asserts defaults and per-host override w1 file has port=8080; w2, with host var webapp_port=9000, has port=9000 role parameter overrides default vars: {webapp_workers: 7} produces workers=7 idempotent second run: exit 0 and changed=0 for every host handler fires only on change first run: exactly one RUNNING HANDLER; second run: none invalid port fails before changing anything webapp_port=70000: non-zero exit, the message webapp_port must be ... appears, and the output directory does not exist zero workers rejected webapp_workers=0: non-zero exit check mode writes nothing --check: exit 0, output directory not created role parameter beats vars/main.yml passing webapp_config_mode: "0600" yields a file with mode 0600 lint ansible-lint roles/webapp exits 0 (production profile)
