The harness writes an inventory in a temporary directory so each test is isolated, points ANSIBLE_ROLES_PATH at the role, sets ANSIBLE_HOME inside the project to keep temp files out of the real home directory, parses the PLAY RECAP, and skips itself if Ansible is not installed.

docs.title: The wrong assumption
docs.text: I first intended a test showing that vars/main.yml "protects" an internal constant from callers: pass webapp_config_mode: "0600" as a role parameter and expect 0644. I was not sure what would happen, so I wrote the assertion loosely (either value accepted) to see, then measured: the file ended up 0600. Role parameters outrank the role's own vars/main.yml, consistent with Ansible's documented precedence order, and consistent with the Lesson 02 experiment, which did not include role parameters (it covered vars/main.yml as source 5). The test now asserts the measured outcome and its comment says why. Takeaway: vars/main.yml is for constants that should not be overridden by accident (an inventory variable loses to it), not a security boundary against callers who pass role parameters or -e.

docs.title: Another finding: lint on the scaffold
docs.text: ansible-galaxy role init produces a role that fails ansible-lint: sample metadata and a numeric min_ansible_version: 2.2 that YAML reads as a float (schema[meta]: ... 2.2 is not of type 'string'). After editing meta/main.yml, removing the sample tests/ scaffold, and rewriting the tasks with FQCNs, names and quoted modes, the role passed the production profile.

docs.title: How to extend this role realistically
docs.text:
For a role that manages a real service, add (each is a Level 2/3 topic):

  1. A package task and a service task, with ansible_facts.os_family branching via include_vars for package names; test in containers for the files, in a VM for the service.
  2. validate: on the template to check the config before replacing the live file.
  3. A meta/argument_specs.yml describing the role's variables (types, required, choices): Ansible validates role arguments against it before running tasks, which replaces much of the hand-written assert and documents the interface in machine-readable form.
  4. Handlers that restart only when configuration changed, plus meta: flush_handlers before a health check.
  5. A verify.yml playbook that checks the end state and can run read-only against production.
  6. A changelog and version tags if you publish it to a collection (Lesson 06).

docs.title: Reading the results
docs.text: When all tests pass, you have evidence for these claims: the interface works as documented; invalid input is rejected before any change; repeated runs converge; handlers fire once per real change; check mode is safe; and the role meets the community lint profile. You do not have evidence that the managed service works, that permissions are right for a real service account, or that the role survives an upgrade of ansible-core. Those need a real target and a version matrix.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• The role's interface is defaults/main.yml and a README table, nothing else.
  • Inputs are validated before any change, and a test proves it.
  • Every host-specific path includes inventory_hostname.
  • The second run reports changed=0, and a test asserts it.
  • The handler fires only on a real change, and a test counts it.
  • Check mode writes nothing, and a test proves it.
  • ansible-lint passes the production profile in CI with a pinned version.
  • The role's tests run in under a minute so people run them.
  • Behaviour you were unsure of (precedence, defaults) is measured and pinned by a test.

docs.title: Running a subset
docs.text:
python3 -m pytest -q src/l2/test_role.py                      # the role suite (about 16 s)
python3 -m pytest -q src/l2/test_role.py -k "idempotent or handler"
python3 -m pytest -q src/l2/prec                              # the precedence experiment (a few runs of Ansible)

The tests skip themselves with a clear reason if ansible-playbook or ansible-lint is missing, so a plain pytest on a machine without them does not fail spuriously.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The tests are an outer loop around Ansible: each one builds a tiny project in a temp directory (an inventory file and a playbook that applies the role), invokes ansible-playbook as a subprocess, and inspects two things: the process's exit status and output, and the resulting files. Ansible's own contract provides the signals: changed counts in the recap (for idempotency), the RUNNING HANDLER marker (for handler behaviour), the exit status (for failure), and the filesystem (for effects). Because role loading is by name along ANSIBLE_ROLES_PATH, the test needs no copying of the role into each temp project, and because each project uses its own temporary sandbox directory, tests are independent and can run in any order.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing tests that only check the happy path.
  • Asserting what you hope is true about precedence instead of measuring it.
  • Sharing a sandbox across tests, causing order dependence.
  • Not running lint on generated scaffolds.
  • Treating vars/main.yml as unoverridable.
  • Skipping the second-run test.
  • Tests that are so slow nobody runs them; keep a fast subset.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run python3 -m pytest -q src/l2/test_role.py (with ansible-core and ansible-lint installed) and read each test.
  2. Add meta/argument_specs.yml for the role and remove the assert task; write a test that an invalid type is rejected.
  3. Add a webapp_enabled boolean that controls whether the config is rendered, with tests for both values and for a string "false" passed with -e.
  4. Add a second role webapp_logrotate and a playbook that applies both; test that applying both is idempotent and that each role's handler fires independently.

docs.title: Level 3 · Extending Ansible
docs.text:
Level 3 goes beyond using Ansible to extending and operating it: writing modules and plugins, building inventories from live sources, handling the awkward corners of command and shell, running long tasks, measuring performance, orchestrating rolling updates safely, and reasoning about state, drift and convergence.

What was run, and what wasn't

ansible-core 2.21.5 on a Mac, local connections only. Measured here: two custom modules (25 tests), three filters, a lookup and two forms of dynamic inventory (23 tests), command/shell pitfalls, async behaviour and messages, forks and fact-gathering timings on 20 local hosts, a rolling update over eight simulated servers (11 tests), and orphan/conflict/drift experiments. Not run: SSH and real network latency, pipelining, Windows and network devices (their collections were installed only to read documentation), Molecule, real cloud inventories, and Ansible's own ansible-test.

Prerequisites: Levels 1 and 2.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Writing a Custom Module: argument spec, check and diff modes, a pure core, 25 tests.
  2. Filter and Lookup Plugins: and the comma-join surprise of lookup().
  3. Dynamic Inventory: a script and a plugin producing identical inventories.
  4. Command and Shell Without Breaking Idempotency: injection, pipefail, argv, creates.
  5. Async Tasks and Polling: and the confusing message when a job outlives async.
  6. Performance: forks from 50 s to 4.5 s, and what fact gathering costs.
  7. Rolling Updates and Failure Budgets: and an always: section that defeated max_fail_percentage.
  8. State, Drift and Convergence: orphans, flip-flopping tasks, purge patterns.
  9. Network and Windows Targets: connection types and collections, read offline.
  10. Project: A Tested Custom Module: the capstone for the level.

docs.title: After Level 3
docs.text: Level 4 is operations: controllers and execution environments, Ansible in CI/CD, secrets at scale, pull mode, Terraform together with Ansible, a drift auditor built on check mode, automation incidents, migrating scripts and anti-patterns, governance, and a capstone managing a simulated fleet.

docs.title: 01 · Writing a Custom Module
docs.text:
When no module does what you need and command would be fragile, write a module. A module is a Python program that reads arguments, compares current and desired state, changes the system if needed, and prints a JSON result. Writing one yourself is also the best way to understand why built-in modules behave as they do.

What was run

Two modules were written and run with ansible-core 2.21.5 on a Mac: filehash (read-only) and kvfile (manages key=value lines, Lesson 10's project). Both were exercised standalone with a JSON argument file, through ansible-playbook, in check and diff mode, and by 25 pytest tests (all passed on the first run). Modules in other languages, Windows (PowerShell) modules, and modules shipped in a collection were not written.

docs.title: The minimum module
docs.text:
#!/usr/bin/python
from __future__ import annotations
from ansible.module_utils.basic import AnsibleModule
import hashlib, os

def main():
    module = AnsibleModule(
        argument_spec=dict(
            path=dict(type="path", required=True),
            algorithm=dict(type="str", default="sha256", choices=["sha256", "sha1", "md5"]),
        ),
        supports_check_mode=True,
    )
    path = module.params["path"]
    if not os.path.isfile(path):
        module.fail_json(msg="file not found or not a regular file: %s" % path, path=path)
    digest = hashlib.new(module.params["algorithm"], open(path, "rb").read()).hexdigest()
    module.exit_json(changed=False, digest=digest, size=os.path.getsize(path), path=path)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Place it in a library/ directory next to the playbook (or in a role's library/, or in a collection's plugins/modules/) and call it by name. In a playbook, with ANSIBLE_LIBRARY=./library:

- {name: hash, filehash: {path: ".../app.conf", algorithm: sha1}, register: h}
-> "7e4a5db2c83fccbca9c1eb994cbdbbd4a51e67d3 17"        # digest and byte size

The pieces:

  • AnsibleModule parses the arguments Ansible passes, validates them against argument_spec (types, required, choices, defaults, mutual exclusion, required_if), and gives you exit_json and fail_json.
  • module.params is the validated dictionary.
  • exit_json(**kwargs) prints the JSON result and exits; fail_json(msg=...) reports failure. Always include changed.
  • supports_check_mode=True declares that you handle module.check_mode correctly (do not change anything when it is true). A module that does not declare it is skipped in check mode.
  • Documentation goes in module-level strings: DOCUMENTATION, EXAMPLES, RETURN (YAML). ansible-doc -M library kvfile renders them (I ran it; the first lines show the description and options with types and defaults). Keep them accurate; ansible-test sanity (not run) checks them against the argument spec in the real Ansible project.

docs.title: Where the work happens
docs.text: The module runs on the target with the target's Python. It is shipped as a self-contained bundle with its dependencies from ansible.module_utils. Consequences: use only the standard library and module_utils unless you install other libraries on the target; the module cannot read files on the controller (that is what lookups do); and Python-version differences between targets matter (use from __future__ import annotations and avoid very new syntax if you support old targets).

docs.title: Design rules for a good module
docs.text:
1. Idempotent by construction. Compute the desired content/state from the current state; write only if different. kvfile builds the new file text in memory and compares it with the old text. Returning changed=True only when a write is needed is what makes check mode and drift audits honest.
  2. Pure core, thin shell. Put the decision logic in a pure function (kvfile.apply(lines, key, value, state) returns the new lines and before/after values). Test it with ordinary unit tests; keep I/O in main.
  3. Check mode. Compute changed and the diff as usual, skip the write when module.check_mode. In my module, --check on a file needing change reported changed and left it untouched (test passes).
  4. Diff mode. Return diff={"before": old, "after": new, "before_header": path, "after_header": path}; Ansible prints it under --diff. Real runs showed +workers=4 and so on.
  5. Validate input early and clearly. kvfile rejects keys that are not letters/digits/underscore/dot/dash (invalid key 'bad key') and values containing newlines (a newline in a value would let one setting inject another line). Fail with a message naming the problem. Do not build shell commands from user data.
  6. Use module_utils helpers where they exist: add_file_common_args=True plus set_fs_attributes_if_different gives mode, owner, group handling and reports a mode-only difference as a change (a test confirms a mode-only change is reported and applied). module.run_command() runs external programs safely (no shell by default).
  7. Atomic writes. Write to a temporary file in the same directory and os.replace it, so a crash never leaves a half-written file.
  8. Return useful data. before and after let playbooks and humans see what changed.
  9. Unknown arguments are errors. The argument spec rejects typos: a test passes valeu and gets Unsupported parameters.

docs.title: Testing a module
docs.text:
Three levels, all in test_modules.py:

  1. Unit tests of the pure function (10 cases): add missing key; replace value; unchanged input returns the same lines; remove; absent when missing is a no-op; comments and blank lines preserved; duplicates collapsed; spaces around =; empty file; a key that is a prefix of another is not confused (ab=1 vs a).
  2. Run the module as Ansible does: a JSON file {"ANSIBLE_MODULE_ARGS": {...}} passed as argv[1], executed with Python, output parsed. The tests cover create-then-idempotent, check mode leaves the file alone, diff content, mode setting, mode-only change, rejection of bad input (three parametrised cases), missing file without create, absent on a missing file, unknown argument, and filehash output and errors. Special keys such as _ansible_check_mode and _ansible_diff switch the modes.
  3. One real playbook run asserting changed=1 then changed=0.

Total: 25 tests, 2.6 seconds, all passed on the first run (after the code was written; I did not need to fix the tests). A fast, pure test suite like this is the reason to structure a module with a pure core.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Forgetting changed, so results are unreliable.
  • Doing work in check mode.
  • Not handling exists=False paths, crashing with a traceback; wrap I/O and use fail_json.
  • Printing to stdout other than the final JSON; stray prints corrupt the result. Use module.debug/module.warn or return data.
  • Relying on controller-side state; the module sees the target.
  • Huge return values (entire files); Ansible stores them in memory for every host.
  • Writing a module when a filter, lookup or role would do. A module is for managing state on the target; formatting data is a filter's job (Lesson 02).

docs.title: Packaging
docs.text: A module used by several playbooks belongs in a collection (plugins/modules/ with the same code) with meta/runtime.yml, a changelog, and documentation built from DOCUMENTATION. Add unit tests under tests/unit and run ansible-test (not run here) for sanity and unit checks in the Ansible-supported way.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When a task calls your module, the controller finds library/kvfile.py, builds an AnsiballZ payload (a Python zip with your file, the needed module_utils, and a wrapper), writes it to a temporary file on the target through the connection plugin, and executes it with the target's interpreter. The wrapper unpacks the zip, calls your main(), and your AnsibleModule reads its arguments from the wrapper's embedded JSON (when run standalone, from argv[1]). The final exit_json prints one JSON object to stdout and exits with code 0 (fail_json exits 1); the controller parses the last JSON object, applies keywords like changed_when, failed_when and register, and deletes the temporary files. Everything the module needs from Ansible for validation and file handling comes from module_utils.basic, which is why a module is portable across connection types.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run python3 -m pytest -q src/l3/test_modules.py, then break apply (for example make it append duplicates) and see which tests fail first.
  2. Add backup: true to kvfile that copies the old file to path.bak before changing it. Write the tests first, including that no backup is made when nothing changes.
  3. Add validate (a command run on a temp file, like copy's) and a test with a validator that rejects the file.
  4. Write a read-only info module portcheck that reports whether a TCP port accepts connections (with a timeout argument) and test it with a real local socket.

docs.title: 02 · Filter and Lookup Plugins
docs.text:
Filters transform data inside Jinja2 expressions. Lookups fetch data from outside the play (a file, an environment variable, a secrets store). Both run on the controller, and both are pure Python, which makes them far easier to unit-test than a long Jinja expression.

What was run

Three filters (human_bytes, kv_to_dict, mask_secrets) and one lookup (envfile) were written in src/l3, loaded with ANSIBLE_FILTER_PLUGINS / ANSIBLE_LOOKUP_PLUGINS, and exercised in a playbook and in pytest (23 tests across plugins and inventory, all passing after two corrections described below). They were not packaged in a collection.

docs.title: Filter plugins
docs.text:
A filter plugin is a Python file with a FilterModule class whose filters() method returns a dictionary of names to callables:

def human_bytes(value, base=1024):
    n = float(value) ...
    return "1.5 KiB"

class FilterModule(object):
    def filters(self):
        return {"human_bytes": human_bytes, "kv_to_dict": kv_to_dict, "mask_secrets": mask_secrets}

Put it in filter_plugins/ next to the playbook or inside a role/collection. Results from a real playbook:

sizes:  [0 B, 1023 B, 1.0 KiB, 1.5 KiB, 5.0 GiB]       # [0, 1023, 1024, 1536, 5368709120] | map('human_bytes')
kv:     {a: "1", b: "two"}                              # 'a=1\n# c\nb = two' | kv_to_dict
masked: {user: u, db_password: "********", nested: {api_token: "********", ok: 1}}

Errors should be AnsibleFilterError with a clear message; Ansible adds the task location. -5 | human_bytes produced The filter plugin 'human_bytes' failed: human_bytes expects a non-negative number, got -5.

Design points:

  • Make filters pure (no I/O, no global state). They then compose, cache, and test trivially.
  • Return native types (dict, list) not strings that need re-parsing.
  • Validate input types and raise AnsibleFilterError instead of a Python traceback.
  • Don't mutate arguments. mask_secrets returns a copy (a test asserts the original is unchanged).
  • Document with a DOCUMENTATION block when shipping in a collection (plugins/filter/x.py plus a .yml doc file in recent versions).

mask_secrets is worth a comment: it masks values whose keys look sensitive (password, secret, token, key), recursing through dictionaries and lists. It is a convenience for logging, not a security control: a secret under an innocently named key (data) is not masked. Use no_log: true for real protection (Level 2 · 05).

docs.title: Why a filter instead of Jinja
docs.text: kv_to_dict could be done with split, map and dict, but the Jinja version is unreadable and untestable. As a plugin it has ten pytest cases: comments, blank lines, spaces around =, values that contain = (u=http://x?a=b keeps everything after the first =), and a clear error for a line with no =. A rule of thumb: when an expression needs more than one level of nesting or more than a line, move it to a plugin.

docs.title: Lookup plugins
docs.text:
A lookup runs on the controller and returns a list. lookup('envfile', 'DB_HOST', 'DB_PASS', file='app.env') reads a dotenv-style file there:

class LookupModule(LookupBase):
    def run(self, terms, variables=None, **kwargs):
        self.set_options(var_options=variables, direct=kwargs)
        path = self.get_option("file")
        ... parse the file ...
        for key in terms: out.append(data[key]) or default or raise AnsibleLookupError
        return out

with DOCUMENTATION declaring the options (file required; default optional) so set_options/get_option validate them. Results:

lookup('envfile', 'DB_HOST', 'DB_PASS', file='app.env')       -> "10.0.2.21,s3cret"     (one STRING)
lookup('envfile', 'NOPE', file='app.env', default='fallback') -> "fallback"
lookup('envfile', 'NOPE', file='app.env')                      -> "The lookup plugin 'envfile' failed: envfile: key 'NOPE' not in .../app.env"

docs.title: The comma-join surprise
docs.text: The first line is the gotcha I hit: I expected a list of two values and got the string 10.0.2.21,s3cret. By default lookup() joins multiple results with commas into a single string (a legacy of with_* loops). To get a list, use wantlist=True (the test checks "1" and "two" come back separately and the comma form disappears) or the query() function (query('envfile', ...)), which always returns a list. A value that contains a comma would then be indistinguishable from two values if you took the default form. The fix is to always use query() or wantlist=True when you want a list.

docs.title: Lookups run on the controller
docs.text:
lookup('file', 'x'), lookup('env', 'HOME'), and my envfile all read the controller's files and environment, not the target's. A frequent bug is expecting lookup('file', '/etc/hosts') to read the remote machine. To read data on the target, use a module (slurp, command, stat) and register. Another consequence: a lookup runs once per templating of the expression, so an expensive lookup (an API call) repeated in a loop is slow; cache with set_fact or run_once.

Secrets and lookups: lookup('ansible.builtin.env', 'API_KEY') is a common way to inject CI secrets without writing them to a file. Combine with no_log: true. Lookups to secret managers exist in collections (not run here).

docs.title: Loading and precedence
docs.text: Plugin directories are searched in this order: those set by environment/config (ANSIBLE_FILTER_PLUGINS), the playbook-adjacent filter_plugins/, role-local directories, then collections by FQCN, then built-ins. A plugin with the same name as a built-in can shadow it; prefer unique names, or give yours a collection namespace (mycompany.platform.human_bytes) so there is no ambiguity.

docs.title: Testing plugins
docs.text: Filter functions are ordinary functions: parametrised pytest cases cover them (six human_bytes cases including exactly 1024 and a decimal base, three invalid inputs, kv_to_dict edge cases, nested masking, non-mutation). Importing a plugin file needs ansible-core importable for AnsibleFilterError, so the test module skips itself if it is missing. Lookups need a bit more: instantiate LookupModule and call run with a minimal stub, or (as I did) run ansible localhost -m debug -a "msg={{ lookup(...) }}" in a subprocess and assert on the output, which tests the real loading path.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: At start-up, the plugin loader builds a registry per plugin type by scanning the search paths. For filters it imports each file and calls FilterModule().filters(), registering the returned names (and, for collections, the fully qualified names). During templating Ansible adds those callables to the Jinja2 environment's filters mapping, so {{ x | human_bytes }} is a plain Python call of your function with x as the first argument. Lookups are registered the same way but exposed as the lookup() and query() functions; a lookup receives the terms and keyword options from the template, plus the current variables, and its return is wrapped as a list (and joined into a string unless wantlist is set). Both run in the controller's worker process, so a crashing plugin shows up as a task failure with the plugin name in the message.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Expecting a list from lookup() without wantlist=True.
  • Expecting lookup() to read the target.
  • Filters with side effects or hidden state.
  • Tracebacks instead of AnsibleFilterError.
  • Names that shadow built-ins.
  • Long Jinja instead of a tested plugin.
  • Treating mask_secrets as security.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a filter chunk(list, n) that splits a list into lists of at most n, with tests for empty lists, exact multiples and invalid n.
  2. Write a lookup lastline that returns the last non-blank line of a controller-side file; test with wantlist and without.
  3. Demonstrate with a playbook that lookup('file', ...) reads the controller by creating different files on controller and target (use two connection: local hosts in different directories) and explaining the outcome.
  4. Move a long Jinja expression from one of your templates into a filter and test it.

docs.title: 03 · Dynamic Inventory
docs.text:
Static inventories rot: servers are created and destroyed by autoscalers, and a hand-edited file can never keep up. A dynamic inventory asks an authoritative source (a cloud API, a CMDB, a database, Terraform state) for the hosts every time, so the inventory is always current.

What was run

The authoritative source here is a small CSV file (cmdb.csv, four hosts). I built the inventory both as an executable script and as a custom inventory plugin, ran them through ansible-inventory, and wrote tests (including one proving the two produce the same data). Real cloud inventory plugins (AWS, Azure, GCP, VMware) were not run (no accounts); their usage is described from the documentation.

docs.title: The source data
docs.text:
name,address,role,env,port
web-01,10.0.1.11,web,prod,8080
web-02,10.0.1.12,web,prod,8080
db-01,10.0.2.21,db,prod,5432
web-stg,10.1.1.11,web,staging,8081

Each row should become a host with variables (ansible_host, http_port) and membership of two groups, role and env.

docs.title: Option 1: an inventory script
docs.text:
Any executable that prints JSON in the right shape to --list (and answers --host NAME) can be used with -i ./script. The JSON format: group names map to {hosts, vars, children}, and a special _meta.hostvars key supplies all host variables in one call so Ansible does not run the script once per host.

def build(path):
    inv = {"_meta": {"hostvars": {}}, "all": {"children": ["ungrouped"]}}
    for row in csv.DictReader(open(path)):
        inv["_meta"]["hostvars"][row["name"]] = {"ansible_host": row["address"], "http_port": int(row["port"]), "ansible_connection": "local"}
        for g in (row["role"], row["env"]):
            inv.setdefault(g, {"hosts": []})["hosts"].append(row["name"])
    return inv

Real output of ansible-inventory -i ./inventory_script.py --graph:

@all:
  |--@ungrouped:
  |--@web:   web-01, web-02, web-stg
  |--@prod:  web-01, web-02, db-01
  |--@db:    db-01
  |--@staging: web-stg

and --host web-01 returned {"ansible_connection": "local", "ansible_host": "10.0.1.11", "http_port": 8080}. A pattern 'web:&prod' listed web-01 and web-02, so groups from the script work in patterns like any others.

Script rules (all tested): --list exit code 0 and valid JSON with _meta; --host prints a JSON object (here {}, because _meta already supplied everything); an unknown flag prints usage to stderr and exits non-zero (I used 2). The script must be executable (chmod +x), print only JSON to stdout, and exit non-zero on any failure (an inventory script that prints an error and exits 0 produces an empty inventory and a green run that did nothing).

Scripts are simple and language-agnostic, but each invocation has no caching or configuration framework unless you build it.

docs.title: Option 2: an inventory plugin
docs.text:
An inventory plugin is Python code loaded by Ansible, configured by a small YAML file whose plugin: key names it:

# cmdb.csv.yml
plugin: csvinv
csv_file: cmdb.csv

The class subclasses BaseFileInventoryPlugin, implements verify_file (decide whether this file is mine; mine requires the name ending csv.yml) and parse, which calls self.inventory.add_host, add_group, add_child and set_variable. Documented options (DOCUMENTATION) are read with _read_config_data. The graph and host variables were identical to the script's, and a test runs both through ansible-inventory --list and asserts the same hosts, groups and variables.

Measured differences worth knowing:

  • Inventory plugins must be enabled: by default only built-in plugins are tried. I set ANSIBLE_INVENTORY_ENABLED=script,csvinv,ini,yaml and ANSIBLE_INVENTORY_PLUGINS=./inventory_plugins (in ansible.cfg: [inventory] enable_plugins).
  • Strings set by the plugin with set_variable showed up in --list JSON as {"__ansible_unsafe": "10.0.1.11"}. As I understand the documentation, the marker means "untrusted text, do not template it": values from external inventory data are treated as unsafe so that a hostile CMDB entry such as {{ lookup('pipe', ...) }} cannot execute code (I did not test that scenario). For ordinary use you read them normally in playbooks ({{ ansible_host }}); my test unwraps the marker explicitly. The script form returned plain JSON values, since its output goes through a different path.
  • A plugin can use the inventory cache (cache: true, with a cache plugin) to avoid hitting a slow API on every run.

docs.title: Cloud and other built-in inventory plugins
docs.text:
Collections provide plugins such as amazon.aws.aws_ec2, azure.azcollection.azure_rm, google.cloud.gcp_compute, community.vmware.vmware_vm_inventory, kubernetes.core.k8s. Their configuration files look like plugin: amazon.aws.aws_ec2 with regions, filters, keyed_groups (create groups from tags) and compose (derive variables with Jinja2) sections. These are not run here; read the collection docs (ansible-doc -t inventory -l lists installed ones). Typical design:

  • Group by tag (keyed_groups: [{key: tags.role, prefix: role}]) so a new instance joins role_web automatically.
  • Set ansible_host from private IP or DNS with compose.
  • Filter to the environment you intend (running against an unfiltered account inventory is how people change the wrong machines).
  • Cache results (a few minutes) to speed up repeated runs, and refresh with --flush-cache when you have just created hosts.

docs.title: Combining static and dynamic
docs.text: -i can be repeated, or -i can point at a directory containing several sources: static files for fixed infrastructure, a plugin config for the cloud. group_vars/ next to the inventory directory apply to groups from any source, so you can attach variables to the role_web group created dynamically. That is the usual way to keep data in Git while membership is dynamic.

docs.title: Safety rules
docs.text:
1. Fail loudly. If the API is down, the inventory command must fail the run, not return an empty list.
  2. Never run against "all" in a dynamic inventory without a filter or limit; all includes things you did not intend.
  3. Test the inventory like code: assert expected groups exist and counts are sane (a pre-run check that fails if prod has zero hosts).
  4. Treat inventory data as untrusted input: a tag or hostname written by someone else flows into variables. Keep unsafe handling on, and quote values used in shell commands.
  5. Be careful with secrets: do not put them in dynamic inventory output, which can be logged.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: On start-up Ansible iterates the -i sources and tries each enabled inventory plugin in order, calling verify_file to let the plugin claim the source; the first plugin that accepts and parses it populates the in-memory inventory. The script plugin executes the file with --list, parses the JSON, and creates groups, hosts and (from _meta) host variables; without _meta it would call --host once per host, which is slow for big inventories. The yaml plugin handles YAML inventories, and a config file like cmdb.csv.yml is claimed by the plugin whose verify_file accepts it (mine accepts names ending csv.yml), which then reads its options from the file's plugin:, csv_file: keys. After parsing, group_vars/ and host_vars/ are layered on, then patterns and --limit select hosts. Because everything is assembled per run, there is no inventory state to sync, which is why a stale inventory is solved by re-running, not by repairing a file.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Scripts that exit 0 on error, producing empty inventories.
  • Missing _meta, so Ansible calls the script for every host.
  • Plugin not enabled, then the config file is parsed as ordinary YAML and ignored.
  • No filter on a cloud inventory.
  • Slow API calls on every run with no cache.
  • Trusting inventory data in shell strings.
  • Relying on host order or on names that change.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run ansible-inventory -i src/l3/inventory_script.py --graph and --list; then break the script (exit 0 with {}) and see what a playbook does.
  2. Extend the CSV with a zone column, add zone as a group source in both forms, and update the tests.
  3. Read ansible-doc -t inventory -l for your installed collections; pick one cloud plugin and write the config file for your environment, with a filter and keyed_groups.
  4. Write a pre-run check that fails when any production group has fewer than two hosts.

docs.title: 04 · command and shell Without Breaking Idempotency
docs.text:
Sometimes no module exists and you must run a command. ansible.builtin.command and ansible.builtin.shell are the escape hatches, and they are where most Ansible bugs come from: wrong quoting, hidden failures in pipes, injection from variables, and tasks that report changed forever. This lesson runs each hazard.

What was run

All outputs come from src/l3/cmd.yml on macOS (zsh is the user's shell, but Ansible's shell module used /bin/sh, and /bin/bash where I set executable). Results of shell features can differ on Linux with dash as /bin/sh; test on your target.

docs.title: command versus shell
docs.text:
• command runs a program without a shell: no pipes, no redirection, no &&, no $(...), no globbing.
  • shell runs the line through a shell (/bin/sh by default), so all of those work, and so do their dangers.
  • raw sends text over SSH without Python (for bootstrapping); script copies and runs a local script.

My experiment: echo $HOME | wc -c.

command: stdout = "/Users/bhanuja | wc -c"      # $HOME was expanded; the pipe and wc were passed as literal arguments
shell:   stdout is a number (the character count)

Two surprises: first, command still expanded $HOME (it expands environment variables in arguments; I had assumed it did not), while the | became a plain argument to echo. Second, $(basename $PWD) earlier in Lesson 08 was not evaluated by command. Do not rely on partial shell behaviour; if you need shell syntax use shell, and if you do not, use command with the argv form.

docs.title: argv: no quoting problems
docs.text:
- ansible.builtin.command:
    argv: [echo, "a b", "c;d"]

printed a b c;d: each list element is one argument, with no shell and no splitting. This is the safest form when arguments contain spaces or special characters, or come from variables.

docs.title: Injection through variables
docs.text:
- ansible.builtin.shell: echo {{ evil }}
  vars: {evil: "ok; echo INJECTED"}

Output lines: ok and INJECTED. The variable's text was pasted into the shell line, so ; echo INJECTED ran as a second command. In real life the variable comes from inventory, a facts value, a user-provided -e, or an API, and the injected command could be rm -rf. With the quote filter:

- ansible.builtin.shell: echo {{ evil | quote }}

the output was one line, ok; echo INJECTED, treated as data. Rule: every variable interpolated into shell: must go through | quote, or use command with argv, or pass data through environment variables (environment: {NAME: "{{ value }}"} and "$NAME" in the script). The CI/CD course's script-injection lesson (Level 2 · 10 there) is the same bug in another place.

docs.title: Pipes hide failures
docs.text:
- ansible.builtin.shell: false | cat

Result: rc=0. The pipeline's status is the status of the last command, so the failing false was invisible. With bash and pipefail:

- ansible.builtin.shell: set -o pipefail; false | cat
  args: {executable: /bin/bash}

rc=1. Always set executable: /bin/bash and set -o pipefail for pipelines you depend on (ansible-lint has a rule for this, risky-shell-pipe). /bin/sh may be dash, which lacks pipefail.

docs.title: Making commands idempotent
docs.text:
1. Use a module instead (file rather than mkdir, get_url rather than curl, lineinfile rather than echo >>). Check ansible-doc -l | grep and collections first.
  2. creates / removes: skip the command if a path exists / does not exist.
touch made with creates -> changed=True  (file did not exist)
rm made  with removes   -> changed=True  (file existed)

Both fired in my run because the sequence creates and then removes the same file, so every run created and removed it again: a good reminder that creates/removes look at a file, not at the intent, and combined carelessly they make a task pair that flips on each run (Lesson 08). 3. Check first, act second: stat (or a read-only command) registers the state; the action task has when:. 4. changed_when: derive changed from the output. A script printing created or unchanged:

- ansible.builtin.shell: "test -f flag && echo unchanged || { touch flag; echo created; }"
  register: ch
  changed_when: "'created' in ch.stdout"

First run changed=True, second run changed=False (measured). Use changed_when: false for read-only commands. 5. failed_when for tools whose exit codes mean something else (grep returns 1 for "no match"). 6. Make the command itself idempotent (mkdir -p, ln -sfn, useradd guarded by id), and still add changed_when.

docs.title: Environment, working directory, and privilege
docs.text:
• chdir: sets the working directory; environment: sets variables; args: {executable: ...} picks the shell.
  • become applies to the command like any task.
  • command runs with a minimal environment; PATH may not include what your interactive shell has. Use absolute paths or set environment: {PATH: ...}.
  • Output is captured in stdout/stderr and printed in logs; do not echo secrets (no_log).

docs.title: Check mode
docs.text: command and shell are skipped in check mode (unless check_mode: false on the task), so tasks after them may not see their output. For a read-only command whose output later tasks need, set check_mode: false and changed_when: false. For commands that change things, you can pair with creates/removes, which Ansible can evaluate in check mode.

docs.title: A pre-flight review checklist for every shell:
docs.text:
1. Is there a module that does this?
  2. Does it need shell features? If not, use command + argv.
  3. Is every interpolated variable quoted?
  4. If it has a pipe, is pipefail on and bash selected?
  5. How does it report changed? Is it guarded by creates, removes, when or changed_when?
  6. What does it do when run twice? When run in check mode?
  7. Does it print or leak secrets?

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The command module splits its argument string with shlex-like rules into an argument vector and calls module.run_command which executes it with subprocess (no shell), after applying os.path.expandvars-style expansion to the arguments, which is consistent with $HOME being replaced. shell calls the same helper with use_unsafe_shell=True, which hands the string to /bin/sh -c (or executable), so the shell interprets everything. Both return rc, stdout, stderr and always set changed: true, because the module has no idea what the command did, unless creates/removes short-circuits it before running. That is the whole story behind "command is never idempotent": idempotency has to be supplied by you (guards or changed_when), not by the module.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unquoted variables in shell.
  • Pipelines without pipefail.
  • changed_when: false on a command that changes something.
  • command with shell syntax, half working.
  • Relying on a login shell's PATH.
  • Commands that print secrets.
  • A creates path that is never created, so the command re-runs forever.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run src/l3/cmd.yml. Which task in it changes state on every run? Fix the pair so both runs report changed=0 on the second run.
  2. Write a shell task with a pipeline and prove with a failing first command that pipefail changes the result.
  3. Convert three shell: tasks from a playbook of your own to modules or command + argv, and say what you gained.
  4. Write the injection test: a variable containing ; touch /tmp/pwned run through shell with and without quote, and verify the file is created only in the unsafe case.

docs.title: 05 · Async Tasks and Polling
docs.text:
Normally Ansible keeps a connection open for the whole life of a task. A task that takes ten minutes (a large download, a database restore, a long build) risks a dropped SSH connection or a timeout, and blocks everything else behind it. Async runs the task in the background on the target and lets the controller check on it.

What was run

src/l3/asy.yml run on macOS with a local connection and sleep as the "long job". With connection: local there is no network to drop, so the reasons to use async (flaky or long connections) were not reproduced; the mechanics and messages are real for ansible-core 2.21.5.

docs.title: The three modes
docs.text:
- name: fire and forget style (poll 0)
  ansible.builtin.command: sleep 3
  async: 10          # allow up to 10 seconds
  poll: 0            # do not wait; return a job id immediately
  register: job
  1. async: N, poll: M (M > 0): start the task, then check every M seconds until it finishes or N seconds pass. The task still blocks the play, but the connection is not held open the whole time (Ansible polls). Use this for long tasks on unreliable connections.
  2. async: N, poll: 0: start it and move on. The task result contains ansible_job_id; you check later with async_status. Use this to start work on many hosts in parallel and to do other work meanwhile.
  3. No async: ordinary blocking behaviour.

docs.title: Starting and checking
docs.text:
My run started a 3-second job with poll: 0 and printed started job j443061854556.15009 finished=False. Then a normal task ran (echo working) while the job continued. Then:

- ansible.builtin.async_status: {jid: "{{ job.ansible_job_id }}"}
  register: res
  until: res.finished
  retries: 6
  delay: 1

Output: three FAILED - RETRYING ... (5, 4, 3 retries left) lines (these are expected, the job was not done yet), then finished=True rc=0 attempts=4. The retries are until retries, not failures. Set retries * delay comfortably above the job's expected duration.

Details:

  • The async_status task polls the status file the job writes on the target (under ~/.ansible_async/<jid>); the job id identifies it.
  • You can start jobs on all hosts with poll: 0, then collect them with a loop of async_status over the registered results: a simple way to do parallel work within a single play beyond forks.
  • Use ansible.builtin.async_status with mode: cleanup to remove status files when many jobs run, so they do not accumulate.
  • The task's own changed/failed outcomes appear in the final status; with poll: 0 the start task is reported ok even if the job later fails, so you must check the final status.
  • Handlers, notify and register on the start task refer to the start, not the finish.

docs.title: When the job exceeds async
docs.text:
- ansible.builtin.command: sleep 5
  async: 1
  poll: 1
  ignore_errors: true

The result on this version was an error that is not very informative:

ASYNC FAILED on localhost: jid=j779617292782.15095
fatal: [localhost]: FAILED! => {"async_result": {"ansible_job_id": "...", "finished": false, "started": true, "results_file": "~/.ansible_async/...", ...}, "msg": "async task produced unparsable results"}

So an exceeded time limit appears as async task produced unparsable results, with finished: false inside async_result as the real clue (I did not investigate why this version words it so; other versions may say something different). Treat finished: false plus that message as "the job outlived async". The background process may be killed or may continue; check the target. The lesson: set async higher than the longest legitimate run, and alert on this error.

docs.title: When to use async
docs.text:
Good uses:

  • A long task (more than the connection's idle timeout, or more than a few minutes) such as a backup, a big package upgrade or an image pull.
  • Starting a slow operation on every host at once and doing other tasks while it runs.
  • Operations that restart the SSH daemon or the network (the connection will drop; start with poll: 0, wait with wait_for_connection).

Poor uses:

  • Short tasks. Async adds overhead and complexity.
  • As a general way to speed up playbooks; raising forks or reducing fact gathering is simpler (Lesson 06).
  • Tasks whose result you need immediately to continue.

docs.title: Related tools
docs.text:
• wait_for waits for a port, a file, or a string in a file, with a timeout; wait_for_connection waits until the host can be managed again (after a reboot).
  • ansible.builtin.reboot reboots and waits for the host to return (not run here).
  • throttle limits concurrency of a specific task.
  • For work lasting hours, a job scheduler or a pipeline is better than a playbook. Playbook runs should be bounded.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• Async plus check mode: async tasks do not run in check mode like others; treat their check-mode results as unreliable.
  • Async plus become and files: the status file lives in the user's home directory on the target; with a different become_user use async_dir consistently.
  • Variable lifetime: job.ansible_job_id is only available from the register; if the playbook fails between start and check, the job keeps running orphaned. Put start and status in the same block with always: cleanup.
  • Idempotency: the command in the job must itself be safe to repeat. A failed run that starts the job again may start a second copy while the first still runs.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: With async, the controller wraps the module in an async wrapper (async_wrapper) shipped to the target. The wrapper forks into the background, runs the real module, and writes its JSON result to a file named after a generated job id in the async directory (default ~/.ansible_async/). It returns immediately with the job id. Polling is just repeated execution of a tiny module (async_status) that reads the file: if it is missing or incomplete the job is still running (finished: 0); if complete it returns the saved result. With poll: N > 0 the controller does that polling loop itself, sleeping N seconds between checks. A job that runs past async seconds is terminated by the wrapper's timeout logic, leaving an incomplete result file, which explains why the controller reports it as unparsable rather than as a timeout.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• async shorter than the job.
  • Starting with poll: 0 and never checking, so failures go unnoticed.
  • retries too small for async_status.
  • No cleanup of status files and orphaned jobs.
  • Using async to hide a slow design.
  • Assuming the start task's ok means the job succeeded.
  • Ignoring the finished: false clue in the error.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the three runs (poll 0 plus async_status; poll: 1; timeout) and list the exact messages for your version.
  2. Start the same 2-second job on 10 hosts with poll: 0, then collect them with a loop. Compare the total time with a normal run.
  3. Wrap start and status in a block with always: that cleans up status files, and force a failure between them.
  4. Write a task that restarts a service which drops the connection, using poll: 0 and wait_for_connection.

docs.title: 06 · Performance: Forks, Pipelining and Facts
docs.text:
Ansible's speed is rarely a problem for ten servers and often a problem for a thousand. Most of the time goes to three things: waiting on tasks (parallelism), gathering facts, and connection overhead. This lesson measures the first two and describes the third.

What was run, and how to read the numbers

I timed real ansible-playbook runs (ansible-core 2.21.5) against 20 inventory hosts that all use ansible_connection=local on one 8-core Mac, each task being sleep 1 or a fact gather. Each configuration was run once, so treat the figures as indicative, not as benchmarks; repeat several times for decisions. With the local connection there is no SSH, so connection setup, pipelining, ControlPersist and network latency (the other big costs in real fleets) are not captured. Those are described from the documentation and not measured.

docs.title: Forks: how many hosts run in parallel
docs.text:
forks (default 5) is the number of worker processes handling hosts at once. The playbook: 20 hosts × 2 tasks of sleep 1, facts off.

-f Wall time 1 50.1 s 5 11.1 s 10 6.6 s 20 4.5 s

The ideal times are 40 s (1 fork: 20 hosts × 2 s), 8 s (5), 4 s (10) and 2 s (20); the measured values are higher by a roughly constant per-run and per-host overhead (about 0.5 s of process start-up plus per-task bookkeeping). Notes:

  • Scaling is close to linear until forks reaches the host count, and then stops: 20 forks cannot help 20 hosts beyond one round.
  • -f 20 isn't free: each fork is a separate Python process holding inventory data. On a small controller, hundreds of forks use a lot of memory and CPU; on a real SSH fleet, the controller's CPU and the network become the limit. Increase gradually and watch.
  • The default of 5 is conservative and is often the cheapest single tuning (forks = 20 or more in ansible.cfg).
  • Under the linear strategy a slow host holds up the others at each task (Level 2 · 08); free helps when host speeds differ.

docs.title: Facts: the hidden fixed cost
docs.text:
gather_facts runs the setup module on every host at the start of each play. Same 20 hosts, -f 20:

Configuration Wall time facts off (gather_facts: false), one debug task 0.4 s gather_facts: true, gather_subset: all (default) 2.3 s gather_subset: min 2.1 s gather_facts: smart + JSON fact cache, first run (fills cache) 2.3 s same, second run (cache hit) 0.4 s

Reading it: gathering all facts added about 1.9 seconds to a play that does nothing else, so a playbook with ten plays that each gather facts spends 19 s on facts alone, even on a local machine. Real hosts over SSH take longer. Three ways to cut it:

  1. Turn it off where you do not use facts (gather_facts: false). Many plays only copy files.
  2. Limit it with gather_subset (for example min, or !all,!min,network). On this Mac, min saved only 0.2 s (2.1 vs 2.3), so the dominant cost was the process and the base facts; the saving is larger on hosts where hardware or network discovery is slow. Measure on yours.
  3. Cache it: with gathering = smart and a cache plugin (jsonfile, redis, ...), facts gathered on one run are reused, and the second run skipped gathering (0.4 s). The cache for 20 hosts was 20 JSON files totalling 400 KB. Caches go stale: the value of ansible_facts.memtotal_mb may be days old; set a timeout (I used 600 s) and gather fresh facts when you need current values (for example setup explicitly, or gather_facts: true in the plays where it matters). A stale cache can also hold facts about a host's previous OS after a rebuild.

Fact caching also lets a play read other hosts' facts through hostvars without gathering them in this run.

docs.title: Connection costs (described, not measured)
docs.text:
Over SSH every task does: copy the module (one or more SFTP/scp operations), execute it, and clean up. Settings from the Ansible documentation that reduce the round trips:

  • SSH pipelining (pipelining = True): sends the module through the existing SSH session's stdin instead of writing a temporary file first, cutting round trips substantially. It needs requiretty to be disabled in sudoers on the target when using become.
  • ControlPersist / ControlMaster: reuse one SSH connection for many tasks (Ansible enables this by default through ssh_args).
  • strategy = free, async for long tasks, and mitogen (a third-party strategy plugin, not maintained for current versions as far as I know; check) are other options.
  • Lower-latency placement: run Ansible from a host close to the fleet (a controller in the same network, not a laptop on a VPN).

If you tune only one SSH setting, pipelining is usually the biggest; verify with timing on your own infrastructure.

docs.title: Reduce the work, not just the time
docs.text:
The cheapest speed-up is to run fewer tasks on fewer hosts:

  • Limit and tags (Level 2 · 07): apply one role to one group.
  • Avoid redundant tasks: replace a loop that calls a module 50 times with a module call that takes a list (one package call with a list rather than a loop).
  • Use when guards that avoid an expensive module instead of letting it figure out nothing is needed.
  • Template once, not per host, when the output is identical (run_once with delegate_to).
  • Short-circuit with stat only if the stat is cheaper than the work.
  • Split playbooks by lifecycle: provisioning once, configuration often, deployment constantly.

docs.title: Measuring properly
docs.text:
1. Use ansible-playbook with the profile_tasks callback (ANSIBLE_CALLBACKS_ENABLED=ansible.posix.profile_tasks, from the ansible.posix collection; not run here) to see time per task, or timer for a total.
  2. Repeat runs and report the median.
  3. Change one variable at a time.
  4. Keep the target conditions identical (cold vs warm caches, load).
  5. Measure on the real connection type before choosing a setting.

My timing harness was a small shell function recording date before and after a run, with output discarded, which includes Python and Ansible start-up (a run with facts off and one trivial task took 0.4 s). That is adequate for 2× effects, and not for 5% ones.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The controller's task queue manager starts a fixed pool of worker processes (forks). For each task, the strategy plugin hands each host's work item to an idle worker; a worker templates the arguments, opens or reuses the connection, ships the module, and reports the result back to the main process over a queue. With forks smaller than the number of hosts the strategy runs hosts in waves, so total time ≈ ceil(hosts / forks) × per-host task time, which matches the table (20 hosts at 5 forks is four waves of 2 s plus overhead, so roughly 8 s + 3 s). Fact gathering is just another task (the setup module) executed for every host before the first task; its output is stored in memory per host, and the cache plugin interface lets that storage persist between runs. The 1.9 s difference between 0.4 s and 2.3 s is the fact module's work (starting it on 20 hosts and enumerating hardware, network, mounts and environment); I did not profile it further.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Leaving forks at 5 for large fleets.
  • Gathering facts in every play when they are never used.
  • Caching facts without expiry and acting on stale data.
  • Optimising before measuring, or measuring once.
  • Raising forks beyond what the controller can handle.
  • Loops of single-item module calls where a list-taking module exists.
  • Running Ansible over a high-latency link and blaming Ansible.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the forks table with your own inventory of local hosts, three runs each, and report medians.
  2. Measure gather_subset: min versus all on a real remote host if you have one.
  3. Enable the JSON fact cache with a short timeout and demonstrate stale data: change a custom local fact and show the old value is served until expiry.
  4. Pick a slow playbook of your own, list its five slowest tasks (use profile_tasks), and propose one change for each.

docs.title: 07 · Rolling Updates and Failure Budgets
docs.text:
A rolling update changes a fleet in stages so that capacity stays up and a bad change is stopped early. Ansible's tools are serial, a failure budget, and per-batch checks. This lesson builds a rolling update over eight simulated servers, tests it, and reports a surprising result about how failure budgets interact with block/always.

What was run

src/l3/rolling/rollout.yml runs against eight inventory hosts (n1..n8, local connection). Each "server" is a directory with a version file and an in_rotation marker file, and the "smoke test" is an assert that fails for hosts listed in a bad_hosts variable. No real service, load balancer or health check was involved. 11 pytest tests drive the real ansible-playbook; all passed after I changed the abort mechanism as described below.

docs.title: The playbook shape
docs.text:
- name: Rolling update
  hosts: app
  serial: [1, "50%", "100%"]
  any_errors_fatal: true
  tasks:
    - name: Rollout block
      block:
        - Drain (remove from rotation)      # delete in_rotation marker
        - Log drain
        - Install new version               # write version file
        - Smoke test                        # assert host not in bad_hosts
      rescue:
        - Roll back to previous version
        - Log rollback
        - Fail the host so the batch is marked failed
      always:
        - Return to rotation                # recreate in_rotation marker

serial: [1, "50%", "100%"] on eight hosts gives batches of 1, 4 and 3: the first is the canary, the second is 50% of the fleet (4), and the third is whatever is left (3). A test extracts the host counts per batch from the output and asserts [1, 4, 3].

Principles in the structure:

  1. Drain first, re-enable last. The host leaves rotation before its software changes and returns only after the smoke test. The always: section guarantees that a host is returned to rotation even when the update fails (it was rolled back to a working version), so a failure never leaves the fleet short of capacity because hosts were forgotten in a drained state. The test checks that after a failure every host is back in rotation.
  2. Roll back locally, then fail loudly. The rescue restores the previous version on that host, logs it, and then deliberately fails the host. Without that final fail, a rescued host counts as recovered, the run would report success, and the next batch would proceed. Failing marks the batch failed.
  3. A canary first. The batch of 1 reveals a bad build with minimal exposure.
  4. Verification is part of the batch. The smoke test runs before the host is returned to rotation. Real ones: an HTTP health check with retries, a synthetic transaction, a check of error-rate metrics.

docs.title: Results from the tests
docs.text:
Scenario Outcome All healthy All eight at 2.0, all in rotation, three batches ran, exit 0 Canary (n1) fails smoke test Exit non-zero; all hosts at 1.0 (the canary rolled back, nobody else touched); all in rotation; only one batch started; the canary's event log reads drained, rolled back n3 fails (second batch) Exit non-zero; n1 stays at 2.0 (first batch succeeded); n3 back at 1.0; n6, n8 (third batch) still at 1.0; all in rotation Re-run after the fix Finishes: all eight at 2.0 (hosts already updated are no-ops) Run twice when healthy Second run changes no versions

The re-run case is why the playbook must be idempotent: the production workflow is "fix and run the same playbook again".

docs.title: A real finding: max_fail_percentage did not stop the rollout
docs.text:
My first version used max_fail_percentage: 0, expecting any failure to stop later batches. The test for "failure in the second batch" failed: the third batch ran (all of n6..n8 were updated) even though n3 had failed. To find out why, I wrote variants of a minimal play with serial: [1, "50%", "100%"] and max_fail_percentage: 0, failing only n3, and recorded which hosts started:

Failure handling in the batch Hosts that started Plain task fail n1..n5 (third batch stopped, as expected) block with rescue: fail (no always) n1..n5 (stopped) block + always: (no rescue) n1..n8 (did not stop) block + rescue: fail + always: n1..n8 (did not stop) Any of the above with any_errors_fatal: true n1..n5 (stopped)

So on ansible-core 2.21.5, a block with an always: section that ran after a failure let the play proceed to later batches despite max_fail_percentage: 0 and a recap showing failed=1. I do not know whether this is intended or a bug, and I did not read the strategy source to find out; I measured it and pinned it in a test (test_which_batches_start_after_a_failure_in_batch_two, parametrised over four shapes). any_errors_fatal: true stops correctly in every shape, so the playbook uses that. If a future version changes the behaviour, the test fails and this section needs updating.

Lessons: (1) a failure budget is a safety feature you must test, not assume; (2) write a test that injects a failure in the middle batch and asserts later batches did not run; (3) the combination of serial, budgets and error-handling constructs is subtle, so prefer the simplest mechanism (any_errors_fatal) when the policy is "stop on any failure".

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• Percent ramp. serial: [1, "5%", "25%", "100%"] starts very small on large fleets.
  • Partial tolerance. max_fail_percentage: 20 allows a few failures within a batch (useful when machines are individually flaky), with the caveats above. Check what it does with your error-handling shape.
  • Wait between batches. ansible.builtin.pause (interactive) or wait_for on a metric check, to let monitoring see the new version before proceeding. Automate the decision with a health query where possible; a canary analysis loop is covered in the CI/CD course (Level 3 · 01).
  • Zero-capacity risk. If capacity per host is high, draining 50% at once may overload the rest. Compute the headroom (CI/CD course, Level 3 · 01) and choose batch sizes so the fleet can serve peak load with the hosts removed.
  • Database migrations are not rolling; run them once (run_once) before the app rollout with expand/contract (CI/CD course, Level 3 · 03).

docs.title: Operating the playbook
docs.text:
1. Start with --check --diff --limit canary-host.
  2. Run on the canary alone, watch metrics.
  3. Run the full playbook; keep a human watching the first batch and the 50% batch.
  4. On failure: do not just re-run. Read the failure, decide fix vs revert. A re-run after a fix is safe by design; a re-run of a broken change just fails again and burns a canary.
  5. Record what was deployed (version, hosts, time, who) as evidence (CI/CD course, Level 4 · 05).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: serial splits the host list of a play into batches and executes the full task list for each batch in sequence, as separate runs of the play (the output shows a new PLAY header per batch). Between batches the executor evaluates whether the run should continue: it counts hosts that failed in the batch and compares the percentage with max_fail_percentage, and any_errors_fatal makes any host failure abort the play for all hosts immediately. The observed discrepancy suggests that hosts which ran an always: section after a failure are bookkept differently from hosts that stopped at the failure, so the batch's failed count did not exceed the limit; I have not confirmed the cause. Blocks, rescue and always are implemented by the same iterator that tracks per-host state, so a host in the "always" phase is still running tasks.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• No failure test for the abort path.
  • Trusting max_fail_percentage with complex error handling constructs.
  • A rescue that doesn't fail, so the run proceeds as if healthy.
  • Forgetting to return hosts to rotation after a failed update.
  • A single large batch for a risky change.
  • Smoke tests that always pass (not checking the thing that changed).
  • Rolling out a change that is not backward compatible, since old and new versions run together.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/l3/rolling and read the parametrised test. Change serial to [2, "100%"] and predict, then verify, the batch sizes.
  2. Add a post_tasks metric check that fails the batch if a (simulated) error rate file exceeds a threshold.
  3. Make the rollback itself fail on one host and decide what the playbook should do (alert, leave it drained, stop the world). Implement and test it.
  4. Add a --tags drain-only mode that only drains the hosts, for maintenance, and ensure always does not return them to rotation in that mode.

docs.title: 08 · State, Drift and Convergence
docs.text:
Terraform records what it created, so removing a resource from the code removes it from the world. Ansible records nothing. It looks at the host, compares, and fixes only what your tasks mention. That makes Ansible simple and flexible, and it makes three problems your job: orphans (things you used to manage), conflicts (two tasks managing the same thing differently), and drift (the host changing between runs).

What was run

The three experiments below are real runs of small playbooks (state_v1/v2/v3.yml, flip.yml in src/l3) in a sandbox directory on a Mac with ansible-core 2.21.5. They manage files; the same logic applies to packages, users, services and firewall rules, whose modules were not run.

docs.title: No state file: orphans
docs.text:
Version 1 of a playbook manages two files:

- copy: {dest: "{{ d }}/a.conf", content: "a\n"}
- copy: {dest: "{{ d }}/legacy.conf", content: "legacy\n"}

Run: ok=2 changed=2; both files exist. Version 2 removes the legacy task because the feature was retired:

state_v2.yml: ok=1 changed=0
files after v2: a.conf legacy.conf        <-- legacy.conf is still there

Ansible has no record that it ever created legacy.conf, so deleting the task changes nothing on the host. The retired configuration keeps working on every machine that received version 1 (and does not exist on new machines, so your fleet is now inconsistent). This is the most important difference from state-based tools.

docs.title: Fix 1: explicit removal
docs.text:
Add a task for the retirement and keep it until every environment has run it:

- ansible.builtin.file: {path: "{{ d }}/legacy.conf", state: absent}

Remove it later when you are sure nothing needs it (tracked in a changelog). This is the normal approach for packages, users and services (state: absent).

docs.title: Fix 2: allow-list purge
docs.text:
For directories where only managed files should exist, enumerate and delete everything else:

vars: {managed: [a.conf]}
tasks:
  - ansible.builtin.copy: {dest: "{{ d }}/a.conf", content: "a\n"}
  - ansible.builtin.find: {paths: "{{ d }}", patterns: "*.conf"}
    register: found
  - ansible.builtin.file: {path: "{{ item.path }}", state: absent}
    loop: "{{ found.files }}"
    loop_control: {label: "{{ item.path | basename }}"}
    when: item.path | basename not in managed

In --check the purge showed changed: [localhost] => (item=legacy.conf) and nothing was deleted; the real run removed it (files after v3: a.conf). This is powerful and dangerous: a typo in the allow-list or the wrong directory deletes real files. Safeguards: restrict paths and patterns tightly, always preview with --check, make the playbook refuse to run if managed is empty, and keep backups. Many tools use this pattern for sudoers.d, cron.d, conf.d directories ("drop-in" directories where each managed item is a file).

docs.title: Fix 3: markers and ownership
docs.text: For shared files, blockinfile and managed markers (# BEGIN ANSIBLE MANAGED BLOCK) identify what Ansible owns, so you can remove just that part. For resources with tags (cloud), tag everything Ansible creates (managed_by: ansible) and reconcile by listing tagged resources.

docs.title: Conflicts: two tasks, one resource
docs.text:
Two roles both want to set a file's mode, one to 0600 and one to 0644:

- file: {path: shared.conf, state: touch, mode: "0600", ...}   # team A
- file: {path: shared.conf, state: touch, mode: "0644", ...}   # team B

Run twice: ok=2 changed=2 the first and the second time. Each run, task A changes the mode to 0600 and task B changes it back to 0644: the playbook never converges. Every run reports changes, check mode always shows drift, and a handler notified by either task fires every time. This is a bug only the second run can reveal, and the "run twice and expect changed=0" test catches it (Level 1 · 10).

Causes: duplicated ownership of a resource across roles (/etc/ssh/sshd_config managed by a baseline role and an app role), copy-pasted tasks, and variable defaults that differ by role. Cure: assign each resource to exactly one owner (a role), make others depend on it via variables, and use a drop-in directory so independent roles manage independent files.

docs.title: Drift: the world changes between runs
docs.text:
Drift sources: manual edits during incidents, other automation (package managers' post-install scripts, configuration agents), unattended upgrades, applications rewriting their configs, and tasks with unpinned versions (state: latest). Drift is normal; the goals are to detect it and decide.

  • Detect: run the playbook in check mode on a schedule; the changed tasks are the drift report (Level 4 · 06 builds an auditor around this).
  • Classify: a change reported on app.conf means someone edited it; a change reported on a task that touches /etc/hosts every run might be a conflict or a legitimately dynamic file.
  • Decide: re-converge (apply), or accept the manual change by encoding it in the playbook.
  • Prevent: limit who may log in and edit by hand, and when they do, require an incident ticket that ends in a pull request.

Enforcement frequency is a policy choice. Applying automatically every hour keeps machines honest and risks overwriting a deliberate emergency fix. Applying on demand allows drift to accumulate. Many teams run check mode continuously and apply only through a reviewed pipeline.

docs.title: Convergence properties to test
docs.text:
1. Idempotent: second run changed=0.
  2. Convergent from any starting state: start from several states (empty, partially configured, wrongly configured) and check each ends at the same final state. The Level 1 project tested a drifted state.
  3. Order-independent where possible: tasks managing different resources should not depend on each other's order; tasks that do depend on order should be in one role with a documented sequence.
  4. Reversible changes: removing something from the playbook should be an explicit step (state absent), tested in a scenario "v1 then v2".
  5. No dependence on the previous run: a clean machine and an old machine converge to the same result.

A good test for item 4 is exactly the experiment above: run v1, then v2, then assert the retired file is gone. The test fails until v2 contains the explicit removal or the purge.

docs.title: Modeling desired state when Ansible is not the source of truth
docs.text: Where an external system owns the truth (a CMDB, Terraform state), generate the Ansible variables from it (dynamic inventory, Lesson 03), so playbooks consume state without storing it. That avoids a second source of truth.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each module is a function from (current state read from the target, requested arguments) to (actions, result). There is no memory between runs: the "state" is the host itself, read fresh. A removed task simply never executes, so its previous effects remain, and nothing in Ansible can tell which effects came from which version of the playbook. Convergence arises from every task being a pure "ensure X" operation; two tasks that ensure incompatible things about the same X make the system a fixed-point-free loop. The recap's changed count is the number of tasks whose modules found a difference, so a persistent non-zero count on an unchanged system is direct evidence of either non-idempotent tasks or conflicting owners.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Deleting a task and assuming the thing is gone.
  • Purge patterns that match too much.
  • Two roles owning one file.
  • Ignoring a task that changes on every run ("it's just noisy").
  • Auto-applying over a manual emergency fix.
  • No scheduled drift detection.
  • Treating state: latest as convergent.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce v1 → v2 → v3 and write the pytest that asserts the retired file is removed after v3 but not after v2 (documenting the orphan).
  2. Reproduce the flip-flop, then fix it so one task owns the file and the other consumes a variable. Prove changed=0 on the second run.
  3. Write a purge for a conf.d-style directory that refuses to run when the allow-list is empty and shows a count of files it would delete in check mode.
  4. Design a drift-detection schedule for your environment: frequency, who reads the report, and the criteria for auto-apply.

docs.title: 09 · Network and Windows Targets
docs.text:
Ansible manages more than Linux servers over SSH. Windows hosts, switches, routers and firewalls, cloud APIs and appliances each need a different connection plugin and a set of modules designed for them. Because the model is "run a task, get JSON", the playbook language stays the same; what changes is where and how the work executes.

What was run, and what wasn't

No Windows host, network device or API endpoint was available, so nothing in this lesson was executed against such a target. What I did do: install the ansible.windows (3.9.1) and ansible.netcommon (8.7.1) collections from Galaxy, count their modules with ansible-doc, read module documentation offline, and list the connection plugins. Everything about behaviour on real devices is from the Ansible documentation (October 2026) and general knowledge; read it as a map for where to look, not as tested advice.

docs.title: What the collections contain
docs.text:
$ ansible-doc -l ansible.windows | wc -l
      81
$ ansible-doc -l ansible.netcommon | wc -l
      16
$ ansible-doc ansible.windows.win_copy | head -5
> MODULE ansible.windows.win_copy (.../ansible/windows/plugins/modules/win_copy.py)
  The `win_copy' module copies a file on the local box to remote windows locations.
  For non-Windows targets, use the [ansible.builtin.copy] module instead.

ansible.windows supplies 81 modules on this version (that is the number of lines ansible-doc -l printed; I did not check whether it also lists plugins), prefixed win_ (win_copy, win_file, win_service, win_feature, win_user, win_registry, win_shell, win_package ...). ansible.netcommon listed 16 entries (generic network modules such as cli_command, cli_config, netconf_config; its connection plugins are listed separately by ansible-doc -t connection -l). Vendor collections (Cisco, Juniper, Arista, Palo Alto, F5 ...) add resource modules for their devices. The connection plugins visible with ansible-doc -t connection -l included ansible.builtin.winrm, ansible.builtin.psrp, ansible.builtin.ssh, ansible.builtin.local, ansible.netcommon.network_cli, netconf, httpapi and libssh.

docs.title: Windows
docs.text:
Two protocols are supported for managing Windows from a control node (the control node itself must be Linux or macOS; Windows is not supported as a controller for the full tool, per the docs):

  • WinRM (ansible_connection=winrm): Windows Remote Management over HTTP(S), using the pywinrm Python library on the controller. Authentication options include NTLM, Kerberos and certificate/basic with HTTPS; Kerberos is the common choice in domains and needs system libraries on the controller.
  • PSRP (ansible_connection=psrp): PowerShell Remoting Protocol, a library (pypsrp) with generally better performance for file transfer.
  • SSH on Windows is supported by newer builds of Windows with OpenSSH enabled (ansible_shell_type: powershell or cmd).

Typical inventory variables:

[windows]
win01 ansible_host=10.0.3.10
[windows:vars]
ansible_connection=winrm
ansible_winrm_transport=ntlm
ansible_winrm_server_cert_validation=validate
ansible_user=svc_ansible
ansible_password={{ vault_win_password }}      # from a vaulted variable

(An example only; not run.) Differences to expect:

  • Modules are PowerShell scripts, named win_*; most Linux modules do not work. Check the module list for the equivalent.
  • Paths use backslashes and drive letters; in YAML, quote or double them ('C:\Temp').
  • File ownership and modes are ACL-based, not POSIX modes.
  • become uses runas, with different semantics from sudo.
  • Reboots are common (ansible.windows.win_reboot), and the connection drops, so wait for it to return.
  • Fact gathering uses ansible.windows.win_setup or the same setup entry point; the fact names differ (ansible_os_family: Windows).
  • Credentials and certificates are the main operational risk: WinRM over plain HTTP with basic authentication sends credentials in clear text; use HTTPS and a modern transport.

docs.title: Network devices
docs.text:
Network devices usually cannot run Python modules, so Ansible's network model runs modules on the controller, which connects to the device (via CLI over SSH, NETCONF, or an HTTP API) and parses/sends commands:

  • network_cli: SSH to a CLI, sending commands and reading text. Set ansible_connection=ansible.netcommon.network_cli and ansible_network_os=<platform> (for example cisco.ios.ios).
  • netconf: NETCONF over SSH with XML, for devices that support it.
  • httpapi: REST-style APIs (Arista eAPI, others).

Typical group variables:

# group_vars/switches.yml
ansible_connection: ansible.netcommon.network_cli
ansible_network_os: cisco.ios.ios
ansible_user: netops
ansible_become: true
ansible_become_method: enable

Concepts that matter:

  1. Resource modules (for example ios_interfaces, ios_vlans) manage a section of configuration as structured data with states such as merged, replaced, overridden, deleted, gathered, rendered, parsed. They are idempotent by comparing the structured data to the device's current configuration. merged adds, replaced makes a resource match exactly, overridden makes the whole device section match exactly (and deletes anything not listed, which is the dangerous one). gathered reads the config into the same structured format, useful to bootstrap source-of-truth data.
  2. Generic command modules (cli_command, ios_command, ios_config) send text commands; they are the escape hatch and have the same idempotency issues as command and shell (Lesson 04). ios_config can compare the intended lines against the running config.
  3. Parsing: network output is text. ansible.utils.cli_parse and parsers like TextFSM, TTP or xmltodict turn it into data. Those need extra Python libraries on the controller (the same dependency lesson as Lesson 03 and Level 2 · 06).
  4. Persistent connections: since each task would otherwise log in again, Ansible keeps a persistent connection process (ansible-connection) per host with a timeout (persistent_command_timeout), so a long-running task can fail with a timeout error that does not appear on servers.
