  5. Check mode and diff are supported by many network modules (they can compute the config diff, and some devices can "commit confirmed" for a safe rollback), which makes them natural candidates for staged changes. Whether yours does depends on the platform and module.
  6. Safety: a network change can cut off your own management access. Use out-of-band access, commit confirmed or rollback timers where the platform has them, and apply changes to one device (a --limit, Level 2 · 07) before the fleet. Back up configurations before change (*_config with backup: true).

docs.title: APIs and "localhost" modules
docs.text: Many modules (cloud providers, SaaS, Kubernetes, load balancers) run on the controller against an API, with hosts: localhost and connection: local (or delegated). Credentials, rate limits and API pagination matter more than SSH. The same principles hold: use modules that take state, register results, check mode where supported, and no_log for tokens.

docs.title: Choosing the connection and keeping inventory clear
docs.text:
• Put connection details in group_vars for the group (windows, switches), not on every host.
  • Test connectivity with the right ping module: ansible.windows.win_ping, ansible.netcommon.net_ping/vendor equivalents, ansible.builtin.ping for Linux. (I confirmed win_copy's docs offline; I did not run win_ping.)
  • Keep the Python libraries needed by each connection (pywinrm, pypsrp, ncclient, paramiko/ansible-pylibssh) pinned in your requirements and in the execution environment (Level 4 · 01).
  • Write per-platform roles with a common interface (role: ntp with variables) and platform task files, rather than one role full of when: os == ....

docs.title: Why this is mostly "the same Ansible"
docs.text: The playbook, inventory, variables, handlers, roles and templates work identically. The differences concentrate in four places: the connection plugin, the module set, the facts, and the failure modes (timeouts, authentication, reboots, device quirks). If you can reason about idempotency, check mode and blast radius on servers, you can reason about them for network gear; what you need to learn is each platform's resource model and how it is safely changed.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: For servers, the controller ships a module to the target and runs it there. For network devices and APIs, there is no place to run Python on the target, so the module runs on the controller inside a persistent-connection helper: the connection plugin (network_cli, httpapi, netconf) opens a long-lived session to the device in a separate process and exposes a socket to the module worker. The module sends commands over that socket, receives text or structured data, and returns JSON. For Windows, the module is a PowerShell script (or C# in newer ones) sent to the host over WinRM or PSRP and executed there by PowerShell, and its JSON output is returned. Task scheduling, variables and templating on the controller are unchanged in every case.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using Linux modules on Windows (or the reverse).
  • WinRM over HTTP with basic auth in production.
  • overridden state on a network resource without a preview.
  • No out-of-band access when changing network config.
  • Persistent-connection timeouts misdiagnosed as device failures.
  • Missing Python libraries for the connection or parser.
  • Putting device credentials in plain inventory instead of Vault or a secrets lookup.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Install ansible.windows and ansible.netcommon and use ansible-doc to find the module that manages (a) Windows services, (b) Windows registry keys, (c) a generic CLI command on a network device. Read each one's state options.
  2. Write the group_vars for a Windows group and a switch group, with credentials from a vaulted file.
  3. Explain, for a network resource module, the difference between merged, replaced and overridden using a three-line example config.
  4. Draft the rollout plan for changing an interface description on 40 switches: pre-checks, backup, canary, --check --diff, batches, verification, rollback.

docs.title: 10 · Project — A Tested Custom Module
docs.text:
This project brings Level 3 together around one deliverable: a custom module, kvfile, that manages key=value entries in a settings file. It has a pure decision function, correct check and diff behaviour, input validation, atomic writes and a thorough test suite. Around it sit the other Level 3 artefacts (plugins, dynamic inventory, rolling update), each with its own tests.

What was run, and what wasn't

Everything here ran on a Mac with ansible-core 2.21.5. kvfile and filehash were executed standalone (the way Ansible runs a module: a JSON argument file), and through ansible-playbook. Test counts from the final run: 25 module tests (test_modules.py), 23 plugin and inventory tests (test_plugins.py), 11 rolling-update tests (rolling/test_rollout.py). Not done: running the module on a remote target over SSH, Windows/PowerShell versions, packaging in a collection, ansible-test sanity.

docs.title: Requirements for kvfile
docs.text:
1. state: present ensures exactly one key=value line for the key with the given value; state: absent removes it.
  2. Idempotent: no change reported when the file already matches.
  3. Preserve comments, blank lines and unrelated settings; collapse duplicate definitions of the managed key.
  4. Check mode never writes. Diff mode returns before and after content.
  5. Reject invalid keys and values containing newlines; report missing files unless create: true.
  6. Support mode, owner, group and report a mode-only difference as a change.
  7. Write atomically.

docs.title: Structure
docs.text:
• apply(lines, key, value, state): pure; returns (new_lines, before_value, after_value). Only this function decides content.
  • main(): builds AnsibleModule with required_if=[("state", "present", ["value"])], add_file_common_args=True, supports_check_mode=True; validates; reads the file; calls apply; computes changed by comparing old and new text; writes via a temp file and os.replace when not in check mode; applies file attributes; returns changed, before, after, diff.

Playbook run (real output) on a two-line file # header / port=80:

set workers=4 (mode 0640)  -> changed
set workers=4 again        -> ok                      (idempotent)
change to 8                -> changed, before/after = 4/8
remove                     -> changed
changed flags: [True, False, True, True]
bad key "bad key"          -> failed: invalid key 'bad key'
missing value              -> failed: state is present but all of the following are missing: value
missing file, create=false -> failed: .../nofile does not exist and create=false

and --check --diff printed the +workers=4 / +workers=8 hunks without altering the file.

docs.title: The 25 tests
docs.text:
Group Count Examples Pure function 11 add, replace, unchanged returns same lines, remove, absent-when-missing no-op, comments preserved, duplicates collapsed, spaces around =, empty file, prefix key not confused, hash equals hashlib Module as Ansible runs it 13 create-then-idempotent; check mode does not write; diff content; mode set; mode-only change reported; three rejected inputs (parametrised); missing file; absent on missing is a no-op; unknown argument rejected; filehash missing file and output Real ansible-playbook 1 second run changed=0

Properties the tests give you: the pure function is correct for edge cases; the module obeys the Ansible contract (JSON, changed, failed, check and diff modes); and the whole thing works through the real engine. The suite takes under three seconds because only one test starts Ansible.

docs.title: A design decision worth defending
docs.text: apply collapses duplicates of the managed key to the first occurrence's position, and changed is determined by comparing complete file text. A consequence: a file with a=1 twice is changed by state: present, value: 1 because the second line is removed. That matches the requirement "exactly one line for the key" and is tested (a=1,a=2,a=3 becomes a=5). A different design could treat duplicates as someone else's responsibility; the point is that the behaviour is specified and tested, not accidental.

docs.title: Companion artefacts and their tests
docs.text:
Artefact Tests What they establish Filter plugins (human_bytes, kv_to_dict, mask_secrets) 16 Edge cases, errors, no mutation, registration Lookup plugin (envfile) 2 Reads a controller file; default join gives 1,two, wantlist=True gives a list; missing key errors Dynamic inventory (script and plugin) 5 Protocol (--list, --host, usage exit 2); the script and the plugin yield identical hosts, groups and variables Rolling update 11 Batch sizes 1/4/3; canary failure rolls back only the canary; failure in batch 2 keeps batch 1 updated and stops batch 3; nobody left drained; re-run after a fix finishes; abort-semantics pins

Two things went wrong on the first run of the plugin tests and are worth remembering: the plugin-sourced inventory values were wrapped in __ansible_unsafe in JSON output, and the lookup's default output joined results with a comma. In both cases my expectation was wrong, not the code, and the tests now pin the real behaviour with comments.

docs.title: Extending the module
docs.text:
1. backup: true creating path.bak before a change (tests: no backup on no-op).
  2. validate: command, like copy, run on a temporary file.
  3. Support key: value with spaces or INI sections as a separate module rather than overloading this one.
  4. Return warnings when duplicates were collapsed.
  5. A diff that shows only the changed lines for large files.
  6. A Windows-compatible version would need a PowerShell implementation; the Python module cannot run on a target without Python.
  7. Publish in a collection with ansible-test sanity and unit-test hooks.

docs.title: When not to write a module
docs.text: Write one when you manage state on the target and need check mode, idempotency and structured results. Don't write one to: format data (a filter), fetch data from the controller side (a lookup), wrap a single command (use command with guards, Lesson 04), or call a REST API once (the uri module). The best sign you need a module is a long chain of command/shell + register + changed_when tasks that you keep copying between roles.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Tests exploit three seams in Ansible's design. A module is a program with a documented contract (JSON in, JSON out), so it can be run without Ansible by feeding the JSON. A pure function inside the module can be imported directly. And the engine's recap and exit status are observable outputs, so end-to-end tests can assert on changed=N. The module's check mode works because AnsibleModule exposes check_mode from the _ansible_check_mode key of the arguments; the controller sets it for --check. File attributes use set_fs_attributes_if_different, which returns True when it changed something, folding mode changes into the same changed flag so users see one honest signal. The temp-file-and-rename write relies on os.replace being atomic on a single filesystem on POSIX.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Writing logic inside main(), which is hard to test.
  • Doing work in check mode.
  • Returning changed=True unconditionally.
  • Not validating inputs that reach file content or commands.
  • Tests that exercise only the happy path.
  • Tests that start Ansible for everything, making the suite slow.
  • Forgetting documentation, so nobody can use the module.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run python3 -m pytest -q src/l3 (this runs the module, plugin and rolling tests; the rolling suite takes about 40 seconds) and read the three test files.
  2. Implement backup: true with tests first.
  3. Add ansible-doc text for the mode option and check that ansible-doc -M library kvfile shows it.
  4. Write a short design note for a second module of your own: its arguments, its pure core, and the five tests you would write first.

docs.title: Level 4 · Operating Ansible
docs.text:
Level 4 is about running automation as a service for a team: where playbooks execute, how they are tested in CI, how secrets are handled, when hosts pull their own configuration, how Ansible fits with Terraform, how to audit drift, how to limit and respond to incidents, how to migrate scripts, how to keep standards, and a capstone that operates a simulated fleet.

What was run, and what wasn't

ansible-core 2.21.5 and ansible-lint on a Mac; all fleets are simulated with local connections. Run for real: ansible-builder create (no image built), a six-step CI script, an executable vault password script, ansible-pull against a local Git repository, a drift-report callback plugin and audit tool, a no_log linter, a Terraform-output inventory script (on a hand-written fixture), a preflight guard, a script-to-playbook migration comparison, ansible-lint configuration behaviour, and a twelve-node capstone. Not run: AWX or Ansible Automation Platform, container builds, GitHub Actions, Terraform, secret managers, remote hosts, Windows and network targets.

Prerequisites: Levels 1 to 3. The CI/CD Mastery Path course is a good companion for Lessons 02, 03 and 07.

docs.title: Modules
docs.text:
1. Controllers, AWX and Execution Environments: what a controller adds; pinning with ansible-builder.
  2. Ansible in CI/CD: a six-step script and the non-idempotent task it caught.
  3. Secrets and Credentials at Scale: vault password scripts, a no_log linter and its limits.
  4. Pull Mode and Bootstrap: ansible-pull, and why --only-if-changed does not repair drift.
  5. Terraform and Ansible Together: division of labour and a tested output-to-inventory script.
  6. Auditing Drift with Check Mode: a callback plugin and an audit tool with three exit codes.
  7. Automation Incidents and Blast Radius: a preflight guard that failed its own first test.
  8. Migrating Scripts and Avoiding Anti-Patterns: script versus playbook, measured; 24 anti-patterns.
  9. Governance, Review and Standards: lint profiles, ratchets and a config result that surprised me.
  10. Capstone: Managing a Simulated Fleet: detect, scope, repair narrowly, verify.

docs.title: After Level 4
docs.text: You have a working model of Ansible from a single module call to fleet operations, a set of tested tools that make the ideas concrete, and a clear record of which claims were measured on ansible-core 2.21.5 and which come from documentation. The next step is to apply them to real machines.

docs.title: 01 · Controllers, AWX and Execution Environments
docs.text:
On a laptop, ansible-playbook is enough. For a team it raises questions: who may run what against which hosts, where do credentials live, how do runs get scheduled and logged, and how do we make sure everybody uses the same Ansible version with the same collections? An automation controller answers those questions, and an execution environment pins the software.

What was run, and what wasn't

No automation controller was installed or run (no AWX, no Ansible Automation Platform, no container runtime, no Kubernetes). The platform concepts below are from the Ansible and AWX documentation as I know it (October 2026); product details change quickly, so check current docs. What I did run: ansible-builder 3.2.0 to generate an execution environment build context (no container image was built or started).

docs.title: What a controller adds
docs.text:
Capability What it means Projects A link to a Git repository with playbooks; the controller syncs it before jobs Inventories Static or dynamic sources, with credentials for cloud syncs Credentials Encrypted stores for SSH keys, vault passwords, cloud tokens; users can use a credential without seeing it Job templates A saved combination: playbook + inventory + credentials + limit + extra vars + execution environment RBAC Who can run, edit, or read each template, inventory and credential Scheduling Cron-like runs, for drift audits and maintenance (Lesson 06) Workflows Chains of templates with success/failure branches and approval steps Logging and history Every run's output, who started it, with what parameters; usually an API and a UI API / CLI Trigger jobs from CI or other systems Execution isolation Jobs run in separate containers (execution environments) rather than on a shared shell

AWX is the upstream open-source project; Red Hat's Ansible Automation Platform is the commercial product built on it. Open alternatives and supplements exist, and plain CI/CD systems (GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Jenkins) can also run ansible-playbook (Lesson 02). The right choice depends on how much RBAC, credential isolation and scheduling you need versus how much infrastructure you want to run.

docs.title: The credential idea
docs.text: The most valuable feature is separation: an operator can launch "Deploy web" without ever seeing the SSH key or vault password. The controller injects them into the job's container at run time. That turns "who has the production key?" from "everyone with the repo" into "the platform, and auditable use of it". It also makes the controller itself a high-value target: it holds credentials for the whole estate and needs hardening, backups, patching and monitoring (Lesson 07 treats incidents).

docs.title: Execution environments
docs.text:
An execution environment (EE) is a container image holding a specific ansible-core, ansible-runner, collections, Python libraries and system packages. The controller (or ansible-navigator on a laptop) runs each job inside an EE, so the same playbook runs with the same software everywhere, solving "works on my laptop".

ansible-builder builds EE images from a definition. My definition:

version: 3
images:
  base_image:
    name: quay.io/fedora/fedora:42
dependencies:
  ansible_core:
    package_pip: ansible-core==2.21.5
  ansible_runner:
    package_pip: ansible-runner
  galaxy: requirements.yml
  python: requirements.txt
  system: bindep.txt

with requirements.yml listing ansible.utils 6.1.1, requirements.txt netaddr==1.3.0, and a bindep.txt for system packages. Running ansible-builder create produced a build context (context/Dockerfile and context/_build/ with bindep.txt, requirements.txt, requirements.yml and helper scripts). The Dockerfile, which I read but could not build, has stages: a base stage that installs pip and ansible-core==2.21.5 ansible-runner, a galaxy stage that runs ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml into /usr/share/ansible/collections, a builder stage that compiles Python dependencies, and a final stage that copies the results. Observations:

  • The pins from the definition appear literally in the image build, so the version of Ansible in the image is whatever you wrote: EE definitions are the pinning mechanism (the same advice as Level 2 · 06 for collections).
  • The base image tag is mutable; pin by digest for reproducibility.
  • Collection dependencies listed in requirements.yml are installed at build time, so a job never downloads collections at run time (faster, and works in air-gapped networks).
  • Building requires a container runtime (Podman or Docker), which I did not have; so the image was never built and the Dockerfile was not tested.

Run an EE locally with ansible-navigator run site.yml --execution-environment-image my-ee:1.0 -m stdout (not run here) to replicate controller behaviour on a laptop. When EEs and a controller are used, remember: the playbook sees the container's filesystem and network; files on the host and SSH agent sockets are not available unless mounted or provided as credentials.

docs.title: Designing the project for a controller
docs.text:
1. Repository layout with a playbooks/ directory, roles/, collections/requirements.yml and inventories in inventories/<env>/. The controller syncs the project and can install collections from collections/requirements.yml (if enabled).
  2. Parameterise with survey variables rather than free text where possible (choices, ranges). Operators fill in a form; the template maps answers to extra_vars. Remember that extra_vars beat all other variables (Level 2 · 02), so any value an operator can set can override your safety checks. Validate inputs with assert.
  3. One template per operation, with minimal credentials (for example "restart service" with a restricted account).
  4. Limits by default. A template for production should require a limit or approval, and use the preflight idea from Lesson 07.
  5. Notifications to chat/email on failure, and an external audit trail for production changes.
  6. Idempotent playbooks so a retry is safe; the controller will retry or re-run.

docs.title: Operating the controller itself
docs.text:
• Capacity: each running job uses a container and some memory; the number of concurrent jobs and forks is bounded by controller nodes. Plan like a CI runner pool (CI/CD course, Level 4 · 02 on queue time).
  • High availability and backup: the controller stores configuration in a database; back it up and test restores. A lost controller means lost credentials and job history.
  • Upgrades: the controller, the EEs and the ansible-core in them have separate lifecycles. Test new EE images on non-production templates first.
  • Network position: the controller reaches your entire estate and often internal APIs. Limit inbound access, use SSO and MFA, and treat it as tier-0 infrastructure.
  • Secrets lifecycle: rotate credentials stored in the controller; consider short-lived credentials or external secret lookups (Lesson 03).
  • Auditing: export job events; review who changed templates and credentials (CI/CD course, Level 4 · 05).

docs.title: When you do not need a controller
docs.text: If you have a handful of operators and a CI system, running Ansible from CI with secrets stored in the CI vault and an EE or pinned virtualenv may be simpler: the pipeline provides scheduling, approvals and history, and you avoid another service. Move to a controller when you need credential separation for non-experts, self-service for other teams, or workflow orchestration across many templates. Whichever you choose, the playbooks stay the same.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A controller keeps jobs as database records. When a job is launched, it checks out the project at a revision, resolves the inventory (possibly by running dynamic inventory plugins in an EE), creates a private directory with the project, inventory and an env/credentials bundle, and starts an ansible-runner process inside the EE container. Runner executes ansible-playbook with the requested options and streams structured events (each task start, result and stat) back as JSON, which the controller stores and displays live. Credentials are exposed to the process through temporary files and environment variables that exist only for the job's lifetime. This design is why the output in the UI is equivalent to the CLI output, why job isolation depends on the container runtime, and why an EE image is a hard dependency of every job.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unpinned EEs, so job behaviour changes without a commit.
  • Credentials that are too broad, shared across all templates.
  • Surveys that accept free text feeding shell commands.
  • No limit or approval on production templates.
  • No backups of the controller database.
  • Treating the controller as just another web app instead of a tier-0 asset.
  • Running playbooks that depend on files on the operator's laptop.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write an execution-environment.yml for your project's collections and Python libraries and run ansible-builder create; read the generated Dockerfile and identify where each pin is applied.
  2. Design the job templates and credentials for three operations (deploy, patch, rotate secrets): who may launch each, with which credential and which limits.
  3. List what you must back up and monitor on a controller, and what the recovery time objective would be.
  4. Decide, for a team of 8 with a CI system, whether a controller is justified. Write the argument both ways.

docs.title: 02 · Ansible in CI/CD
docs.text:
Treat automation code like application code: every change is linted, tested on disposable targets and promoted through environments. This lesson builds a CI script for an Ansible repository, runs it, shows what it catches, and ties it to the CI/CD course on this site.

What was run

src/l4/ci.sh is a six-step script, run with ansible-core 2.21.5 and ansible-lint against the Level 1 baseline playbook on two local "servers". The GitHub Actions workflow (src/l4/workflow/ansible-ci.yml) was written and checked with this site's sister course's workflow linter (wflint.py: 0 findings), but was never run on GitHub; its two action references use obviously fake SHAs that you must replace with real, reviewed ones. See the CI/CD Mastery Path course for the underlying CI/CD concepts.

docs.title: The pipeline, cheapest check first
docs.text:
1 syntax-check      ansible-playbook --syntax-check
2 ansible-lint      production profile
3 secret hygiene    nologlint.py (tasks using secret variables need no_log)
4 converge          first run on a disposable target
5 idempotence       second run must report changed=0
6 check mode        --check must report changed=0 (no drift)

The ordering follows the CI/CD course's rule (Level 1 · 05): run the fastest, most likely to fail checks first. Steps 1 to 3 need no target and take seconds; steps 4 to 6 need a target and take longer.

docs.title: What each step caught
docs.text:
• Step 2 failed on the Level 1 baseline playbook as I first wrote it: Failed: 7 failure(s) with name[play] (the play was unnamed) and six name[casing] findings (task names started with lowercase). The script stopped there, exactly as intended. I produced a lint-clean copy (baseline_ci.yml) by naming the play and capitalising the task names, after which the production profile passed.
  • Steps 4 to 6 on the clean copy: first run changed=6 on both nodes, second run changed=0, check mode changed=0, and the script printed CI OK. About 3 seconds in total on a Mac with two local nodes.
  • Step 5 catches non-idempotent tasks. I added a task that writes the current nanoseconds into a file (lookup('pipe', 'date +%N')). The pipeline got through steps 1 to 4 and then printed:
== 5 idempotence (second run)
node1 : ok=6 changed=1
node2 : ok=6 changed=1
FAIL: second run reported 2 change(s)

and exited non-zero. A change that would flap on every run in production was stopped in review. The same defect passes steps 1 to 4 because nothing in them runs the playbook twice.

docs.title: Where Ansible runs in the pipeline
docs.text:
• Test stage: run against throwaway targets. Options: connection: local and a sandbox (as in this course), a container started per job, or a VM/cloud instance created for the job and destroyed afterwards. The cheaper the target, the faster the feedback; the more realistic, the more it proves.
  • Staging/pre-production: run for real against an environment that mirrors production, ideally from the same Execution Environment image (Lesson 01).
  • Production: run via a controller job or a protected pipeline environment with approval (CI/CD course, Level 2 · 07), with --check --diff output attached for the approver and a limit/batching strategy (Level 2 · 08, Level 3 · 07).
  • Scheduled: a nightly drift audit in check mode (Lesson 06).

docs.title: The workflow file
docs.text:
name: ansible-ci
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
permissions:
  contents: read
concurrency:
  group: ansible-ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
jobs:
  verify:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@<full commit SHA>
      - uses: actions/setup-python@<full commit SHA>
        with:
          python-version: "3.12"
      - run: |
          python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
          ansible-galaxy collection install -r requirements.yml -p ./collections
      - run: ./ci.sh playbooks/site.yml inventories/ci/hosts.ini

(The real file in src/l4/workflow has the same content.) The CI/CD workflow linter reported 0 findings: least-privilege token, a job timeout, SHA-pinned actions (with obviously fake values here), and a concurrency group that cancels superseded runs (right for CI, wrong for a deploy job, CI/CD course Level 2 · 07).

Key decisions embedded:

  • Pinned tooling: requirements.txt pins ansible-core, ansible-lint and Python libraries; requirements.yml pins collections. An unpinned install makes CI break when a new lint rule appears (a lint upgrade adds rules and fails old code).
  • Collections installed per project, not globally.
  • Secrets: the vault password comes from CI's secret store through an executable password script (Lesson 03), never from the repository.
  • Read-only token for pull requests from forks; do not expose secrets to fork builds (CI/CD course, Level 4 · 01).

docs.title: Testing against containers: what it proves and does not
docs.text: A container job (for instance a Debian or Rocky image) can verify package names, file templates, users and many config files across distributions quickly. It cannot verify behaviour that depends on a real init system, kernel settings (sysctl), firewalls, SELinux/AppArmor enforcement, or reboots. For those, use VMs, and consider testing a representative subset. Say clearly in your documentation what the CI tier covers. I did not run container jobs; the local-connection tests here have the same limitation, more strongly.

docs.title: Promotion and review
docs.text:
• Pull request: steps 1 to 6 on disposable targets; attach the lint and recap output.
  • Merge to main: apply to staging automatically; run smoke tests.
  • Release to production: a manual approval, with a --check --diff against production attached; then apply with batching.
  • Changes to roles are versioned and released like libraries (Level 2 · 06; CI/CD course Level 3 · 07), with a changelog, so consumers pin versions.

docs.title: Make the pipeline testable and fast
docs.text:
• Keep each job under a few minutes; fast feedback matters (CI/CD course, Level 4 · 02).
  • Cache the pip and collection downloads (CI/CD course, Level 2 · 02 for key design).
  • Run roles' tests in parallel (a matrix over roles), and only the roles that changed (path filters, CI/CD course Level 2 · 09).
  • Fail on warnings you care about: ANSIBLE_DEPRECATION_WARNINGS, lint warn_list aging (Lesson 09).
  • Record artifacts: lint report, JUnit-style results (ansible.builtin.junit callback; needs the junit_xml Python library, not run), and the drift report from Lesson 06.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: The script is a sequence of commands whose exit statuses set -e propagates; the pipeline system treats a non-zero exit as a failed step. The idempotence assertion reads the PLAY RECAP lines (host : ok=.. changed=..), extracts each host's changed count with sed, sums them with paste -sd+ | bc, and fails if the sum is not zero. That parsing is only as reliable as the recap format; a more robust version uses a callback plugin that writes JSON (as Lesson 06 does) or the junit callback. The same facts that make the Level 1 tests work make this work: modules report changed truthfully, so a second run with zero changes is evidence of convergence.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Unpinned CI tooling.
  • No second-run test, so non-idempotent tasks reach production.
  • Running the real pipeline against production on every pull request.
  • Secrets passed to fork builds.
  • Believing a container test proves service behaviour.
  • Parsing the recap with brittle shell and never testing the parser.
  • One giant job that takes 40 minutes and gets skipped.
  • Using cancel-in-progress: true on a production deploy group.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run src/l4/ci.sh on a playbook of yours (set PATH to include a virtualenv with ansible-core and ansible-lint). Record which step fails first and fix it.
  2. Add a deliberately non-idempotent task and prove step 5 fails, then fix the task with changed_when or a module.
  3. Replace the shell recap parser with the JSON drift report from Lesson 06 and write a test for it.
  4. Adapt ansible-ci.yml to a matrix over three roles with path filters; run the CI/CD course's workflow linter on it.

docs.title: 03 · Secrets and Credentials at Scale
docs.text:
Level 2 showed how Vault encrypts files. At scale the questions change: where does the vault password come from in CI, how do you stop people from printing secrets, how do you rotate hundreds of credentials, and when do you stop storing secrets in Git at all?

What was run, and what wasn't

Run for real: an executable vault password script supplied by an environment variable (success and failure), and nologlint.py, a text-based linter for missing no_log (12 tests). Not run: HashiCorp Vault, cloud secret managers, SSH certificate authorities, OIDC federation or the lookups that talk to them. Their descriptions come from documentation and general practice and are marked as such.

docs.title: Where the vault password comes from
docs.text:
Level 2 used a password file. In CI a file is awkward, so Ansible lets --vault-password-file point to an executable: if the file is executable, Ansible runs it and reads the password from its standard output.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
import os, sys
pw = os.environ.get("ANSIBLE_VAULT_CI_PASSWORD", "")
if not pw:
    print("vault_pass: ANSIBLE_VAULT_CI_PASSWORD is not set", file=sys.stderr); sys.exit(1)
print(pw)

Real results:

with the variable set:    encrypt succeeds, playbook runs: ok=1 changed=1
without the variable:     [ERROR]: Vault password script .../vault_pass.py returned non-zero (1): None

and the file written by the playbook had mode 0600 (-rw-------). The script fails closed: a missing secret is an error, never an empty password. Replace the body to fetch from your CI secret store, a keychain, or a secret manager CLI; the interface to Ansible stays the same. Rules for the script: print only the password and a newline, send diagnostics to stderr, exit non-zero on any failure, never write the password to disk or logs, and keep the script free of the secret itself.

Multiple passwords (--vault-id dev@dev_pass.py --vault-id prod@prod_pass.py) let a repository hold secrets for several environments, with CI jobs for non-production given only the non-production password.

docs.title: Keeping secrets out of logs: no_log and a linter
docs.text:
Vault protects secrets at rest. At run time a secret appears as an ordinary variable and is easy to print: a debug task, a failing command that includes it in cmd, -vvv output, or --diff of a file that contains it. Level 2 · 05 measured this. The countermeasure is no_log: true on every task that handles a secret, and an automated check that it is there.

nologlint.py parses playbooks with PyYAML and flags a task when its arguments, environment or vars reference a variable whose name matches secret patterns (password, passwd, secret, token, api_key, private_key, credential, or a vault_ prefix) and neither the task, an enclosing block, nor the play sets no_log: true. A debug task using such a variable is flagged even with no_log because the purpose of debug is to print. On a sample playbook:

secrets/sample.yml:sample:tasks: 'leaks' uses db_password -> missing no_log
secrets/sample.yml:sample:tasks: 'prints' uses api_token -> debug prints it
2 finding(s)          (exit status 1; the task with no_log: true was not flagged)

12 tests cover: a plain flagged task; no_log on the task, on an enclosing block, and on the play clearing it; nested blocks; handlers; secrets in environment; the vault_ prefix; secret names inside filter expressions (db_password | b64encode); non-secret names ignored; a literal word like "password policy" without {{ }} not flagged.

Limits of this heuristic, stated plainly: it works on names, so a secret stored in a variable called data is invisible to it; it does not follow include_tasks or roles into other files unless you lint them too; it flags use, not exposure through register (a registered result containing a secret printed later); and it cannot tell whether no_log hides the specific failure you need to debug. It is a net for common mistakes, not a proof.

no_log has its own cost: it hides the error message too (the failing task printed only censored). When you must debug, reproduce in a safe environment without no_log, or log a sanitised message yourself.

docs.title: Secrets from a secret manager (described, not run)
docs.text:
Instead of encrypting values into Git, fetch them at run time:

  • Lookup plugins such as community.hashi_vault.hashi_vault (HashiCorp Vault), and cloud collections for AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault and GCP Secret Manager. A task reads lookup('...', 'secret/data/app'). Lookups run on the controller (Level 3 · 02), so the controller needs credentials to the secret manager, and the value is then sent to the target in the module arguments.
  • Benefits: central rotation, access policies, audit logs, dynamic or short-lived secrets (database credentials generated per run), no ciphertext in Git history.
  • Costs: the controller depends on the secret manager being up; the identity that fetches secrets becomes the crown jewel; and a lookup in a loop can call the API many times.
  • Combine with no_log, and avoid writing the secret into files that outlive the run unless needed.

docs.title: Short-lived credentials (described, not run)
docs.text: The best secret is one that expires. Options: cloud role assumption with OIDC from CI (CI/CD course, Level 1 · 08 and Level 3 · 08); SSH certificates signed by a CA with a short validity instead of long-lived keys on every host; database credentials issued per job; tokens limited to one scope. Ansible itself does not issue these; it consumes them from the environment or a lookup. Design so that the playbook never needs a credential that lives longer than the run.

docs.title: SSH keys and the control node
docs.text: The control node's SSH private key is the master key to the estate. Practices: use an agent or a hardware-backed key; one key per environment; restrict what the key can do on targets (authorized_keys options, a dedicated ansible user with narrowly scoped sudo); use ssh-agent forwarding carefully (it lets a compromised intermediate host use your key); and rotate when people leave. Configure host_key_checking deliberately: disabling it removes protection against man-in-the-middle attacks and is a common shortcut that should not reach production.

docs.title: Rotation as a playbook
docs.text:
A rotation procedure should be automated and idempotent:

  1. Generate or fetch the new secret.
  2. Distribute it (update the secret manager or re-encrypt the vault file).
  3. Update consumers in an order that avoids outage (accept both old and new first, then switch, then remove old).
  4. Verify consumers work.
  5. Revoke the old secret.
  6. Record the rotation (who, when, what, evidence), not the secret.

Test the procedure on a non-production copy. Rotation is a rolling update with rollback (Level 3 · 07): do not revoke the old secret until the new one is verified everywhere.

docs.title: Handling a leak
docs.text: Revoke first, investigate second (CI/CD course, Level 4 · 07). For Ansible specifically: rekeying a vault file does not help if the plaintext secret leaked; change the secret itself. Search logs and job history on the controller for the leaked value; vault-encrypted old versions in Git remain decryptable by anyone holding the old vault password.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: When --vault-password-file names an executable, the vault secret loader runs it with subprocess, captures stdout, strips the trailing newline and uses it as the password; a non-zero exit becomes the Vault password script ... returned non-zero error shown above. Ansible then tries the password against each encrypted blob it encounters, using the vault ID label from the header to choose among multiple secrets. no_log is enforced in the task executor: when a result for a no_log task is produced, the callback layer replaces its content with a censored message before any display or callback sees it, while the registered variable still holds the real data for later tasks (so a later debug of the registered variable still prints it unless it too is protected).

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Vault password in the repository or in an unprotected CI variable visible to fork builds.
  • Password scripts that fail open (print nothing and exit 0).
  • Missing no_log on tasks that handle secrets.
  • Registered variables that hold secrets, printed later.
  • Disabling SSH host key checking permanently.
  • Rekeying after a leak instead of changing the secrets.
  • Long-lived shared credentials when a short-lived alternative exists.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Write a vault password script that reads from your OS keychain or a CLI of your choice and test the success and failure paths.
  2. Run nologlint.py on your playbooks and roles. For each finding decide fix, suppress with reason, or false positive; extend the secret-name patterns for your organisation.
  3. Write the rotation playbook for one credential in your estate, in the order old-and-new, switch, verify, revoke, with a test.
  4. Draw where each secret in one deployment lives at rest, in transit, in memory and in logs, and what protects it at each point.

docs.title: 04 · Pull Mode and Bootstrap
docs.text:
Normally a control node pushes to many hosts. With ansible-pull the host pulls its own configuration from a Git repository and applies it to itself. Pull mode scales to large fleets without a central controller, handles machines that cannot be reached from outside (laptops, edge devices, autoscaled instances behind NAT), and repairs drift automatically when scheduled.

What was run

Real runs of ansible-pull (ansible-core 2.21.5) against a local Git repository (file:///tmp/pullrepo) on a Mac, applying a playbook to localhost. A scheduler (cron, a systemd timer) and real remote machines were not involved; that part is described.

docs.title: How it works, shown
docs.text:
A tiny repository with local.yml:

- hosts: localhost
  connection: local
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - name: managed file
      ansible.builtin.copy:
        dest: /tmp/pullout/motd
        content: "version {{ release | default('1') }}\n"
        mode: "0644"

$ ansible-pull -U file:///tmp/pullrepo -d /tmp/pullwork -i localhost, local.yml
Starting Ansible Pull at ...      -> clones the repo, runs local.yml:  ok=1 changed=1     (motd: "version 1")
$ (same command again)             -> repository unchanged; playbook runs again:  ok=1 changed=0

Options used: -U repository URL, -d working directory for the checkout, -i localhost, an inventory containing just the local host (the trailing comma makes it a literal host list). By default ansible-pull looks for a playbook named after the host (<hostname>.yml) or local.yml; here I named it explicitly. The first run cloned the repository into -d, subsequent runs updated it with a fetch, then ran the playbook.

docs.title: --only-if-changed and drift
docs.text:
--only-if-changed (-o) skips the playbook if the repository has not changed since the last pull. My measurements:

Situation Command Result No new commit ansible-pull ... --only-if-changed Repository has not changed, quitting; playbook not run New commit (release default changed 1 → 2) with --only-if-changed playbook ran, changed=1, motd now version 2 Someone edits motd by hand (hacked) plain ansible-pull playbook ran, changed=1, motd restored to version 2 Someone edits motd by hand --only-if-changed nothing happened; the hand edit remained

The last row is the important gotcha: --only-if-changed is an optimisation for "apply when the code changes", and it does not repair drift, because drift is a difference between the host and the repo, and the repo did not change. For drift repair you must run the playbook on every pull (no -o), or run it on a schedule with a periodic forced apply (for example every pull without -o, but pulling rarely).

docs.title: Scheduling
docs.text:
ansible-pull is meant to run from a scheduler on each node: a cron entry such as every 15 minutes, a systemd timer, or a configuration agent. Considerations (described, not run here):

  • Splay: add random delay (--sleep N randomises up to N seconds) so hundreds of nodes do not hit the Git server at the same moment.
  • Locking: prevent overlapping runs (use flock or a systemd unit that won't start twice).
  • Logging: capture output to syslog/journal and ship it; there is no central controller log by default.
  • Reporting: pull mode has no built-in central view; send a heartbeat or run result to a monitoring system (for example write a metrics file or post to an endpoint at the end of the playbook), and alert on nodes that haven't reported.
  • Failures: a broken commit on the main branch will run on every node. Roll out from a branch/tag per ring (canary nodes track canary, the rest stable) and pin the checkout with -C <ref> (--checkout).
  • Security: the node needs read access to the repository (a deploy key or token with read-only scope; keep it away from the playbook's own secrets) and should verify what it runs. ansible-pull supports --verify-commit to require signed commits (not run here). Secrets in the repo must be vaulted, and each node needs the vault password somehow (a file placed at bootstrap, or fetched from a secret manager with the node's identity).

docs.title: Push versus pull
docs.text:
Push (ansible-playbook from a controller) Pull (ansible-pull on each node) Who initiates Operator or CI The node, on a schedule Reachability Controller must reach nodes (SSH, WinRM) Node must reach Git Scale Bounded by controller and forks Scales with nodes; Git server load Orchestration (ordering across hosts, rolling batches) Natural (serial, delegate_to) Poor: nodes act independently Drift repair Only when you run it Automatic if scheduled and run without -o Visibility Central output You must build reporting Credentials Controller holds access to all nodes Each node has only its own access Fast response Immediate Up to one interval

Choose pull for large, loosely coupled or hard-to-reach fleets where each node's configuration is independent; push for coordinated changes (rolling updates across a cluster, database failover). They combine: pull for the baseline on every node, push for orchestrated operations.

docs.title: Bootstrap patterns
docs.text:
A new machine needs Ansible and a first run. Patterns:

  1. Image bake: build the OS image with Ansible (baseline role) once, with Packer or similar; machines boot already configured, and pull mode maintains them.
  2. cloud-init / user-data: a small script installs Python and Ansible and runs ansible-pull once, which then installs the scheduler (so the machine keeps itself updated). A common sequence: install packages, ansible-pull the bootstrap playbook, which configures the cron/timer.
  3. Provisioning tool: Terraform creates instances and triggers a push run (Lesson 05).
  4. Manual seed for a handful of special machines: run ansible-pull by hand.

The bootstrap playbook should itself be idempotent and small: install the dependencies, place credentials (for example a read-only Git deploy key delivered through the cloud's metadata or a secret service, not stored in the repository), and install the periodic job. Keep it separate from the full configuration so you can reason about the trust chain: the first run determines what the machine will trust afterwards.

docs.title: Pitfalls
docs.text:
• A single broken commit affects every node within one interval. Protect the branch, require review and CI (Lesson 02), and use rings.
  • Time skew and partial runs: nodes converge at different times, so versions differ during a rollout; design changes to be backward compatible.
  • Inventory: with -i localhost, playbooks cannot see other hosts; anything needing groups or hostvars of other nodes does not work as in push mode.
  • Roles from Galaxy are fetched at run time unless vendored (needs network access and trust), and collection dependencies must be installed on each node (an EE is not used).
  • Unattended breakage is more serious than in push: no one is watching. Use any_errors_fatal-style guard rails, health checks and automatic rollback tags where possible.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: ansible-pull is a small program that first runs the git module (via an ad-hoc call to ansible) against localhost to clone or update the repository, and records whether the repository changed (before and after commit IDs, which you can see in the quit message). Then, unless -o applies, it runs ansible-playbook on the playbook path inside the checkout with the supplied inventory. Because the second step is just a normal playbook run, everything about idempotency, check mode and variables is unchanged. The --only-if-changed logic compares only the repository's commit IDs, which explains why local drift is invisible to it.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Using -o and expecting drift repair.
  • No splay, creating thundering herds on the Git server.
  • No reporting, so silent failures persist for weeks.
  • All nodes tracking main with no rings.
  • Storing the deploy key or vault password in the repository.
  • Playbooks that assume other hosts are visible.
  • No lock, so slow runs overlap.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Reproduce the four-row table with a local repo. Then add --verify-commit handling in your design notes (what would you need to set up?).
  2. Write a bootstrap.yml that installs a cron entry (as a file in a sandbox directory) running ansible-pull with a splay, and test it for idempotency.
  3. Design the ring rollout for 1,000 nodes: canary tag, soak time, promotion, and how you stop a bad release.
  4. Add a heartbeat task at the end of a playbook that writes a timestamp and result to a file; write a check that finds nodes whose heartbeat is older than two intervals.

docs.title: 05 · Terraform and Ansible Together
docs.text:
Terraform (or OpenTofu) is good at creating infrastructure and tracking it in state. Ansible is good at configuring what runs on it, and at orchestrating operations. Using both is common, and the join between them is where problems arise: how does Ansible learn which machines Terraform created, and who owns what?

What was run, and what wasn't

Terraform was not installed, so no terraform apply ran and no state was produced. I built and tested an inventory script that consumes the JSON shape produced by terraform output -json (as documented in the Terraform CLI docs), using a hand-written fixture. The Terraform-side snippets are untested illustrations. For Terraform itself, see the Terraform Mastery Path course on this site; for pipeline safety around plan and apply, the CI/CD Mastery Path (Level 3 · 05) covers a plan guard.

docs.title: Division of labour
docs.text:
Concern Better owned by Why Networks, VMs, load balancers, databases, DNS Terraform State, dependency graph, plan/diff, destroy OS packages, config files, users, services on a host Ansible Fine-grained on-host modules, templates, handlers Application deployment steps and orchestration Ansible (or a deploy tool) Ordering, batches, delegation Bootstrapping (first boot) cloud-init / images, then Ansible The machine must exist and be reachable first Secrets storage A secret manager Neither tool is a secret store

The overlap: both can create cloud resources. Pick one owner per resource, or the two will fight (Level 3 · 08 conflicts). A decent rule: if the resource has an identity in a cloud API and a lifecycle independent of the OS, Terraform; if it is inside the OS, Ansible. Avoid having Ansible cloud modules and Terraform both manage security groups.

docs.title: The handoff patterns
docs.text:
1. Output → inventory. After apply, terraform output -json yields machine addresses; a script or inventory plugin turns them into Ansible hosts and groups. Static, simple, and explicit.
  2. Cloud inventory plugin. Ansible queries the cloud API (aws_ec2, azure_rm, ...) for instances tagged role=web. Terraform tags instances; Ansible discovers by tag (Level 3 · 03). Decoupled from Terraform state, which is good when others create machines too.
  3. Terraform inventory provider/plugin. A community plugin reads Terraform state directly (not run here). That couples Ansible to the state file and requires access to it; state may contain secrets, so restrict who can read it.
  4. Provisioner / local-exec calling ansible-playbook from Terraform. Terraform's own docs advise provisioners as a last resort: failures leave resources tainted, the run is not part of the plan, and re-running configuration is awkward. Prefer a separate pipeline stage.
  5. User-data / ansible-pull at first boot (Lesson 04): Terraform only needs to start instances with the right user-data; machines configure themselves.

docs.title: An output-to-inventory script, built and tested
docs.text:
terraform output -json prints an object whose keys are output names, each with value, type and sensitive. The script tfinv.py accepts that JSON and builds a script-protocol inventory (Level 3 · 03):

{"web_ips": {"value": ["10.0.1.11", "10.0.1.12"], "type": ["tuple", ["string", "string"]], "sensitive": false},
 "db_hosts": {"value": "10.0.2.5", "type": "string", "sensitive": false}}

becomes hosts web-01, web-02 (group web) and db-01 (group db), each with ansible_host and a tf_output variable naming the source. ansible-inventory -i ./tfinv.py --graph (with TFINV_FILE set, because Ansible calls an inventory script with only --list) printed @web: web-01, web-02 and @db: db-01. Design choices, each with a test (10 tests, all passing):

  • Refuse sensitive outputs. If "sensitive": true, the script raises an error: addresses are not secrets, but anything marked sensitive should not be copied into an inventory, which can be logged.
  • An unknown or empty result is an error, not an empty inventory. {"other": ...} gives no known outputs found and a non-zero exit. Silently returning zero hosts would make a downstream playbook succeed on nothing (Level 1 · 03: zero matching hosts exits 0).
  • Validate addresses (non-empty strings).
  • Predictable names (web-01...) that do not depend on the address, so changing an IP doesn't rename hosts.
  • Exit codes: 0 on success, 1 on bad input, 2 on usage error; --host prints {}.
  • It reads from a file named by TFINV_FILE or stdin. This is a teaching tool: real outputs would be richer (instance IDs, zones, tags).

Because the fixture is hand-written, the script has never read an actual Terraform output. If your Terraform version formats output differently from the documented shape, the tests will not tell you; run it once against a real output -json before relying on it.

docs.title: Ordering in a pipeline
docs.text:
1. terraform plan   (PR: review the plan; guard destructive changes)
2. terraform apply  (protected branch; creates/updates machines)
3. wait for readiness (SSH reachable, cloud-init done)
4. ansible-playbook (configure; inventory from outputs or cloud tags)
5. smoke tests

Points that go wrong:

  • Readiness. The instance exists but SSH is not ready. Use wait_for_connection or wait_for as the first task, with a timeout, rather than sleep.
  • Replaced machines. If Terraform replaces an instance, its IP changes, host keys change (host_key_checking failures), and Ansible's configuration is gone; the playbook must re-run on the new machine. Make the Ansible run part of the same pipeline after each apply, and it must be idempotent so re-runs on unchanged machines are no-ops.
  • Drift between layers. Terraform does not know what Ansible did and Ansible does not know what Terraform created beyond the inventory. Do not use Terraform to change files on machines and Ansible to resize disks.
  • Variables shared across tools. Port numbers and names used in both should come from one place. Terraform can write a vars.json/group_vars file (via local_file) or Ansible can read Terraform outputs; keep a single source of truth.
  • Destroy order. Before destroying machines that Ansible registered elsewhere (monitoring, load balancers, DNS), run a deregistration playbook; Terraform will not.
  • State access. Anything reading state needs access to a sensitive file; prefer outputs (an explicit contract) over reading state.

docs.title: Idempotent infrastructure plus idempotent configuration
docs.text: Both tools aim at convergence, but they differ in how they detect change: Terraform by comparing the plan with recorded state and refreshed real attributes, Ansible by inspecting the host. A full run of both after an unrelated change should produce no changes; that is a useful nightly test (a scheduled terraform plan -detailed-exitcode and an Ansible check run, Lesson 06).

docs.title: Alternatives and neighbours
docs.text:
• Packer builds machine images with Ansible as a provisioner: bake once, replace instead of patching. Terraform launches the image; Ansible runs only at build time and for rare tweaks.
  • Kubernetes shifts configuration into manifests and controllers (GitOps, CI/CD course Level 3 · 06); Ansible still bootstraps nodes and manages out-of-cluster pieces.
  • Cloud-native config (SSM, Run Command) can replace SSH-based pushes; Ansible has connection plugins and inventory plugins for some of these (not run here).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Terraform writes its outputs from the state file after apply; terraform output -json reads them back as JSON without contacting the cloud. Ansible's inventory is evaluated at the start of each run, so it sees the machines that exist then. The script protocol runs the script with --list and parses the JSON. The inventory therefore is a snapshot taken at playbook start: if Terraform changes machines mid-run, Ansible does not notice. This one-way, snapshot-based coupling is a good thing: the only contract between the tools is data (a list of addresses and attributes), which you can validate, test, version and inspect, rather than shared mutable state.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Two tools managing the same resource.
  • Provisioners as the main integration.
  • Empty inventory silently accepted.
  • Copying sensitive outputs into inventories or logs.
  • Forgetting readiness waits.
  • Reading the state file directly instead of outputs.
  • No test of the join between tools.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/l4/test_tfinv.py and add a new output (bastion_ip, group bastion) with tests for both list and string values.
  2. If you have Terraform, run it for a trivial config with an output of a list, feed terraform output -json to tfinv.py and fix any difference from the fixture.
  3. Write the pipeline outline (stages, credentials per stage, approvals) for apply then configure.
  4. Decide who owns security groups, DNS records, OS firewall rules and application ports in your estate, and record it in one table.

docs.title: 06 · Auditing Drift with Check Mode
docs.text:
Level 3 explained drift: the difference between what your automation says and what a machine actually has. Check mode (--check --diff) makes Ansible report those differences without changing anything, so a scheduled check run is an audit. This lesson builds a small auditing tool around it and measures what it can and cannot see.

What was run

src/l4/callback_plugins/driftreport.py (a custom callback plugin) and src/l4/audit/driftaudit.py (a runner and summariser) were written and run against the Level 1 baseline on two simulated servers, and 9 pytest tests passed on the first run. Everything was local-connection with file-based "servers"; real services, packages and remote hosts were not audited.

docs.title: Why not parse the console output?
docs.text: The screen output is for humans: it mixes task headers, item lines, diffs and warnings. On this install ansible-doc -t callback -l listed only default, junit, minimal, oneline and tree: setting ANSIBLE_STDOUT_CALLBACK=json failed with Could not load 'json' callback plugin (a JSON callback lives in a separate collection, ansible.posix, which I did not install), and junit needs an extra Python library. A callback plugin is a few dozen lines and gives exactly the data needed.

docs.title: The callback plugin
docs.text:
A callback plugin receives events as the run proceeds. The aggregate plugin driftreport:

class CallbackModule(CallbackBase):
    CALLBACK_TYPE = "aggregate"; CALLBACK_NEEDS_ENABLED = True
    def v2_runner_on_ok(self, result):           # record only results with changed: true
    def v2_runner_on_failed(self, result, ignore_errors=False): ...
    def v2_runner_on_unreachable(self, result): ...
    def v2_playbook_on_stats(self, stats):       # at the end: write the JSON report

It must be enabled (ANSIBLE_CALLBACKS_ENABLED=driftreport) and found (ANSIBLE_CALLBACK_PLUGINS=<dir>). For each changed result it stores host, task name, the diff (when the module supplied one), and, for looped tasks, the labels of the items that changed. At the end it writes report.json with per-host summaries, the list of findings, drifted_hosts and failed_hosts.

docs.title: The runner and its exit codes
docs.text:
driftaudit.py playbook inventory [args] runs the playbook with --check --diff and the plugin enabled, reads the report, prints a summary and exits:

Exit Meaning 0 No drift on any host 1 Drift found (at least one task would change something) 2 A task failed or a host was unreachable: the audit result is not trustworthy

The third code matters. A failed task in an audit may hide drift behind it, and an unreachable host was not audited at all. A cron job that treats "non-zero" as "drift" would miss those; reporting them separately lets you alert differently.

docs.title: What it found, for real
docs.text:
On the two-node baseline after a clean converge: hosts audited: 2 drifted: 0 failed: 0, exit 0. Then I vandalised the sandbox: appended a line to node2's app.conf, set its var/lib/app directory to 777, and deleted node1's motd. The audit printed:

hosts audited: 2  drifted: 2  failed: 0
- node1
    [changed] message of the day
- node2
    [changed] directory tree items=['var/lib/app']
    [changed] app configuration
    [changed] restart app

exit 1. Note three things: the looped task reports which item drifted (var/lib/app, not all three directories); the handler restart app appears because the config change would notify it, so the report previews the restart; and nothing was repaired (a test confirms a hand-edited file is left as it was).

The nine tests: clean fleet exits 0; drift found per host with exit 1; the audit does not repair; diff text is captured (PermitRootLogin yes and no both present); looped items are identified; an undefined variable gives exit 2; a first run on an empty machine is "all drift"; and two for the summary formatter.

docs.title: Interpreting results
docs.text:
• A change on a run you expected clean could be: a manual edit (true drift), a non-idempotent task (always changes; fix the playbook), a conflict between two roles (Level 3 · 08), or a time-dependent value. Run the idempotence test first (Lesson 02); an audit on a playbook that fails it is noise.
  • Group by task name across hosts. If the same task shows on 80% of hosts, it is probably the playbook, not 80 people editing files.
  • Distinguish expected variation (a per-host cache file) and exclude it from management, rather than filtering the report.
  • The diff is evidence. It shows what differs; it may contain secrets, so protect the report as you would the files (diff: false or no_log on sensitive tasks, and access control on stored reports).

docs.title: Blind spots of check mode (measured or known)
docs.text:
1. command and shell are skipped in check mode (Level 1 · 05), so they contribute no drift information. Replace with modules or add check_mode: false for read-only probes.
  2. Dependent tasks: a task that depends on a previous task's real effects may report misleadingly (a service start that would only succeed after a package install). Package/service modules usually handle this with care but not always.
  3. Things the playbook does not manage are invisible. An audit tells you whether managed resources match, not whether the machine has an unmanaged cron job or an extra user. Add find/stat based "unexpected item" checks (the purge pattern in check mode from Level 3 · 08) and security scanners.
  4. Failed hosts are not audited (the exit 2 case).
  5. Modules with imperfect check support may under-report. Test: for each module you rely on, change the thing by hand and confirm check mode notices.
  6. Time: the audit is a snapshot; drift can occur a minute later.
  7. Handlers in check mode are simulated; the report shows them as changes because they would run.

docs.title: Running audits
docs.text:
• Schedule nightly or weekly in CI or on a controller with read-only credentials where possible (check mode still needs the access to read state, and become for privileged files).
  • Store reports with timestamps; trend the count of drifted hosts and tasks.
  • Alert on exit 2 immediately (audit blind) and on exit 1 according to severity (changes to sshd_config and sudoers matter more than a log level).
  • Respond: re-converge (apply), or investigate the manual change. For compliance-sensitive settings, make an incident out of it.
  • Close the loop: for each drift cause found, decide a prevention (fewer people with shell access, a pipeline-only change policy).

A pipeline for the audit can reuse ci.sh's check-mode step as a gate (Lesson 02), but the audit's value is in the report and trend, not just the exit code.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Check mode is a flag (_ansible_check_mode) passed to each module in its arguments; modules that support it compute their result and skip the write, setting changed accordingly. The task executor passes each module result to the registered callbacks; v2_runner_on_ok fires for results that did not fail, with the full result dictionary including changed and (in diff mode) diff. The aggregate plugin accumulates findings in memory, so in one run on a big fleet the report grows with the number of changes and diff sizes. At v2_playbook_on_stats the stats object provides per-host summaries (ok, changed, failures, unreachable, skipped, rescued, ignored) used to compute failed_hosts. The wrapper is a normal subprocess run with environment variables enabling the plugin, which keeps the audit logic out of the playbook.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Auditing a non-idempotent playbook, producing permanent noise.
  • Treating exit 2 as drift (or ignoring it).
  • Auto-repairing on every audit without review.
  • Believing a clean audit means a clean machine.
  • Storing diffs with secrets in plain reports.
  • Not testing check-mode support of the modules you rely on.
  • Never alerting on unreachable hosts.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run driftaudit.py against a playbook of yours (use --limit for one host first) and categorise each finding: manual change, playbook bug, or expected.
  2. For three modules you use, change the managed state by hand and confirm check mode reports it.
  3. Extend the plugin to include the task's file and line (result._task.get_path()), and update the summary.
  4. Write the alert policy: which findings page someone, which open a ticket, which are logged.

docs.title: 07 · Automation Incidents and Blast Radius
docs.text:
Automation multiplies mistakes as well as effort. One wrong hosts: pattern or one bad variable can change every server in minutes. The goal of operating Ansible safely is to make the blast radius of any single run small, visible and deliberate, and to be ready when something goes wrong anyway.

What was run

The preflight.py guard (9 tests) was run against small inventories using the real ansible and ansible-inventory commands; the first end-to-end test failed because of a bug in the guard itself (below). The incident runbooks are general practice, not drawn from a real incident, and have not been exercised. See the CI/CD course (Level 4 · 07) for pipeline incident handling.

docs.title: How playbooks cause incidents
docs.text: Cause Example Control Wrong target hosts: all in a play meant for staging; a --limit forgotten Preflight, protected groups, inventory per environment Wrong variable -e version= empty; a default overridden by -e or set_fact (precedence, Level 2 · 02) Input validation (assert), no free-text -e in templates Non-idempotent task A "fix" that restarts a service on every run Idempotence test in CI (Lesson 02) Batch too large 200 hosts restarted at once serial, failure budget, tested abort semantics (Level 3 · 07) Conflicting owners Two roles flip a setting each run (Level 3 · 08) One owner per resource; audit Drift repair that overwrote an emergency fix Scheduled apply reverted a hot patch Drift audit before apply; change freeze flags Stale facts / cache Acting on cached facts about a rebuilt host Short fact cache expiry; gather before destructive tasks Secret exposure debug or -vvv log with a token no_log, linter, log access control (Lesson 03) Dependency drift A collection or ansible-core upgrade changes behaviour (this course found when: on a string became an error in 2.21.5) Pin versions; test upgrades; EEs Inventory error Dynamic source returns the wrong set or an empty set Inventory sanity checks, fail on empty Lack of rollback A destructive task with no way back Backups, state: absent as a deliberate step, rehearsed rollback Credentials too powerful The Ansible user can do anything everywhere Least privilege, per-environment keys

docs.title: A preflight guard: compute the blast radius first
docs.text:
preflight.py inventory pattern [--max-hosts N] [--protected groups] [--allow-protected] resolves the pattern to hosts using ansible --list-hosts, adds the group memberships from ansible-inventory --list, and refuses when:

  • the pattern matches no hosts (so a typo in CI does not become a green no-op);
  • the host count exceeds --max-hosts (default 5);
  • any target is in a protected group (default production) and --allow-protected was not given.

Example output:

targets: 1 host(s): w1
REFUSED: touches protected group(s): production (use --allow-protected)      exit 1

docs.title: The bug the tests found
docs.text:
My first version built group membership from each group's hosts list only. The end-to-end test used an inventory like:

[web]
w1
w2
[production:children]
web

w1 is in web, and web is a child of production, so w1 is in production, but production has no hosts list of its own. The guard allowed w1 to be touched without --allow-protected: a safety check that approved the very case it exists to stop. The test (expecting exit 1 and the word "protected") failed with exit 0. I rewrote groups_of to include all ancestor groups via the children relationship (cycle-safe), and added tests: ancestors included, multi-level nesting (leaf → mid → production), and cyclic definitions. After the fix, all 9 tests passed.

Lessons: (1) a guard rail needs a negative test for each way to hit the thing it protects, including indirect ones; (2) inventory group nesting is common (production:children), so any tool that reasons about groups must resolve it transitively; (3) the cheapest time to find such a bug is before the first production run.

Wire the guard in front of risky runs: a make deploy target, a CI job, or a controller template pre-step. Pair it with --check --diff (Lesson 06) for the content of the change.

docs.title: Making the blast radius small
docs.text:
1. Separate inventories per environment with no shared groups across them, and different credentials. The protected-group mechanism helps, but it is a second line of defence.
  2. Default to limits. A playbook run for production requires a --limit or a controller survey value; assert on ansible_limit is defined (Level 2 · 07).
  3. Batches and budgets (Level 3 · 07) with any_errors_fatal on irreversible steps.
  4. Canary first: a designated host or group gets every change first.
  5. Check mode before apply with the diff attached for review.
  6. Rate limit changes: throttle, serial, and a pause between batches for monitoring to react.
  7. Staged credentials: the credential used by a CI job for staging cannot reach production.
  8. Break-glass and change freezes: a switch (a file or flag the playbook checks via assert) that blocks scheduled applies during an incident or holiday freeze.
  9. Kill switch: an obvious, documented way to stop a running rollout (cancel the job; the playbook structure must leave hosts in a safe state, Level 3 · 07's always).

docs.title: Detection
docs.text:
• Monitor the effects (error rate, latency, capacity) during and after rollouts; a change window without monitoring is a blind change.
  • Alert on unusual automation activity: runs outside the schedule, runs against production by unusual users, a surge in changed counts (e.g., the drift report finds 80% of hosts drifted after a run: your own change did something unexpected).
  • Keep run logs with who ran what, with which parameters and revision (a controller does this; for CI it is the pipeline history).

docs.title: Response runbook for a bad run
docs.text:
1. Stop the run. Cancel the job; if it is a rolling update with a serial batch, the playbook should stop after the current batch (confirm).
  2. Freeze automation: disable schedules and other jobs that could compound the damage.
  3. Assess scope: which hosts changed? Use the run log and a --check --diff against desired state to see differences; the drift audit tool (Lesson 06) helps compare reality to the intended state.
  4. Decide: roll back (previous playbook revision, if the change is reversible and the rollback tested), roll forward (a fix), or repair manually on the most affected hosts.
  5. Execute in small batches with verification; use the same guard rails you used to roll out.
  6. Communicate: status, scope, next update time.
  7. Restore normal operations only when the cause is understood and a test or guard prevents recurrence.
  8. Review (blameless): why did the change pass review and CI? Which guard would have stopped it? Add it (a test, a lint rule, a preflight check) and record the action items with owners.

Everything in the CI/CD course's pipeline-incident runbooks (broken main, leaked secret, compromised build input) applies to the pipeline that runs Ansible; the Ansible-specific parts are the blast radius, the idempotence of repair and the verification of end state.

docs.title: Rehearse
docs.text: Run a game day: pick a harmless change, run a "bad" playbook against a staging fleet (one that deletes a managed file everywhere), and practise detection, stopping, assessing with the drift audit, and repairing with a targeted --limit run. The capstone test (Lesson 10) does exactly this on twelve simulated nodes: audit finds three drifted nodes, repair touches only those three, and untouched nodes' files keep their modification times.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: preflight.py asks Ansible itself which hosts a pattern selects (ansible PATTERN -i INV --list-hosts), instead of reimplementing pattern evaluation, so it honours !, &, ranges and group nesting exactly as a real run would. It reads group structure from the JSON that ansible-inventory --list prints: each group object may have hosts and children. Resolving ancestors is a graph walk over the children edges from each host's direct groups upward, with a visited set so cycles terminate. Asking the real tool for the pattern and using the data only for membership is the design choice that keeps the guard small and correct.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Guards that don't resolve nested groups.
  • Protected-group checks that can be turned off by default (--allow-protected in scripts).
  • No limit on production templates.
  • Rollback plans never rehearsed.
  • Automation credentials shared across environments.
  • Alerts that fire only on failure, not on unexpected success at scale.
  • No freeze mechanism for scheduled applies during incidents.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/l4/test_preflight.py; add a test for a pattern with an exclusion (web:!w2) and one for a range pattern.
  2. Create an inventory with two overlapping environment groups and show a host that belongs to both; make the guard refuse it unless both are allowed.
  3. Write a freeze.yml check (an assert against a file or variable) and show a scheduled run refusing to apply during a freeze.
  4. Plan a game day for your own estate: the injected fault, the signals, who acts, and the success criteria.

docs.title: 08 · Migrating Scripts and Avoiding Anti-Patterns
docs.text:
Most teams arrive at Ansible with a pile of shell scripts, wiki instructions and muscle memory. Migrating them well means translating intent into declarative tasks, not transliterating commands into shell: tasks. This lesson shows the difference with a measured example and then lists the anti-patterns that appear again and again.

What was run

A small provisioning script and its playbook equivalent were both run repeatedly on a Mac (sandbox directories under /tmp), ansible-core 2.21.5. The catalogue of anti-patterns draws on this course's measured findings and on general experience; items not measured here are marked as such.

docs.title: The script and its problems
docs.text:
#!/bin/bash
set -e
D=${1:?dir}
mkdir $D
mkdir $D/logs
echo "port=8080" >> $D/app.conf
useradd_sim() { echo "created user" >> $D/users.log; }
useradd_sim
chmod 600 $D/app.conf

Observed:

  • First run: works.
  • Second run: mkdir: /tmp/mig5: File exists, exit status 1 (because of set -e). The script is not rerunnable.
  • Starting from a different state (the directory exists but is empty): the same failure, even though nothing was wrong with the target state.
  • Without set -e, two runs left app.conf containing port=8080 twice (>> appends). The script "worked" and corrupted its own output.

This is the typical profile of a provisioning script: it is correct only from one starting state and only once. Fixing it with guards (mkdir -p, grep -q ... || echo) is possible and tedious, and each guard is a hand-written check of state.

docs.title: The playbook version
docs.text:
- hosts: localhost
  connection: local
  gather_facts: false
  tasks:
    - ansible.builtin.file: {path: "{{ d }}/logs", state: directory, mode: "0755"}
    - ansible.builtin.lineinfile: {path: "{{ d }}/app.conf", line: "port=8080", regexp: "^port=", create: true, mode: "0600"}
    - ansible.builtin.lineinfile: {path: "{{ d }}/users.log", line: "created user", create: true, mode: "0644"}

Measured:

fresh directory, run 1: ok=3 changed=3
run 2:                  ok=3 changed=0
run 3:                  ok=3 changed=0       app.conf: port=8080  (one line)
pre-existing empty dir: ok=3 changed=3      (works from a different starting state)

The playbook converges from either starting state, is safe to repeat, and shows in check mode what it would do. (The directory itself is created by file with state: directory creating parents as needed; the script had a separate mkdir $D.)

docs.title: How to migrate
