docs.text:
1. Inventory the scripts: what do they do, to which hosts, how often, who runs them? Delete dead ones.
  2. Write down the intent as end state: "directory exists with mode 0755", "setting port is 8080", "user exists in group X". If you can't state the end state, you do not yet understand the script.
  3. Map each step to a module (ansible-doc -l, collections). Use command/shell only where none exists, with creates/removes/changed_when (Level 3 · 04).
  4. Keep the data separate: ports, paths and names become variables; hosts differences become inventory variables.
  5. Run side by side: apply the playbook to a copy of a real machine or a staging machine and compare the resulting state with the script's (file lists, stat, package lists).
  6. Test idempotence (Lesson 02) and check mode.
  7. Switch over one environment at a time; keep the script for a rollback window; then delete it.
  8. Document the playbook's variables and the run command.

Resist rewriting and redesigning in one step. A faithful translation that passes tests first, improvements afterwards.

docs.title: Anti-pattern catalogue
docs.text:
Each item has a fix; those measured in this course have a lesson reference.

  1. shell: for everything. No idempotency, no check mode, injection risk. Use modules; if unavoidable, guard and quote (Level 3 · 04).
  2. Unguarded commands that report changed every run. changed_when, creates/removes (Level 1 · 05).
  3. ignore_errors: true as a default. Hides real failures. failed_when with a specific condition; rescue blocks (Level 2 · 04).
  4. Variables defined everywhere. Unpredictable precedence. One definition per variable; defaults in roles, data in inventory (Level 2 · 02).
  5. set_fact used for configuration. Outranks inventory. Use it for computed values only.
  6. God playbook / God role. One file that does everything, run with tags. Split by lifecycle and responsibility (Level 2 · 01, 07).
  7. Dictionaries expected to merge. combine(recursive=True) explicitly (Level 2 · 03).
  8. Deleting a task to remove a feature. Leaves orphans. Explicit state: absent first (Level 3 · 08).
  9. Two roles managing one resource. Never converges. Single owner; drop-in directories (Level 3 · 08).
  10. state: latest in production runs. Non-reproducible upgrades. Pin versions; upgrade deliberately.
  11. Handlers for things that must happen. A failure can skip them (Level 1 · 08). force_handlers, or explicit tasks with when.
  12. No input validation. assert / argument_specs at the top of roles (Level 2 · 01).
  13. Hard-coded shared paths. Hosts race (Level 2 · 01). Per-host paths.
  14. Secrets in plain text, debug, or -vvv logs. Vault, no_log, linter (Lesson 03).
  15. Unpinned dependencies. Pin ansible-core, collections, Python libs; use EEs (Lesson 01).
  16. Short module names. FQCNs; lint enforces (Level 2 · 09).
  17. Tags as dependencies. --tags configure skipping a prerequisite (Level 2 · 07). Independent tagged tasks, or always.
  18. hosts: all with no limit/guard. Preflight, limits, protected groups (Lesson 07).
  19. No tests. Lint, second-run test, drift check (Lessons 02, 06).
  20. Treating the playbook as documentation of what is deployed. It only says what would be enforced; drift and orphans make reality differ. Audit (Lesson 06).
  21. Giant Jinja one-liners. Compute in vars or write a tested filter (Level 3 · 02).
  22. Fact gathering everywhere. Off unless used; cache with expiry (Level 3 · 06).
  23. Running Ansible from laptops with personal keys against production. Controlled runners/controller, per-environment credentials, audit (Lessons 01, 03).
  24. Using Ansible to hold long-lived state. Keep state in the system of record; generate inventory (Lesson 05).

docs.title: When not to use Ansible
docs.text: Honest limits: very large fleets needing sub-minute convergence (SSH-based push is slow, pull helps); highly dynamic container orchestration (use Kubernetes controllers and GitOps); complex stateful infrastructure graphs (Terraform); real-time event-driven remediation (Ansible has event-driven features in some distributions, not run here); and where a vendor's native tool is the supported path. Ansible shines at configuring heterogeneous machines and orchestrating operational tasks across them.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: A shell script is an imperative program: it executes commands in order and its outcome depends on the starting state because each command has an implicit precondition (mkdir requires the directory not to exist). An Ansible task is a desired-state assertion implemented by a module that first reads the current state and acts only on the difference, so preconditions are checked rather than assumed. The migration shifts the burden from the author (writing guards) to the module author (writing the comparison once, tested, in a reusable form). That is why the playbook above has no if statements yet converges from two starting states: file and lineinfile contain them.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Transliterating commands into shell tasks.
  • Migrating without a side-by-side comparison.
  • Redesigning while migrating.
  • Keeping the script as a second source of truth.
  • No owner for the new playbook.
  • Converting everything at once instead of one environment or service at a time.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Pick a script you run today. Write the end-state list for it, then the playbook. Compare the script and playbook on three starting states.
  2. Take five items from the anti-pattern catalogue and find an example in your own repositories; write the fix.
  3. Write a lint rule or test that detects anti-pattern 8 (a removed task without an explicit absent step) in your repo's history, or explain why it cannot be detected statically.
  4. Decide which of your current automation tasks should not be in Ansible and say where they should live.

docs.title: 09 · Governance, Review and Standards
docs.text:
When ten people write playbooks, quality drifts unless the standards are written down and enforced by tools. Governance here means: agreed conventions, automated checks, a review process, and a way to evolve the standards without stopping work.

What was run

ansible-lint was run with a project configuration (.ansible-lint) on the deliberately bad playbook from Level 2 · 09. The observed results, including one I did not predict, are quoted below. Review and organisational practices are general experience and unmeasured. No policy engine beyond ansible-lint was run.

docs.title: Standards worth writing down
docs.text:
A short document (one page to start) covering:

  1. Layout: playbooks/, roles/, inventories/<env>/, collections/requirements.yml, requirements.txt, ci.sh.
  2. Naming: plays, tasks, handlers named in sentence case starting with a capital (lint enforces name[casing]), roles and variables prefixed (webapp_port).
  3. Modules: FQCNs always; command/shell only with justification, guards and changed_when.
  4. Variables: defaults in roles, environment data in inventory, one definition each; no secrets outside Vault or the secret manager.
  5. Safety: no_log on secret-handling tasks; assert for inputs; serial and any_errors_fatal for rolling changes; --check --diff before production.
  6. Testing: lint, syntax check and a second-run idempotence test for every role and playbook; a drift check for production-relevant roles.
  7. Versions: pinned ansible-core, collections and Python libraries; EE image for controller jobs.
  8. Documentation: a README per role with variables, examples, supported platforms.
  9. Release: roles used by many repos are tagged with semantic versions and a changelog (CI/CD course, Level 3 · 07).

Keep rules few and checkable. A rule nobody can check will be ignored; a rule with an automated check becomes habit.

docs.title: ansible-lint as the enforcer
docs.text:
ansible-lint has profiles of increasing strictness: min, basic, moderate, safety, shared and production. The tool prints the highest profile your content satisfies. A project config selects the target:

---
profile: basic
warn_list:            # reported but do not fail the build
  - name[casing]
  - package-latest
skip_list:            # not checked at all
  - no-free-form

I ran this on the bad playbook (13 violations without a config). Result:

Failed: 3 failure(s), 0 warning(s) in 1 files processed of 1 encountered.
Profile 'basic' was required, but 'min' profile passed.        exit status 2

Reading it: the rules in skip_list and warn_list removed some findings (down from 13), but three findings remained and the build still failed: the unnamed play (name[play]) and two unnamed tasks (name[missing]). I had expected my configuration to turn the run green and it did not; the rules I listed were only a subset of the problems. That is the useful behaviour for a ratchet: listing a rule is a visible decision, the remaining violations still block. The summary also shows 0 warning(s), so the entries in warn_list didn't produce counted warnings in this case; I did not investigate why (they may have been counted only when the corresponding rule matched a different category or file). Check your version's behaviour before relying on it.

Using the tool well:

  • Pin the version (a new release adds rules). Upgrade deliberately in a branch.
  • Ratchet: start with basic, record existing violations in warn_list with comments giving an owner and a date, and shrink the list; never grow it casually. Raise the profile when it is clean.
  • Don't blanket-skip. Each skip is a reviewed exception with a reason, like a security exception.
  • Inline exceptions with # noqa: rule-id on a line are possible and should be rare; review them like code.
  • Count and trend violations over time as a health metric.
  • Run in CI and locally (pre-commit hook) with the same config.

docs.title: Code review for Ansible
docs.text:
What a reviewer should look at:

  • Blast radius: does this change affect more hosts than intended? Check hosts: and group variables.
  • Idempotency: would a second run change anything? Did CI's second-run step pass?
  • Check-mode friendliness: new command/shell tasks need check_mode and changed_when thought.
  • Variable precedence: is a new variable defined in a surprising layer? Does it have a prefix?
  • Secrets: no_log, Vault use, nothing printed.
  • Rollback: if this is wrong in production, how do we undo it?
  • Orphans: when removing a task, is there an explicit removal for existing hosts?
  • Tests: new behaviour has a test (a negative case where input is validated).
  • Docs and changelog for shared roles.

A pull request template with these as a checklist raises the floor. For high-risk paths (inventories/production, privileged roles, sudoers/sshd templates), require CODEOWNERS approval from a platform or security team (CI/CD course, Level 4 · 05 on separation of duties).

docs.title: Change management
docs.text:
• Changes are pull requests, linked to a ticket when your process requires; production applies run from a controlled pipeline or controller with an audit trail, not from laptops.
  • Plan-like preview: attach the --check --diff output (Lesson 06) to the change; it is the Ansible analogue of a Terraform plan, with the caveats in that lesson.
  • Environments promote: the same revision goes to dev, staging, then production; the variable data differs (inventories), not the code.
  • Freeze windows and break-glass (Lesson 07): defined, rare, reviewed.
  • Emergency changes are made through the same pipeline with an expedited review, or logged and back-ported immediately.

docs.title: Ownership and lifecycle
docs.text: Every role and playbook has an owner (a team, not a person), a status (supported, deprecated), and a deprecation process: announce, give a migration path and date, remove. Shared roles are versioned; consumers pin; the owner publishes a changelog and tests supported platforms. Without owners, shared roles become communal junk drawers that nobody dares change.

docs.title: Measuring health
docs.text:
Useful metrics, all computable from what this course built:

  • Share of playbooks passing lint at the target profile.
  • Number of entries in warn_list and skip_list, and their age.
  • Idempotence-test pass rate; number of tasks that change on a clean second run.
  • Drift audit results: hosts drifted, tasks drifted, time to repair (Lesson 06).
  • Run outcomes: failures, rollbacks, mean time to repair (CI/CD course, Level 3 · 09 for the delivery metrics).
  • Share of roles with tests and READMEs.

Avoid ranking people by these; use them to find where to invest (the CI/CD course discusses how such metrics get gamed).

docs.title: Compliance as code with Ansible
docs.text: Ansible can also enforce and audit compliance baselines: a role applying CIS-like settings and a check-mode run proving compliance (Level 1's baseline project is a small example). Treat third-party hardening roles like any dependency: review, pin, test, and understand what they change, since a hardening role can lock you out of a machine (disabling password login before keys are in place).

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: ansible-lint loads each file with Ansible's parsers and produces a list of matches, each with a rule ID, tags, severity and a location. The configuration decides how each match is treated: rules in skip_list are not run, rules in warn_list are reported as warnings that do not affect the exit code, and the selected profile defines which rules are mandatory. The exit code is non-zero if any non-warning match remains (the observed exit status 2). Because the profile is cumulative (each profile includes the lower ones), a violation of a min rule such as a syntax error stops everything else, and Profile 'basic' was required, but 'min' profile passed simply reports the highest profile with no remaining violations.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Standards no tool checks.
  • Growing skip lists silently.
  • Unpinned lint versions.
  • Review focused on style rather than blast radius and idempotence.
  • No owner for shared roles.
  • Applying production changes from personal machines.
  • Treating a hardening role as trusted without reading it.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Add a .ansible-lint to a repository at basic, list current violations in warn_list with owner and date comments, and make CI fail on anything new. Check what exit code you get.
  2. Write a pull request template with the review checklist above, adapted to your estate.
  3. Define three metrics for your Ansible health and write the query or script that produces each from your repos and CI history.
  4. Draft the deprecation process for a shared role used in 15 repositories.

docs.title: 10 · Capstone — Managing a Simulated Fleet
docs.text:
The capstone operates a fleet end to end with the tools built across the course. The fleet is simulated: twelve inventory hosts (eight web, four db) that all use ansible_connection=local, each owning a directory tree under a temporary sandbox. The playbook is the lint-clean baseline from Level 1 (baseline_ci.yml). The test file src/l4/capstone/test_capstone.py walks through a realistic operating sequence with real ansible-playbook, ansible-lint and the audit and guard tools.

What was run, and what wasn't

All nine tests passed (about 42 seconds) with ansible-core 2.21.5 on a Mac. No remote hosts, SSH, privilege escalation, packages, services or networks were involved; the "servers" are directories and the managed state is files and modes. The sequence demonstrates the workflow and the tools; it does not prove anything about a real fleet. See the "What this does not show" section.

docs.title: The fleet
docs.text:
[web]  web01..web08   app_port 8001..8008
[db]   db01..db04     app_port 5401..5404
[servers:children]  web, db
[production:children] servers

The fleet inventory is generated (fleet.py) with each host's ansible_python_interpreter set to the Python running the tests. production contains everything via nested groups, which is exactly the shape that broke the first version of the preflight guard (Lesson 07).

docs.title: The sequence, as tests
docs.text:
The tests share one fleet (module-scoped sandbox) and run in order, because operations on a fleet are a story, not independent cases:

# Step Assertion 1 Secret hygiene nologlint finds nothing in the playbook 2 Lint ansible-lint passes (production profile) 3 First converge All 12 nodes changed=6, no failures 4 Idempotence Second run changed=0 on all 12 5 Drift injected and audited Three kinds of drift on three nodes; the audit reports exactly db02, web03, web07, exits 1, and repairs nothing 6 Preflight all is refused (exceeds --max-hosts 5); a single production node is refused without --allow-protected; a three-node list with --allow-protected passes 7 Targeted repair --limit web03,db02,web07: only those three hosts run and change; four untouched nodes' app.conf modification times are unchanged 8 Audit again Clean: exit 0, no drifted hosts 9 Per-node variables survived web03 still has port = 8003, db02 has port = 5402

The drift in step 5 was: overwritten application config on web03 (content drift), mode 777 on db02's data directory (permission drift), and a deleted motd on web07 (missing file). The audit identified exactly the three affected hosts out of twelve and did not touch the broken files (the test asserts the bad config text and the missing file are still as left).

docs.title: What the sequence demonstrates
docs.text:
1. Gates before action. Static checks and idempotence tests give confidence the playbook is safe to run (Lessons 02 and 03, Level 2 · 09).
  2. Observation before intervention. The audit tells you what is wrong without changing anything (Lesson 06), and it identifies hosts and tasks, not just a number.
  3. Constraining the blast radius. The preflight guard stops a fleet-wide run and requires an explicit statement of intent for production (Lesson 07).
  4. Surgical repair. --limit to the drifted hosts leaves everything else alone, shown by unchanged timestamps (Level 2 · 07).
  5. Verification. A second audit proves the repair worked.
  6. Variables survive repair. Per-host data (ports) is the same after repair as before.

This is the shape of routine fleet operations: detect, scope, repair narrowly, verify.

docs.title: What this does not show
docs.text:
State plainly, because a simulation is easy to over-read:

  • Real connections: SSH keys, host keys, latency, timeouts, become, reboots.
  • Real resources: packages and services, whose modules have different check-mode behaviour and failure modes; kernel settings; firewall and network changes.
  • Scale: twelve nodes with local processes say nothing about thousands of hosts, forks, or controller load (Level 3 · 06 measured forks on 20 local hosts only).
  • Concurrency with humans: people changing the machines while automation runs.
  • Rolling updates and failure budgets (Level 3 · 07 tests those separately, with the surprise about always).
  • Credentials and secrets beyond the executable-password-script test in Lesson 03.
  • Controllers, pull mode at scale, or Windows/network targets.

If you carry these ideas into production, rebuild the tests against disposable real targets (VMs or containers for file/package behaviour, a staging fleet for the rest).

docs.title: Everything built in this course
docs.text:
All code is under src/ in the repository, with tests that run the real Ansible (ansible-core 2.21.5) unless noted:

Level Artefacts Tests 1 Baseline playbook with 2 simulated servers; handlers/loops/templates experiments 8 (baseline/test_baseline.py) 2 webapp role (with lint passing); variable-precedence experiment; vault, tags, serial experiments 9 (l2/test_role.py) + 5 (l2/prec/test_precedence.py, covering the measured order and four pairwise rules) 3 kvfile and filehash modules; filter, lookup and inventory plugins; rolling-update playbook 25 + 23 + 11 4 Drift-report callback and audit tool; no_log linter; Terraform-output inventory; preflight guard; CI script; capstone 9 + 12 + 10 + 9 + 9

Counted with pytest --collect-only: 8 + 9 + 5 + 25 + 23 + 11 + 9 + 12 + 10 + 9 + 9 = 130 tests across the course's own code. Several suites start many Ansible processes, so the complete run takes a few minutes (the single biggest are the baseline, rolling-update, drift-audit and capstone suites).

docs.title: Where to go from here
docs.text:
1. Run it on real machines. Create two VMs or containers and port the baseline to real package, service and user tasks. Keep the second-run test.
  2. Put it in CI (Lesson 02), and read the CI/CD Mastery Path alongside.
  3. Learn your platform's collections (cloud, network, Windows) and read their modules' check-mode support.
  4. Try a controller (AWX) and an execution environment build with a real container runtime.
  5. Combine with Terraform (Lesson 05) and Kubernetes/GitOps where they fit.
  6. Read other people's roles critically, with the anti-pattern catalogue (Lesson 08) in hand.

docs.title: How It Actually Works
docs.text: Each capstone step uses an Ansible property you have now seen measured: modules compare state and report changed truthfully (so changed=0 means converged); check mode asks the same modules to report without writing (so the audit changes nothing); --limit evaluates a pattern on the controller and never contacts excluded hosts (so repair touches only the drifted three, visible in untouched modification times); and the callback API exposes per-task results to plugins (so the audit can name hosts and items). The preflight guard asks Ansible itself which hosts a pattern selects and combines that with the inventory's group graph. Nothing here relies on magic: it is the same primitives from Level 1 composed with small, tested programs around them.

docs.title: Common mistakes
docs.text:
• Reading a passing simulation as proof for production.
  • Skipping the audit before repair (so you can't tell what the repair changed).
  • Repairing the whole fleet when three hosts drifted.
  • No verification after repair.
  • Letting a guard rail become a flag everyone passes by default.
  • Letting the tests rot when the playbook changes.

docs.title: Exercise
docs.text:
1. Run pytest src/l4/capstone and read the fixture and each step. Add a thirteenth node and make the tests pass.
  2. Add a fourth kind of drift (an extra unmanaged file in etc/app) and extend the playbook plus the audit to detect it (use the purge pattern in check mode).
  3. Add a rolling-update step to the capstone using src/l3/rolling and assert that capacity (hosts in rotation) never drops below a threshold between batches.
  4. Write the operations runbook for this fleet: daily audit, how to read the report, when to repair, who approves production, and how to roll back.
